issues.body:
## Summary

ChatGPT Desktop is launched with **Run as administrator** and the UAC prompt is accepted. The main process includes the `--do-not-de-elevate` argument, but both ChatGPT/Codex and the Computer Use helper still run at Medium integrity. Computer Use can capture an elevated application's window, but mouse and keyboard input is silently ignored because the target runs at High integrity.

## Environment

- ChatGPT Desktop package: `OpenAI.Codex_26.908.4834.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`
- Windows: Pro, 25H2, build `26200.9445`, x64
- Agent environment: Windows native
- Codex configuration: `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`
- Target: a local Win32 desktop application that requires administrator privileges

## Steps to reproduce

1. Fully exit ChatGPT Desktop and verify that its background processes have stopped.
2. Start ChatGPT Desktop with **Run as administrator** and accept the UAC prompt.
3. Start or select a Win32 application running at High integrity.
4. Ask Computer Use to click a visible control in that application.
5. Observe the integrity levels of the relevant processes.

## Actual result

- The main `ChatGPT.exe` command line contains `--do-not-de-elevate`, but its integrity level is Medium.
- `codex.exe`, `codex-code-mode-host.exe`, and `codex-computer-use-swift.exe` run at Medium integrity.
- The target application runs at High integrity.
- Computer Use successfully captures and displays the target window.
- Click and keyboard calls report no error, but the target receives no input and its state does not change.
- The unified Computer Use interface can also return an empty native-app inventory, while the legacy Sky interface can still capture the elevated window.

## Expected result

When ChatGPT Desktop is explicitly launched as administrator and the UAC prompt is accepted, the Computer Use helper should be able to interact with an approved High-integrity target, or ChatGPT should clearly report that controlling elevated applications is unsupported. Input operations must not report apparent success when Windows has blocked them.

## Diagnostic evidence

```text
ChatGPT.exe (Medium, command line includes --do-not-de-elevate)
├─ codex.exe (Medium)
└─ codex-computer-use-swift.exe (Medium)

Target Win32 application (High)
```

The shell token used by the agent reports `S-1-16-8192` (Medium mandatory level), and the Administrators group is present only as `deny only`. Querying the target's token from the agent process returns Access Denied, consistent with the High-integrity boundary. Repeated Computer Use clicks and an `Alt` keypress leave the target unchanged.

## Security-preserving suggested behavior

Please either provide a supported brokered interaction path for explicitly approved elevated windows, launch the Computer Use input component with the documented inherited elevation while preserving per-app approval boundaries, or detect the UIPI mismatch and return an actionable error instead of reporting a successful input operation.

issues.title: Agent expands cleanup scope into proposal rewrites and consumes usage on repeated rework

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

issues.body:
## What issue are you seeing?

A Codex coding session repeatedly expanded a narrowly scoped cleanup into unrelated changes, then consumed substantial usage correcting its own work and overstated readiness to merge.

The requested work was to remove a superseded room/map implementation while preserving authored content and the existing component architecture, update directly relevant documentation, and address PR review comments. The user repeatedly objected to changes outside that boundary.

Observed behavior in the session:

- The cleanup extended into shared systems and content that the user wanted preserved. Subsequent corrections restored content and reverted unrelated system changes.
- The agent also edited eight future-design proposal documents. Changes included rewriting implementation audits, a foundation-stage row, migration text, compatibility wording and status notes. The user wanted proposal edits limited to individual sentences made false by removing the old implementation; future plans and alternatives were to remain intact.
- Review feedback was treated as authorization for broader proposal rewrites. Some supplied review text was itself later acknowledged to exceed the cleanup scope. The agent did not reliably reconcile those suggestions with the user's narrower instructions.
- The agent started separate full test, safety and GPU runs before the existing push gate, requiring the user to redirect it to use the push gate instead. Long repeated inspections, corrections and status messages compounded the cost.
- After replying to and resolving 27 review threads and obtaining passing local gates, the agent recommended merging. The proposal-scope problem was still present. Passing tests and resolving threads did not establish that the requested scope had been respected.
- When the user objected to the wasted usage, the agent initially stopped instead of completing the requested correction. The user had to explicitly demand that it make the work right. The proposal correction was not completed before the user reported closing the PR.

The user reported spending hours and exhausting a full five-hour usage window on this work. A tool operation also failed because automatic approval review encountered a usage-limit error. The exact account usage total and monetary cost were not independently available in the session.

## What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is an observed long-session instruction-following failure, not a deterministic compiler or client crash. A minimal independent reproduction has not been isolated.

The task sequence was:

1. Provide repository instructions and an explicit cleanup boundary: remove a superseded implementation; preserve content, shared interfaces and planned component support.
2. Ask the agent to fix the PR, keep documentation unambiguous, reply to review comments and resolve only addressed threads.
3. Supply corrections distinguishing necessary current-state documentation updates from changes to unapproved future proposals.
4. Continue the session through multiple repair and review rounds.
5. Inspect the complete diff after the agent reports that the PR is ready to merge.

In this incident, the diff still contained proposal rewrites outside the intended boundary, despite repeated corrections and positive readiness claims.

## What is the expected behavior?

- Preserve the user's exact scope and previously selected outcomes throughout a long session, including after context compaction.
- Treat review suggestions as findings to reconcile with the task, rather than automatic permission to broaden it.
- For a removal task, amend a proposal only where removing code makes a specific sentence false. Preserve its proposed designs, migration plans, alternatives, open questions and cited observations unless their alteration is explicitly authorized.
- Interpret a requirement for clear documentation as a writing constraint, not permission to redesign or rewrite every related document.
- Verify scope and preservation against the complete diff before recommending merge. Passing technical gates and resolving review threads cannot substitute for that check.
- Use the project's existing required validation pipeline without redundant expensive runs, particularly after the user explicitly requests that workflow.
- Respond to reported rework and usage costs with concrete, scoped corrective action and concise communication.

## Additional information

- Environment: Linux, Git worktrees, repository-level `AGENTS.md` instructions, GitHub PR review, and local pre-push gates.
- Model and reasoning setting, confirmed by the reporting user: **Sol 6.1 (`gpt-6.1-sol`), `xhigh` reasoning effort**. The exact client version was not provided.
- The project is private. Repository identifiers, PR links, source snippets, local paths, screenshots and the full conversation are intentionally omitted from this public report.
- The user explicitly requested that this behavior and its usage impact be reported to OpenAI through a GitHub issue. Please investigate the scope-preservation and readiness-reporting failure and the reported usage impact. This report does not establish a billing-calculation defect or a specific internal root cause.

issues.title: dot cannot read user-created Codex threads: “unsupported placement format version” / “unsupported placement region”

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

labels.name: dots
labels.description: Issues involving setting up ChatGPT dots or managing their ongoing work.

issues.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

Summary
I’m trying to use dot to access existing Codex threads that I created myself, rather than tasks originally created by dot. Reading these threads fails with backend errors, even though my Windows desktop is connected and dot can discover my local Codex projects.
This appears inconsistent with the recently announced ability to follow up on existing Codex threads:
Official announcement:
https://x.com/ChatGPT/status/2108636748217770180?s=20
Official release notes:
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/whats-new/dots-october-9-2026
Related documentation:
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots/tasks-and-memory
The announcement describes starting Codex work and following up on existing threads. In my tests, access works for a previously dot-created task, but fails for the user-created threads tested below.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Environment
- Test date: October 10, 2026; earlier attempts also failed before this date.
- Codex/ChatGPT desktop on Windows; requests to dot sent through ChatGPT web on Windows.
- Desktop reported connected, attached, and authorized for tasks.
- I updated the desktop app and requested another test. The same Architect-thread error persisted afterward.
- Reconnecting the computer did not resolve that error either.
- Exact desktop app/build version was not captured during these tests.
Steps to reproduce
1. Connect the Windows desktop to dot.
2. Copy a codex://threads/<thread_id> link from an existing user-created Codex session.
3. Ask dot to read that thread without sending messages or modifying it.
4. dot invokes cloud_threads.read with the supplied threadId and a small limit, such as 2 or 3.
5. The request fails before returning conversation content.
Tools used
- cloud_threads.read — full tool name: mcp__codex_apps__cloud_threads_read.
- cloud_threads.list_threads with children_only=false, limit=50; archived=true was checked separately.
- cloud_threads.list_environments.
- cloud_threads.list_projects with the connected computer’s environmentId.
Observed results
A. Existing project-associated Architect thread:
AppServerBackendRequestError: Client specified an invalid argument: post-cutover thread ID <THREAD_A> has unsupported placement format version 2
This was reproduced repeatedly, including after the desktop update and reconnection.
B. Another existing user-created thread:
AppServerBackendRequestError: Client specified an invalid argument: post-cutover thread ID <THREAD_B> has unsupported placement format version 3
C. An existing session not associated with a project:
AppServerBackendRequestError: thread not found: <THREAD_C>
D. A new session I created specifically for testing after the update:
AppServerBackendRequestError: Client specified an invalid argument: post-cutover thread ID <THREAD_D> has unsupported placement region 10
These read failures returned isError=true and error_code=UNKNOWN. No conversation content was returned.
Successful control checks
- cloud_threads.read successfully returned messages from a previously dot-created task on the same computer.
- cloud_threads.list_environments confirmed the desktop connection and task authorization.
- cloud_threads.list_projects successfully returned my registered local projects, including the relevant project’s ID and root path.
Additional findings and limits
- Account-level list_threads returned 30 IDs with no continuation cursor. The first two failing thread IDs were absent. The archived list was empty. This listing check occurred before the new test session was created.
- That listing exposed IDs, not thread titles or project associations. It therefore did not provide a usable list of chats belonging to my local project.
- Project discovery only confirms access to the sidebar project registry. Its registered root path is an old folder; active worktrees are elsewhere. We did not establish access to those worktrees through this check.
- The read-tool description mentions expanded access to existing threads, but no available status field confirmed whether that capability is enabled for my account.
- No messages were sent to the affected threads. No threads or worktrees were created by dot during this investigation, and no project files were changed.
Expected behavior
dot should be able to resolve and read an authorized existing local Codex thread on the connected computer, consistent with the announced feature. If a thread type, account rollout, or app version is unsupported, the error should explain the requirement or limitation clearly.
Impact
I cannot use dot to follow an existing Architect session and coordinate ongoing project work. I still have to manually copy messages and reports between Codex and dot.
Diagnostic interpretation — not a confirmed root cause
The placement-format and placement-region errors suggest a possible thread-ID compatibility or routing problem. We have not confirmed whether this involves local versus cloud thread storage, rollout state, permissions, or another backend issue. The errors do not establish that the threads were deleted, and “region 10” should not be assumed to represent my geographic location.
Please investigate why existing-thread reads fail while desktop/project discovery and a dot-created-thread read succeed, and confirm whether any account setting or client update is required.

issues.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

Files available through ChatGPT Library cannot reliably be transferred into Codex Cloud tasks started from a saved cloud environment. The parent assistant’s cloud workspace can download and inspect the same files, but consuming cloud tasks fail through the supported Library download/materialization flow.

Observed repeatedly on October 7, 2026 (UTC), including fresh cloud tasks.

Earlier attempts returned:

```text
library file transfer failed: download failed
```

The helper exited with code 1 and exposed no HTTP status. Two newer fresh-cloud attempts returned:

```text
library download request failed: hosted apps tools/list request failed: network
```

Earlier attempts resolved expected Library metadata before failing to obtain bytes. The latest error occurs during the hosted tools-list/download-request path. These may be different failure stages; a common root cause is unconfirmed.

Affected workflow: hosted ChatGPT/assistant-to-Codex Cloud Library transfer. Standalone Codex CLI reproduction is unconfirmed. Hosted runtime/helper build versions were not captured.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence in the affected account:

1. A parent assistant saves a ZIP artifact to Library.
2. The parent cloud workspace downloads and inspects that artifact successfully.
3. Start a fresh Codex Cloud task from a saved cloud environment.
4. Provide the authorized Library reference and request retrieval using the supported consumer-local Library download/materialization workflow.
5. The task fails to obtain bytes with one of the errors above.
6. Repeat in another fresh task from that saved environment: failure persists.

Comparison checks:

- Parent cloud successfully downloaded and inspected the same files.
- Creating a new Library copy did not fix consuming-task retrieval.
- Manually attaching a file directly to a task eventually allowed access in an observed case; this is not established as a universally reliable fix.
- The user also observed intermittent attachment-download failures in the web UI; whether related is unknown.

No explicit authorization or permission denial appeared in the failing output. This does not establish that authorization is uninvolved. A separate minimal synthetic-ZIP reproduction has not yet been established.

### What is the expected behavior?

An authorized Library file should be downloadable into the consuming cloud workspace through the supported flow. On failure, please expose an actionable error and a safe diagnostic correlation identifier for support.

### Additional information

This prevents parallel cloud tasks from inspecting source artifacts despite successful access in the parent cloud workspace.

Possibly related reports:
- #51038: same generic helper download error, connected Mac destination.
- #50679: Library upload failures and a download-side Linux cloud report with HTTP 502.
- #51576: Cloud Work attachment materialization failures with different observed behavior.

Shared root cause is unconfirmed. This report adds the comparison between successful parent-cloud access and failed retrieval in fresh saved-environment tasks.

Please route to the hosted Cloud/Library component owner and advise how to obtain safe diagnostic correlation information when the helper omits it.

Private file contents, filenames, Library IDs, task links, account details, repository names, credentials, signed URLs and full logs have been omitted.

> 无法加载工作空间设置
> 请重试以继续聊天

English: "Couldn't load workspace settings. Please retry to continue chatting."

It is **not yet established** whether the missing Chat entry/switcher and workspace settings failure share a root cause.

- Platform: Windows desktop application (Chinese UI).
- Reported: October 20, 2026.
- App version/build: not yet collected.
- Network/proxy and diagnostic logs: not collected for this specific case.
- Account identifiers: intentionally omitted.

## Observed behavior
1. The user reports that ordinary **Chat** mode is not available in their Windows desktop app.
2. In the **Codex** view, the left sidebar and existing local projects/conversations remain visible (e.g., a local project can be selected).
3. A selected project conversation shows the workspace settings error above and a **重试** (Retry) button.
4. The project and local-computer context is visible above the message composer.
5. The screenshot does not show the dropdown opened or the ChatGPT view, so the exact state of the Chat / Work selector is not verified. No claim is made that the workspace error causes the missing mode.

## Steps to reproduce (based on the observed screen)
1. Open the Windows desktop app, in Chinese.
2. Navigate to Codex and select an existing local project/conversation.
3. Observe the workspace settings error near the composer.
4. Try using the normal Chat mode (the user reports it is not available).

## Expected behavior
- A user with access to ordinary Chat should have a clear, working way to enter it on Windows.
- Workspace settings should load successfully, or offer actionable error details and recovery rather than blocking or disrupting chats.

- #48700 — Windows desktop Chat / Work toggle missing.
- #54601 — Chat vs Work switcher missing.
- #52437 — Windows "无法加载工作空间设置".
- #55513 — October 20 Windows settings error, with diagnostics **from a different reporter**.

## Request
Please investigate the Chat mode entry/switcher availability and the workspace-settings load failure on Windows. Could the app surface actionable diagnostics and recover from transient settings errors without obstructing the Chat experience?

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1007.21159

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro 20x

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

## Description

Codex Desktop consistently reports the following error across all available models on my personal ChatGPT Pro account:

`Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.`

However, another personal ChatGPT account works normally on the **same Mac, network, and Codex Desktop installation**.

The affected account has its full usage allowance available and Codex Web works normally.

The issue persisted for several days, temporarily resolved for approximately one day, and then returned.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Codex Desktop and sign in with the affected Pro account.
2. Start a new conversation and submit a simple prompt, such as `Reply with OK`.
3. Observe the capacity error across all available models.
4. Switch to another personal ChatGPT account in the same desktop application.
5. Submit the same prompt.
6. The second account works normally.

## Expected Behavior

Codex Desktop should process requests normally when the account has available usage allowance.

## Actual Behavior

All models fail on the affected account while another account works on the same machine.

Neither account belongs to a managed Business, Enterprise, or Edu workspace.

## Relevant Logs

Previous logs showed:

```text
WebSocket was closed before the connection was established
closeCode=1006
SSH: codex path probe timed out after 60000ms
app_server_connection.connection_failed_before_ready
app_server_connection.reconnect_failed
```

Repeated connection failures were observed, although their relationship to the capacity error has not been confirmed.

## Feedback Upload Issue

I attempted to submit in-app feedback including diagnostic logs.

Feedback ID:

`01a12321-cbc7-7e12-8fd5-320a3534087a`

However, Codex Desktop displayed:

> Feedback upload not confirmed. We couldn't confirm whether your feedback was received. It may have been delivered, and resubmitting could create a duplicate.

Therefore, the feedback upload status remains unknown.

## Additional Information

- Codex Desktop version: 26.1007.21159
- Subscription: ChatGPT Pro
- Usage: Full allowance available
- Both accounts: Personal accounts
- Codex Web: Working on the affected account
- Failure pattern: Recovered for approximately one day, then recurred
- Switching models: Does not resolve the issue

Please investigate whether this is related to account-specific model access, backend request admission, routing, authentication state, or execution-environment problems.

Thank you.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Codex Desktop version `26.1007.21159` on macOS.
2. Sign in with my affected personal ChatGPT Pro account.
3. Start a new conversation.
4. Select any available model.
5. Enter a simple prompt:

   `Reply with OK`

6. Submit the request.
7. Codex Desktop returns:

   `Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.`

8. Repeat with other available models and new conversations. The same error occurs.
9. Sign out and switch to a different personal ChatGPT account on the exact same Mac, network, and Codex Desktop installation.
10. Submit the same prompt. The second account works normally.
11. Switch back to the affected account. The capacity error occurs again.

### Reproducibility

- The issue has occurred repeatedly over several days.
- It temporarily resolved for approximately one day before recurring.
- All available models are affected on the original account.
- The affected account works normally in Codex Web.
- Neither account belongs to a managed Business, Enterprise, or Edu workspace.

### Session / Feedback Information

- Feedback ID: `01a12321-cbc7-7e12-8fd5-320a3534087a`
- Feedback upload status: Unconfirmed by Codex Desktop.
- Usage allowance: Fully available; no usage limit reached.
- Token limit usage: Not available.
- Context window usage: Not available. The error also occurs in newly created conversations with a minimal prompt.

No special code or repository setup is required to reproduce this issue. A simple text prompt is sufficient.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex Desktop should successfully process prompts and generate responses using the available models when the account has sufficient usage allowance.

Both personal ChatGPT accounts should be able to use Codex Desktop normally under the same device and network conditions.

For example, submitting `Reply with OK` in a new conversation should return a response rather than a model capacity error.

The affected account should behave consistently with its working Codex Web access and the other functioning account.

### Additional information

### Environment

- Codex Desktop version: `26.1007.21159`
- Operating system: macOS
- Subscription: ChatGPT Pro
- Workspace: Personal account (no managed workspace)
- Usage allowance: Fully available
- Codex Web: Working normally
- Another personal account on the same Mac: Working normally

### Relevant Diagnostic Logs

Previous Codex Desktop logs showed:

```text
WebSocket was closed before the connection was established
closeCode=1006
SSH: codex path probe timed out after 60000ms
app_server_connection.connection_failed_before_ready
app_server_connection.reconnect_failed
```

These logs indicate repeated connection failures. However, I cannot confirm whether they directly caused the model capacity error.

I attempted to submit in-app feedback including logs.

`01a12321-cbc7-7e12-8fd5-320a3534087a`

Codex Desktop displayed:

> Feedback upload not confirmed. We couldn't confirm whether your feedback was received. It may have been delivered, and resubmitting could create a duplicate.

The diagnostic upload therefore remains unconfirmed.

### Important Observations

- The problem follows the affected account rather than the computer.
- Switching to another personal account immediately allows Codex Desktop to work normally.
- The affected account has full usage allowance.
- The affected account can use Codex Web normally.
- The problem recovered for approximately one day, then returned.
- The issue affects every available model, not just one model.

### Investigation Request

Could the engineering team investigate possible account-specific model access restrictions, request admission or routing problems, desktop authentication issues, or account-associated execution environment failures?

The controlled comparison between two personal accounts suggests that a general device-wide network or installation issue is less likely.

Thank you.

issues.title: [macOS][app-server 0.162.0-alpha.2] Footprint grows from 8.1G to 20G shortly after launch, with 24.4G peak and severe swap activity

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
<!-- report-key: codex-memory-20261009-010251Z-cb4e4994 -->

### What version are you using?

- Desktop bundle version: `26.1002.52244`, read from the installed application's `Info.plist` (not the About dialog).
- Affected executable: the bundled `CodexCLI.app/Contents/MacOS/codex` under `ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex-cli/`.
- That exact executable reports `codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.2`.
- Executable SHA-256: `cb4e4994627e770800a940b42969c77855a3fc09a6e60b02aa6319f670d6b6ab`.
- The affected process has the `app-server` argument; it is not an MCP child or the renderer.

### What subscription do you have?

Not independently collected for this report. Account identifiers and credentials are intentionally omitted.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 27.0, build `26A428`, ARM64. Physical RAM: `25,769,803,776` bytes (24 GiB).

### What issue are you seeing?

The desktop application's bundled app-server showed rapid, very large memory growth shortly after launch, with substantial compression and system-wide swap activity. This was measured on the running process, not inferred solely from large transcript files or virtual address space.

Measurements on 2026-10-09, Asia/Taipei (UTC+08:00), all for the same app-server PID:

| Local time | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| 08:48:37 | Process launch time reported by `vmmap`. |
| 09:02:51 | `top`: app-server `MEM=8222M`, `CMPRS=7038M`; its uptime was about 14 minutes. |
| 09:02:52 | `vmmap -summary`: physical footprint `8.1G`; physical-footprint peak `24.4G`. |
| 09:04:20 | `top`: the same app-server `MEM=20G`, `CMPRS=20G`, at about 16 minutes of uptime. |

The earlier `vmmap` sample reported about `1.5G` resident versus `8.1G` physical footprint, with `6.9G` swapped writable regions. A resident-only process listing substantially understated the charged footprint. These are the tools' displayed units; physical footprint must not be interpreted as all bytes simultaneously resident in RAM.

Selected sanitized `vmmap` output:

```text
Physical footprint:         8.1G
Physical footprint (peak):  24.4G

REGION TYPE                 VIRTUAL  RESIDENT  SWAPPED
Malloc Large                   3.4G    183.2M     3.0G
Malloc Small                   6.7G    409.2M     3.3G
mapped file                   35.2M      128K       0K

DefaultMallocZone allocation count: 4,111,406
DefaultMallocZone bytes allocated:  6.4G
```

System-wide measurements during the same diagnostic window:

- Swap used rose from `16965.81M` to `23795.25M`; the latter sample had `24576.00M` allocated swap.
- `kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level` changed from `2` to `4`.
- At 09:04:20, `top` reported `23G used`, including `14G compressor`, with `186M unused`.
- A separate approximately 35.1-second `vm_stat` counter comparison (16,384-byte pages) observed 109,092 additional swap-in pages and 421,868 additional swap-out pages: approximately 1,704.6 MiB and 6,591.7 MiB of page-equivalent activity.
- Those counter deltas are system-wide, not per-process attribution or measured physical disk throughput. Other applications were running.

The app-server was the largest process by `top`'s memory metric. At the last sample it was `20G`, versus approximately `1765M` for the largest Codex renderer. This report concerns the backend, not just renderer overhead or an aggregate of helper processes.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is an observed production sequence, **not yet a deterministic minimal reproduction**:

1. Run the desktop application with existing long-lived conversations and tool history.
2. Continue normal task activity after the app-server has launched.
3. Observe app-server footprint, compression, and system swap using the read-only commands below.
4. In this occurrence the backend already had a recorded `24.4G` footprint peak roughly 14 minutes after launch, and the sampled footprint subsequently rose from about `8.1G` to `20G` within about 90 seconds.

```sh
sysctl hw.memsize vm.swapusage kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level
top -l 1 -o mem -n 10 -stats pid,command,mem,cmprs
vmmap -summary <app-server-pid>
vm_stat
```

Do not intentionally replay multi-gigabyte histories on a memory-constrained production machine merely to reproduce this report.

### What is the expected behavior?

The desktop backend should bound peak and retained memory while loading/processing long histories and should not drive the host into severe memory pressure shortly after launch. If a historical thread is too large for a given operation, an explicit bounded failure would be preferable to uncontrolled allocation affecting unrelated active work.

Please investigate which operation owns the large allocations, including whether history readers, background extraction, concurrent requests, or retained state are involved. A model token/context limit alone should not be assumed to bound host-side history parsing memory.

### Additional information

Relevant context, **not a proven cause**:

- This installation has very large historical rollouts. Three ordinary files found under the default sessions directory were approximately 2.25 GB, 710 MB, and 259 MB.
- More importantly, a read-only open-file query of this app-server found three distinct historical rollout paths on an external SSD with sizes `12,052,351,985`, `7,261,386,912`, and `1,507,111,398` bytes. One path appeared on multiple file descriptors; that does not prove multiple in-memory copies.
- Historical rollouts have been relocated outside the default sessions directory. This is not a clean-profile reproduction. MCP/custom tooling and other applications are also present.
- File sizes and open handles do **not** prove entire files were loaded, nor establish the triggering operation. No heap stack attribution, background-memory-job correlation, or source-level root cause has been established for this occurrence.
- No process was killed or restarted, no conversation was archived, and no session database or rollout was modified as part of these diagnostics. The recorded peak predates the `vmmap` inspection. We did not deliberately open the large conversations to force a reproduction.
- No new crash was observed in this measurement window. Prior high-memory incidents were reported by the user, but are not used as primary evidence here.

Potentially related, but not confirmed duplicates/root causes:

- #51233: background extraction of image-heavy rollouts, reported on another version/platform.
- #40175: screenshot/history growth and compressed app-server memory.
- #36431: macOS app-server memory growth in the VS Code integration.

This report adds measurements for the desktop-bundled `0.162.0-alpha.2` backend shortly after launch. Please consolidate with an existing issue if the underlying path is confirmed to be the same.

Privacy: no conversation IDs, transcript contents, repository names, private local paths, account data, environment dumps, or credentials are attached.

issues.title: Windows desktop app: app-server starts a new set of stdio MCP servers for every thread it loads and never stops them

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
**Environment:** Codex desktop app on Windows 11 Pro (10.0.26300); `codex.exe … app-server` runs as a child of ChatGPT.exe; codex-cli 0.162.1. `~/.codex/config.toml` has 9 stdio MCP servers (5 shell-script servers started through a Git-for-Windows bash launcher, plus node_repl, codebase-memory-mcp, a java-based proxy, and npx packages).

**What happens:** the app-server starts a full MCP server set each time a thread is loaded (new, resumed, apparently re-hydrated). None is ever stopped when the thread goes idle, the user switches threads, or the window closes; they live as long as the app-server (days).

On one machine, one app-server (born 10-12 21:33 local) had child MCP sets 2.5 days later born at 10-12 21:35, 10-13 05:10, 07:08, 08:54 (2 sets), 20:43, 10-14 02:16, 08:27, 14:56. Each set: node_repl.exe, node.exe, codebase-memory-mcp.exe, java.exe, cmd.exe→npx, and (before a manual kill) 5 bash servers × 3 processes each (launcher, MSYS exec stub, server) = 15 bash processes per thread. The app-server held 135 bash processes and was the real parent of every one (born before each child; not PID reuse). In a second burst, 120 bash MCP processes (8 sets) appeared in one minute with no new rollout file — this looks like thread re-hydration (unconfirmed).

**Reproduction:**
1. Configure any stdio MCP server (a shell script that logs its PID and loops on `read` suffices).
2. Open the desktop app and open N threads in turn.
3. `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | ? ParentProcessId -eq <app-server pid>` shows N sets.
4. Close/leave the threads and wait — all N sets stay until the app-server exits.

**Evidence the servers are not at fault** (they exit on stdin EOF): each server loop is `while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do …; done`. Four experiments with the exact launcher command line:
1. .NET parent closes stdin after an initialize round-trip → launcher + server exit within 6 s.
2. .NET parent force-killed → whole tree gone within 8 s.
3. `claude.exe -p` parent (another MCP client), normal exit → 0 server processes after 15 s.
4. `claude.exe -p` force-killed with 19 server processes running → 0 left after 15 s.

The servers stay alive only because the app-server keeps their stdin open.

**Impact:** every thread loaded during an app-server lifetime adds ~10–15 processes that accumulate over days. On Windows (costly process creation) this pushes 100–230 idle bash/node processes onto the box and slows anything that spawns processes under a deadline (git hooks, MCP calls).

**Ask:**
- (a) per-thread teardown — close a thread's MCP clients (and so the servers' stdin) when the thread is unloaded, idles past a timeout, or its window closes; or
- (b) one shared set per app-server, multiplexing threads, as the CLI does per session.

A documented lifetime either way; a knob such as `mcp_servers.<name>.idle_timeout_secs` would also help.

issues.body:
### Codex App version
Windows installed package: OpenAI.Codex 26.915.4065.0 (verified on 2026-09-22).

### Summary
Local browser-driven validation previously worked through a loopback HTTP development URL. After moving the prototype into its project directory, the preview entry changed to a file URL and Browser Use rejected it. The rejection also prohibits alternate access methods, leaving no clear supported recovery workflow even though the browser documentation describes local development servers.

Related reports: #45230 and #46729. This report adds a verified historical successful interaction sequence and a shipped-file comparison, rather than claiming a new regression or requesting removal of safety checks. Please consolidate if appropriate.

### Observed evidence
- On 2026-09-19, historical native task records show successful IAB accessibility reads, screenshots, and clicks through a loopback HTTP URL. Observed interactions included pause, a resource-changing control, and reset. This was actual agent interaction, not only manual user preview.
- After project migration, the entry became file:///.../index.html (private directory redacted). Browser Use rejected the file URL. A later attempt to select the existing file-backed tab was also blocked.
- The user can manually preview the project, but that does not establish agent access.
- Exact errors include: "Browser Use rejected this action due to browser security policy. Reason: The browser URL policy blocks this action." and "Blocked browser navigation by Browser Use URL policy: file:///.../index.html".
- The accompanying rejection explicitly prohibits workarounds and alternate browser surfaces. We did not bypass it or switch the denied content to another endpoint.

### Read-only diagnostic findings
The inspected browser-service.mjs contains a URL check accepting about:blank and URLs whose parsed protocol is http: or https:, rejecting file: before page interaction.
The runtime default service file and the corresponding file in the installed Windows application bundle have identical SHA-256:
FA354758746C6D4569A3D63474246BA64DCFB9A3F2572927218AFA281CB281C3
The separately configured cached browser-service copy has the same protocol predicate. This comparison supports that the inspected restriction exists in the shipped file; it does not establish every historical process's effective configuration or prove the entire installation is unmodified.

We have not established that any previous version supported direct file URL automation. Historical HTTP success is not evidence of historical file URL success. We have not established an update regression or a shared cause with earlier network/proxy initialization failures.

### Reproduction sequence from observed records
1. Open a local HTML prototype through a loopback development URL: agent interaction succeeded in the historical run.
2. Later open the migrated prototype using a direct file URL.
3. Ask Browser Use to inspect/interact with that page: URL-policy refusal.
4. Manual preview remains possible, while automated visual validation is blocked.
A standalone minimal reproducer has not been executed after the refusal; the sequence above describes recorded observations, not a fresh experiment.

### Expected behavior / clarification requested
1. Is direct file URL automation intentionally unsupported in this Windows version? If so, please document manual preview versus agent-control support separately.
2. Please expose an actionable diagnostic distinguishing unsupported schemes from user-denied origins and managed policy restrictions.
3. What is the supported way to resume normal local-development browser validation after this explicit refusal? In particular, how can a user obtain an approved development-server workflow without asking the agent to circumvent the earlier refusal?
4. If this is a defect, please identify a fixed version or supported recovery action. We are not requesting a global policy relaxation or a patch that removes safety checks.

### Documentation and impact
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/browser describes local development-server interaction and manual file-backed previews.
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference documents HTTP/HTTPS origin policies; it does not provide a file-scheme approval path.
The practical impact is an incomplete automated visual/interaction acceptance loop, with users otherwise pushed toward manual screenshots and testing. Local code checks are not a substitute for that acceptance.

Only this sanitized summary is published. No project source, private directory paths, raw transcripts, credentials, screenshots, or session identifiers are attached. No browser policy or installed application files were modified for this report.

GPT-6.1 Sol has repeatedly spent excessive time on straightforward coding-agent instructions, while also expanding narrowly scoped requests into unrequested work. This report describes two observed symptoms; they may have different underlying causes.

### Observed behavior
1. **Trivial Git cleanup took approximately 11 minutes.** The instruction was to discard changes and delete a branch. This is a bounded repository-maintenance task, yet the agent's end-to-end completion took about 11 minutes.
2. **Unauthorized scope expansion.** For a separate task, the instruction was to preserve an existing calculation/display structure and numerical invariants. The agent inferred that an API field must also appear in the UI, classified its absence as a bug, asserted that UI changes were needed for 79 records, and produced a frontend change request. The user had not requested this UI behavior. After correction, the agent acknowledged that the requirement was unsupported and retracted the change request.

The second example is intentionally anonymized to avoid disclosing business details.

### Expected behavior
- Execute narrowly scoped Git cleanup promptly, with only necessary safety checks.
- Treat user-specified invariants and scope as binding; do not promote inferred improvements to requirements.
- When a potentially relevant but unrequested change is discovered, report it separately instead of implementing it or issuing follow-on requests.
- Stop reasoning once sufficient information is available to perform the requested operation.

### Actual impact
- Large latency even for routine actions.
- Increased review and correction burden.
- Risk of downstream implementation work based on requirements that were never approved.

### Reproduction / diagnostics
The symptoms have recurred in recent use, but a deterministic reproduction and per-tool timing breakdown are not yet available. Consequently, the 11-minute measurement is **end-to-end elapsed time**, not a confirmed 11 minutes of reasoning-only activity. issues.title: [Windows][26.825.5331.0] Headless startup caused by Application Protected node_repl.exe relocation failure (0x80071770)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Microsoft Store / MSIX package:

- `OpenAI.Codex 26.825.5331.0`
- The same headless-startup behavior was also reproduced on `26.825.4187.0` before updating.
- Standalone CLI available at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\OpenAI\Codex\bin\codex.exe` (`codex-cli 0.150.1`).

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex/ChatGPT Desktop starts several background processes but never creates a visible window.

Observed process state:

- main `ChatGPT.exe`: running, high CPU, `MainWindowHandle=0`
- crashpad: present
- GPU process: present
- network service: present
- storage service: present
- `ChatGPT.exe --type=renderer`: **missing**
- `codex.exe app-server`: **missing**

The desktop log stops after only:

```text
Launching app ... enableSparkle=false enableUpdater=false ...
Appshot hotkey inactive configured=true enabled=false platform=win32
```

Resetting/reinstalling the app, using a standalone CLI via `CODEX_CLI_PATH`, disabling the updater, and resetting the Electron profile did not fix the issue.

### Root cause found

The per-user CUA runtime was stuck in a staging directory such as:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\.staging-426e88130fe66c7e-...\
```

Inside that staging directory, `bin\node.exe` existed and ran successfully:

```text
v24.19.0
```

but `bin\node_repl.exe` was missing.

The packaged source file exists at:

```text
C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\OpenAI.Codex_26.825.5331.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0\app\resources\cua_node\bin\node_repl.exe
```

`cipher /c` reports:

```text
E node_repl.exe
  Compatibility Level:
    Application Protected
```

A normal PowerShell copy fails reproducibly:

```powershell
Copy-Item $src $dst -Force
```

with:

```text
The specified file could not be encrypted.
HRESULT: 0x80071770
```

So the CUA runtime relocation never finishes, leaving the app in a headless startup state before the Codex app-server and renderer are created.

### Confirmed workaround

Only the missing `node_repl.exe` was copied into the existing staging directory using Windows `xcopy /G` (allow decrypted destination):

```powershell
cmd /c "xcopy \"$src\" \"$dst\" /Y /G"
```

Result:

```text
1 File(s) copied
```

After that single-file copy, launching the app immediately succeeded.

The expected processes then appeared:

```text
codex.exe ... app-server
ChatGPT.exe --type=renderer
```

and the desktop window opened normally. Closing and reopening the app also worked.

### Why this looks actionable

This is not only a generic bundled-CLI relocation failure. In this case:

1. `CODEX_CLI_PATH` already pointed to a working standalone CLI.
2. The app still stayed headless because `cua_node` relocation was incomplete.
3. The failure was isolated to an `Application Protected` packaged runtime file (`node_repl.exe`).
4. A decrypted-destination copy of that one file was sufficient to unblock runtime finalization and the entire desktop startup chain.

### Expected behavior

When relocating MSIX/Application Protected runtime resources from `WindowsApps` into `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, the desktop app should use a Windows-compatible copy path that allows a decrypted destination (for example behavior equivalent to `COPY_FILE_ALLOW_DECRYPTED_DESTINATION`) or fall back to buffered read/write.

It should also surface the underlying relocation failure instead of silently remaining headless with only `Launching app` / `Appshot hotkey inactive` in the log.

### Related issues

- #40843 — bundled executable relocation fails with `ERROR_ENCRYPTION_FAILED (0x80071770)`
- #38696 — WSL relocation variant of the same protected-file problem
- #25220 — bundled plugin copy failures from EFS/Application Protected WindowsApps files

This report is specifically about the `cua_node` runtime and `node_repl.exe` causing full desktop headless startup on `26.825.5331.0`.

issues.title: [macOS 26.1007.71326] 8.74 GiB main/renderer state plus agent-launched MLX transcription exhaust swap and reset WindowServer

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex Desktop `26.1007.71326` (build `20398`), bundled Codex `0.162.0-alpha.17.2`, Codex Framework `155.0.8059.40`.

### What subscription do you have?

Paid ChatGPT subscription; exact tier omitted from this public report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.4.1 (25E253), Apple silicon Mac16,1, 16 GiB unified memory.

### What issue are you seeing?

A second system-wide memory incident occurred on October 16. Unlike my earlier #44996, this time a macOS watchdog stackshot preserved per-process memory at the time of failure. **The dominant Codex allocations were the desktop main process and renderer, not MCP helpers. A separate Python ML workload launched by Codex added another 5 GiB immediately before swap exhaustion. WindowServer then timed out and the desktop session was rebuilt, interrupting other applications.**

This report distinguishes three issues that need different investigation: large retained desktop state, the agent's resource-unaware choice of workload, and the OS-wide failure after swap could no longer grow. I am not claiming that all three have one implementation-level cause.

#### 1. Captured process footprints

The system stackshot covers `2026-10-16 04:50:23.588–04:50:29.491 +0800` (`2026-10-15 20:50:23.588–20:50:29.491 UTC`). Its `Footprint` fields report:

- ChatGPT/Codex desktop main process: **3270.41 MiB** (3.19 GiB), suspended.
- Largest, frontmost Codex renderer: **4551.54 MiB** (4.45 GiB).
- All 11 Codex renderers: **5679.47 MiB** (5.55 GiB).
- Main process plus all renderers: **8949.88 MiB** (8.74 GiB).
- Main bundled Codex app-server: **406.56 MiB**.
- 26 processes identified as Node/Node REPL with executable paths inside the installed ChatGPT bundle: **754.01 MiB** combined.
- All 47 processes with executable paths inside that bundle: **10876.86 MiB** (10.62 GiB) combined.
- Separate Python 3.12 inference process: **5094.32 MiB** (4.97 GiB).
- WindowServer itself: **1376.72 MiB**.

These are sums of Apple's per-process footprint fields, not an RSS snapshot or a claim that every summed byte is unique physical RAM. The Python value is separate from the 10.62 GiB bundle-path total. Process attribution is based on executable paths, not just display names.

The main process had been alive for 118274 seconds (32.85 hours). The large renderer had been alive for 118265 seconds. No current-incident renderer minidump/heap snapshot survived; the available stackshot shows the renderer repeatedly entering kernel/APFS/page-fault-related paths, while the main process had already been suspended by memory management. That establishes severe memory pressure, not the identity of a retaining JS object.

#### 2. The 5 GiB Python process was launched by the subtitle task

The task was to download a video and create reviewed bilingual subtitles using the existing YouTube automatic captions. Codex additionally chose to run local MLX Whisper over the entire audio as a cross-check.

The session transcript records this launch at `04:44:43.614 +0800`:

```text
work/asr-venv/bin/python work/check_audio.py > work/audio-check.log 2>&1
```

The original script at that point—not its later revised contents—called:

```python
mlx_whisper.transcribe(
    str(audio),
    path_or_hf_repo='mlx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo',
    language='en',
    word_timestamps=True,
    verbose=False,
    initial_prompt='<interview context>',
)
```

Audio duration was 2374.381 seconds (39m34s); the original compressed audio was about 35 MiB. This was one full-audio inference worker, not an 80-process concurrency storm.

Attribution is supported by independent evidence:

- The stackshot identifies Python PID 68414, footprint 5094.32 MiB, with age 341 seconds. That places its start around `04:44:42.6`, within about a second of the recorded tool launch. The age field is rounded.
- System unified logs show PID 68414 contacting `cfprefsd` at `04:44:43.832` and `trustd` at `04:44:46.424`.
- The Python executable UUID in the stackshot is `4C4C449F-5555-3144-A18E-6A1A7C588299`; `dwarfdump --uuid` on that task's virtualenv interpreter resolves to the identical UUID. The virtualenv points to the uv-managed Python 3.12 executable.
- The recorded tool result returned shell session 35607 for this command. Later polling after the desktop session reset reported `Unknown process id 35607`.

This is a high-confidence correlation; the stackshot does not preserve the complete original PPID/argv chain, so I am not representing the UUID alone as unique to one task.

The package source explains why this was not a 35 MiB workload: `ModelHolder` keeps the model resident; the downloaded weights are about 1.5 GiB; the audio loader decodes the complete source, then computes the whole log-Mel spectrogram before windowed inference. A 16 kHz float32 waveform for the full source is about 145 MiB, and STFT/features/decoder intermediates add allocations. `word_timestamps=True` invokes another forward pass with cross-attention, stacking/normalizing alignment weights and converting them to NumPy for filtering/alignment. Those paths explain the allocation categories, but the available evidence cannot assign each part of the observed 5094.32 MiB to a particular tensor or allocator cache, or prove an MLX leak.

The model download took 2m34s according to the preserved tool output, so recognition started approximately `04:47:18`. Eleven seconds later, the kernel reported failure to create swap. The task polled transcription progress and model-download size but did not measure its own RSS, system memory pressure, or available disk space. It chose full-file large-model inference even though captions already existed and the immediate purpose was verification of names/phrases.

After the incident, the task changed its script at `04:53:33` to 300-second chunks, `word_timestamps=False`, and checkpoints. The new run completed at about `04:56`. That is a successful functional fallback, not a measured before/after memory benchmark. It must not be confused with what ran during the crash.

#### 3. Main/renderer retention and event fan-out

Seven retained desktop main-log segments cover this application lifetime from October 14 to the freeze. A bounded offline scan found:

- **9840 distinct completed reasoning item IDs, delivered 19989 times** across renderer views. 9003 items appeared twice, 573 three times, 264 once.
- **9593 deliveries** explicitly carried `rendererWindowVisible=false`. The latest recorded visibility state for ten non-primary webcontents was hidden; eleven renderer processes were present in the stackshot. Hidden does not establish that a window was closed or its renderer orphaned.
- **6156 `ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications` errors**, first at October 14 `11:59:29.162Z`, last at October 15 `20:47:00.201Z`—before the local model began inference. These are a UI-path symptom, not proof of memory retention by ResizeObserver itself.
- **3206 failed `durable` host reconnection attempts** during the same lifetime. The final retry at `04:47:24` again failed before WebSocket establishment. Request counters near the end showed no pending client/internal requests; the retry count alone therefore does not establish a pending-request memory leak.
- **400 distinct thread/server startup pairs across 92 thread IDs** over the lifetime. These are historical startup records, not 400 simultaneously live processes.
- **16 successful `inactive_thread_unsubscribed` events**. Cleanup does run in some cases; this is not evidence that every unsubscribe or archive leaks.
- Only **185 `thread/turns/list`** and **385 `thread/items/list`** responses over the retained lifetime. This does not show the rapid post-crash history-refetch storm described in #34890.

Two long-lived tasks streaming around the incident had pre-incident rollout sizes of 287045934 and 168225124 bytes. The first included about 210.57 MB of persisted compaction records; the second included about 62.22 MB of tool-output records and a single 8.51 MB tool-output record. The new subtitle task had only about 2.69 MB of persisted history before the freeze.

These file sizes are context, **not proof that the entire JSONL/compaction corpus was loaded into the live UI**. They do show why task-count limits do not bound the size of individual retained conversations and why the newly started subtitle task alone is unlikely to explain the desktop UI footprint.

#### 4. Read-only inspection of the shipped desktop code

I inspected the installed `app.asar` by reading individual archive members without changing the application:

- `.vite/build/src-DCNiwad_.js` contains the conversation-manager/inactivity logic. The inactivity constants are `Zb=108e5` (3 hours) and `$b=10` retained inactive owner conversations. `getInactiveOwnerConversationIdsToUnsubscribe` excludes active views, owned stream followers, and conversations for which `shouldKeepConversationLoaded` is true.
- `shouldKeepConversationLoaded` protects active/in-progress runtimes and pending interaction items. `releaseInactivePassiveConversation` also skips conversations with a stream role, active view, pending requests, or keep-loaded status.
- A successful unsubscribe clears turn data only under additional eligibility conditions. Full `conversationCacheEvictor` removal is called by archive/delete/discard paths. The inspected inactivity policy is based on age/count/state, not a byte budget.
- The same manager/history code is present in `webview/assets/app-shared-8340f229c2b3.js`. It processes `item/completed` and updates the conversation's turn/item state; live logs independently confirm delivery to multiple renderer views, including hidden ones.
- The IPC `sendBroadcast` path serializes the message using `JSON.stringify` and obtains its byte length before rejecting frames over 268435456 bytes. This is the same allocation-risk ordering reported in #52631, but **there are zero oversized-broadcast warnings in this incident's retained logs**. I cannot claim that path caused the observed main-process allocation.

The supported interpretation is retained/replicated large conversation state plus long-lived windows as a likely contributing path. **There is no surviving heap profile or retained-object graph proving what exact objects account for 3.19 GiB main-process and 4.45 GiB primary-renderer memory.** A heap/native allocation capture from an instrumented build is needed to close that gap. Claiming an exact object-level root cause from the stackshot would overstate the evidence.

#### 5. Kernel-confirmed failure timeline

All times below are October 16, UTC+08:00:

```text
04:44:43.614  Agent launches full-audio MLX Whisper worker.
~04:47:18     Model download finishes; full-audio recognition begins.
04:47:28.325  Last retained desktop main-log line.
04:47:29.562  kernel: low swap: failed to create swapfile
04:47:30.246  kernel: memorystatus: suspending ChatGPT [41084] due to swap exhaustion
04:47:35.288  kernel: suspending WeChat due to swap exhaustion
04:47:40.311  kernel: suspending MailMaster due to swap exhaustion
04:47:45.388  kernel: suspending Google Chrome due to swap exhaustion
04:47:50.388  kernel: suspending D-Chat due to swap exhaustion
...          More unrelated apps are suspended; compressor-space-shortage repeats.
04:50:23.588  System stackshot begins.
04:50:46.902  watchdogd saves WindowServer userspace_watchdog_timeout report.
~04:51       New loginwindow/desktop session and application processes start.
```

The watchdog report says WindowServer's main work processor had not checked in for 40 seconds. This was a desktop-session reset, not a full reboot: kernel boot time remained October 13. During diagnosis after the session reset, the data volume reported 99% used and about 8.2 GiB available. That is a material environmental contributor to swap-growth failure; its exact free-space value before the incident was not captured, so I am not claiming disk fullness alone caused it.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deliberate replay to system failure was attempted.

Observed workflow:

1. Keep the macOS desktop app running for about 33 hours while working in several long-lived, tool-heavy local conversations and secondary windows.
2. Continue three visible user tasks; other views remain hidden. The desktop continues to deliver completed-item events to multiple views.
3. Ask for reviewed bilingual subtitles using an available YouTube caption track.
4. Codex additionally installs MLX Whisper and launches full-file `whisper-large-v3-turbo` inference with word timestamps on a 39-minute source without measuring current machine headroom.
5. With large pre-existing desktop state and limited free disk, model loading/recognition is followed by swapfile creation failure, mass application suspension, and a WindowServer watchdog timeout.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Main-process and renderer memory should remain bounded during long-running, multi-window work, including active large conversations and replicated/follower state.
- Desktop reclamation should account for retained bytes, not only inactive-task count and age. Hidden/follower views should not unnecessarily retain full histories or redundant state.
- An agent should choose a resource-appropriate verification method: use the existing captions and targeted ambiguous excerpts rather than unconditionally running a large model over the entire source. Local ML workload selection should account for current memory and disk pressure.
- Please provide a supported way to capture main/renderer heap and native-memory attribution before the next failure, and investigate which state/IPC allocation path retains the observed memory.

### Additional information

Related issues reviewed:

- #44996 is my earlier macOS swap-exhaustion incident. This new report has a different dominant memory breakdown and a separately identified agent-launched ML workload. It should not be treated as proof that archive cleanup failed.
- #34890 covers multi-task renderer memory, fan-out and crash/reload behavior; this incident has a system stackshot but no renderer minidump/refetch storm.
- #52631 has confirmed main-process V8 heap OOM and oversized IPC payload warnings. This incident has large main-process footprint but no matching warning or confirmed V8 OOM trap.
- #53277 covers a Windows renderer memory spike and denied hydration; there are no matching denied-hydration errors here.
- #37653 covers agent-generated MLX workload concurrency failures. Here one full-file worker was sufficient to add about 5 GiB; the trigger was not broken parallel-job counting.

Public evidence is sanitized. Raw stackshots/logs/session files contain other applications, prompts, proprietary project material, local paths and authentication-related metadata and are not uploaded. The preserved watchdog report is the `2026-10-16-045046` WindowServer `userspace_watchdog_timeout.spin` report. Targeted sanitized excerpts or an instrumented capture can be supplied if maintainers identify the fields needed.

issues.body:
## Summary
macOS desktop Computer Use intermittently loses the Apple Simulator window after successful accessibility and screenshot reads. A subsequent operation returns:
```
Computer Use server error -10005: noWindowsAvailable
```
This prevents completion of native UI acceptance testing. Please provide a supported recovery, diagnostic procedure, or fixed build; repeated rebinding has not provided a lasting solution.

## Environment
Read from the installed desktop application metadata during this investigation:
- Desktop bundle identifier: com.openai.codex (installed as ChatGPT.app)
- Desktop app version: 26.1013.40934, build 20770
- macOS 15.7.3, arm64
- Xcode 26.3.0; Apple Simulator, iPhone 17 Pro / iOS 26.3.1 test runtime
- Supported cua_repl interface, target bundle com.apple.iphonesimulator
These are investigation-time values; no desktop-version change at the exact failure timestamp has been established.

## Observed sequence
This is an intermittent field reproduction, not yet a clean-machine reproducer:
1. Bind the existing Apple Simulator application using cua.getApp("com.apple.iphonesimulator").
2. Read a fresh accessibility tree and screenshot. Both successfully show the running test app and two visible choices.
3. Run a helper consisting of fresh getAXState -> select an exact visible button -> App.click -> fresh getAXState, followed by getAXStateAndScreenshot.
4. The call fails after 18.7937 seconds with -10005 noWindowsAvailable.
5. Because the helper contains multiple operations, the failing sub-operation and whether the click reached the app are unknown. No success or business failure is inferred.

The last recorded instance occurred at 2026-10-23 05:17:54 UTC+08:00. The app process remained the same throughout that continuation. Successful native file-picker imports and other UI interactions preceded this failure.

## Bounded recovery already attempted
- Earlier rebinding, a visible Raise action, Escape, and two restarts of only the isolated test app process did not produce lasting stability.
- A later read-only fresh bind from another authorized task successfully captured the Simulator and its system file picker.
- One subsequent bounded continuation closed the picker and completed a series of real UI checks without restarting the app, then hit the error again above.
- After recurrence, retries and restarts stopped. The test checkpoint is preserved.
- No simulator reset, application uninstall, macOS reboot, privacy-permission weakening, helper-process termination, or private IPC workaround was performed for this report.
- A supported XCTest/XCUITest alternative is being evaluated for project continuity. That would not establish that the Computer Use problem is fixed.

## Diagnostic limits
A narrow search of the available desktop app logs for the incident day did not find the exact -10005/noWindowsAvailable error. Other tool-discovery log entries were present but are not treated as a root cause. We cannot distinguish stale window binding, capture failure, input dispatch failure, or Simulator responsiveness from current evidence.

## Requested help
1. Identify the supported diagnostic/log source and how to determine which operation loses the window.
2. Advise a recovery or build that preserves the existing Simulator and app checkpoint.
3. Clarify whether native Simulator/modal file-picker windows have known limitations in app-bound Computer Use.
4. If additional diagnostics are needed, specify the smallest redacted artifact set.

Related symptom reports: #43119, #55335, #56310. These involve other applications or OS versions; this report does not assume an identical cause.

## Privacy
No source code, project names, local user paths, app save data, account identifiers, session IDs, screenshots, raw logs, or full transcripts are attached. Any further diagnostic upload will be reviewed separately.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

issues.body:
# Responses websocket: mid-turn requests intermittently lose the thread's prompt cache (cached_tokens drops to the shared prefix)

## Summary

Within a single turn, on a reused Responses websocket, 0.25% of follow-up requests come back
with `cached_input_tokens` at the model's shared prefix (or 0) instead of the previous request's
input. The previous response completed a few seconds earlier and the next request is incremental.
Misses cluster in time across independent threads. The cause looks like server-side routing or
eviction, which a client setting cannot fix.

## Environment

- codex-cli 0.154.0 through 0.156.1, Linux. Sessions run in a long-lived `codex app-server` daemon;
  TUIs attach with `--remote`.
- Models: gpt-6-sol, gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-luna, gpt-5.6 family. Default websocket transport, no
  transport or timeout overrides.

## Measurements (30 days, 984 rollouts, 100,475 mid-turn requests)

A request counts as cold when `cached_input_tokens < 0.5 × input_tokens` and input > 20k. Mid-turn
means no `task_complete` or `turn_aborted` since the previous request, and a gap under 300 s.

- 252 cold requests (0.25%), 14.3M uncached input tokens.
- The gap does not matter: <10 s 0.24%, 10–30 s 0.30%, 30–120 s 0.19%, 120–300 s 0/392.
- 187/252 fall back exactly to the model's shared prefix, the value the session's first request
  gets (e.g. 12800 on gpt-6-astra, 7808 on gpt-6-sol). 37 fall below it or to 0. The local prefix
  (tools, instructions) is unchanged: a changed prefix would break the cache inside the shared part.
- Young chains are worse: 4.8% at the 2nd request of a session, 2.6% at the 2nd after a compaction,
  down to 0.10% after 20 requests. This dropped around 2026-09-11 with no client change: CLI 0.153.4
  had 31/1455 cold before 2026-09-10 and 0/76 after.
- Misses cluster across independent threads. Among established chains, 56 cold-cold pairs from
  distinct threads fell within ±120 s, against 7.4 expected at the base rate (×7.6). Example:
  2026-09-18 10:14 UTC, two unrelated sessions (different models, same app-server process) went cold
  58 s apart with no reconnect logged.
- In the window covered by `logs_2.sqlite` (6,869 requests, 23 cold), 5 of the 21 requests sent right
  after a server-initiated websocket close and reconnect were cold (23.8%), all partial (26k–52k
  cached). The logged close reasons were "Connection closed normally", "Connection reset without
  closing handshake", "connection limit reached (60 minutes)" and "idle timeout". The other 17 cold
  requests had no reconnect logged (0.25%).

## Example response pairs (previous warm → next cold, same turn)

| UTC | CLI | Model | Previous response (input/cached) | Cold response (input/cached) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-18T10:15:35 | 0.155.0 | gpt-6-astra | `resp_0c41afac3f202152016aad0f2f278887d2928712e0455ce3f2` (124608/119552) | `resp_0c41afac3f202152016aad0f43068087d291a1a2666d7d5f89` (127452/7808) |
| 2026-09-22T22:07:14 | 0.155.1 | gpt-6-astra | `resp_0d458bc92ce39885016ab2fbec656c87d2ae9ab837ba61361b` (44270/41344) | `resp_0d458bc92ce39885016ab2fc07219c87d2b4649dfd48be6e98` (47242/12800) |
| 2026-09-23T14:32:45 | 0.156.1 | gpt-6-sol | `resp_0d75f95810c6f550016ab3e3042c1c87d28d7e9ad10f132033` (166269/163200) | `resp_0d75f95810c6f550016ab3e307963887d2a1e710c1def8496f` (167812/0) |
| 2026-09-23T16:21:01 | 0.156.1 | gpt-6-astra | `resp_0efcfe2e2d592fb1016ab3fbe885ec87d083c49bc8080b2cb7` (82455/80512) | `resp_0efcfe2e2d592fb1016ab3fc25543487d09e27255d3629002f` (87084/32640), after a reconnect |

## Questions and requests

1. Is KV affinity for `previous_response_id` continuations on the same websocket expected to hold
   within a turn? The cross-thread clustering suggests engine-level eviction or rebalancing.
2. After a server-initiated close in the middle of a turn, the reconnect handshake carries
   `x-codex-turn-state`, yet 24% of the next requests are partially cold. Is the turn-state token
   meant to restore affinity?
3. Observability, client side:
   - The TRACE lines "incremental request failed" (`codex_core::client`) are stored in
     `logs_2.sqlite` with a NULL `thread_id` column: the thread id is only in the span body. They
     fall under the 1000-rows-per-process cap and are pruned within about an hour in a long-lived
     app-server, so one cannot tell a failed incremental request from a routing miss after the fact.
     Could they carry the thread id?
   - In `CODEX_ROLLOUT_TRACE_ROOT` bundles, `upstream_request_id` is null for websocket inferences.
     A server-side request id would let users report a miss precisely.
4. The latest alpha (0.158.0-alpha.8) repairs the websocket at shutdown and at turn start (#47701,
   #47709, #47745) and adds Retry-After handling (#47641). We found nothing about mid-turn
   continuation or routing. Is this tracked?
