issues.title: [macOS desktop] Moved project chat retains stale cwd; hidden legacy local registration survives app-server deletion

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS, desktop project membership, working-directory state, legacy project registrations, and the visible sidebar disagreed during a Work/Codex continuation and subsequent project move.

The user started local work from a conversation already in a ChatGPT project. A local project registration with the same display name and a cloud backing link existed alongside the cloud project. After the user moved the local workflow chat to another project, membership changed, but the chat's working directory and multiple saved workspace references still pointed at the original folder.

Later, the sidebar showed **Projects → No projects**, while `list_projects` continued to return the old local registration. Repair required the bundled app-server API plus reconciliation of the legacy desktop settings and a full app restart.

**The initial creation/continuation trigger was not independently reproduced.** This report documents the state inconsistencies and verified recovery, not a confirmed root cause. A linked local registration may be intentional; the problem is the inconsistent identity/path state and lack of a usable visible cleanup path.

## Environment

- ChatGPT/Codex macOS desktop: **26.1016.62342**, bundle build **21477**
- Bundle identifier: `com.openai.codex`
- Bundled CLI: **0.163.0-alpha.11.2**
- macOS **27.0.1**, build **26A434**, Apple Silicon
- Observed and repaired October 22, 2026
- Sidebar grouping: project

## Observed sequence

1. The user launched local workflow work from a chat in an existing cloud project. Local work accumulated in a folder associated with that project's local backing registration.
2. `list_projects` returned separate `local` and `chatgpt` entries with the same display name. The local record had a `chatGptBacking` link to the cloud project.
3. `move_thread_to_project` returned success for a move to the cloud project. Subsequent `list_threads` still reported the original local project ID. This did not establish that the move had persisted.
4. The user moved the workflow chat through the UI to a different existing project. `list_threads` then reflected the destination's local project ID, but the chat's `cwd` remained the original folder.
5. The destination local project's roots included both its own folder and the old folder. Saved `thread-workspace-state-v1:<thread>` contained an old applied cwd/root and a different pending workspace.
6. A later screenshot in the Codex surface showed **Projects → No projects**. Nevertheless, `list_projects` and legacy saved state still contained the unwanted old local registration.
7. An attempt to isolate the old local registration in a custom sidebar section via `move_project_to_sidebar_section` returned the requested local ID, but readback placed its linked cloud project in the section instead. This was immediately reversed; no project was deleted through that tool.

The user-visible names and placement did not provide a reliable way to identify which entry could be safely removed.

## Impact

- Moving the chat did not by itself verify or change its working directory.
- Tool success acknowledgements could disagree with readback.
- A local registration could remain in records without appearing as a removable sidebar entry.
- Installed local tools depended on files in the old workspace, so removing the folder before relocating those dependencies could break the workflow.
- A missing old folder remained referenced by the chat, risking failures on subsequent file operations.
- The user had to reconcile project membership, folder location, and multiple internal state representations manually.

## Expected behavior

- Make the relationship between a cloud project and its local backing registration explicit.
- Make local folder context and the effective working directory inspectable.
- When moving a chat, explicitly preserve or offer to change folder context, and reconcile applied/pending workspace state consistently.
- Make successful mutations observable in readback, or clearly signal asynchronous completion.
- Provide a safe way to remove a local registration even when the sidebar does not display it, preserving cloud projects, conversations, and original files.
- Avoid targeting a linked cloud project when an action was addressed to a distinct local registration, or document that aliasing explicitly.

## Recovery performed and verified

All local files were preserved before registry changes; backups of the affected settings, thread rollout and SQLite state were retained.

1. Copied the entire 85-file workspace to a permanent folder and verified every file hash. Retained the original workspace as a backup.
2. Updated the dependent local MCP application's launcher path. Restarted its connection and verified tool discovery, model-file checks, a local API connection, a reference crop, and a real image upscale.
3. Used the **installed bundled app-server schema**, not guessed RPC parameters:
   - `project/update`: replace the stale folder in the destination local project's roots;
   - `thread/resume` with explicit `cwd` and `runtimeWorkspaceRoots`: update the affected workflow chat without starting a generation;
   - `thread/read`: verify the new cwd;
   - `project/delete`: remove only the old local database project registration.
4. The live desktop tools still reported the old legacy registration after the app-server database removal. Backed up and narrowly reconciled `local-projects`, the legacy-to-app-server ID mapping, old default selection, and affected saved workspace entries in `.codex-global-state.json`.
5. Reapplied the legacy reconciliation after normal desktop shutdown to guard against cached state being written back, then restarted the app.

**Post-restart verification:**
- The old local registration was absent from `list_projects`, the SQLite `projects` table, and legacy saved settings.
- The cloud project remained present and pinned; its original cloud conversation retained its project membership.
- The moved workflow chat retained its new project membership and permanent cwd.
- Applied workspace roots and destination project roots referenced the permanent folder; no pending stale workspace remained.
- All 85 preserved files still matched their hashes.

This is an account of a recovery, **not a recommendation that users edit app databases/settings manually**.

## Related reports

- #53486 — sidebar/project membership disagreement and successful move not reflected in readback.
- #49699 — missing local-project removal control after project UI changes.

No private conversation contents, screenshots, account identifiers, project/thread identifiers, original project names, personal paths, or raw logs are included.

- Password reset on 2026-10-23.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

- Unified ChatGPT/Codex desktop app: **26.1016.51333**, build **21161**, production channel.
- Windows MSIX package: **OpenAI.Codex 26.1016.6573.0**.
- Previous installed release: **26.1013.40934** (MSIX **26.1013.4894.0**).
- The issue began immediately after the update on **October 20, 2026 (PDT)**. It remains unresolved after reinstalling.

### What subscription do you have?

The desktop usage diagnostics report `planType: prolite`. This account already had a working Dot before the update.

### What platform is your computer?

**Windows 11 Pro, x64**, OS version **10.0.26300**, build **26300**.

### What issue are you seeing?

The entire **Dots / Your dot** entry disappeared from the desktop sidebar after the update. It is missing in both the **ChatGPT** and **Codex** views.

A Dot conversation window appeared once during troubleshooting, but after I closed it, there was still no persistent entry to reopen it. The default **Ctrl + .** shortcut also does not open the Dot.

I have now **reinstalled the desktop app**, and the entry is still missing.

Meanwhile, on the same account in Chrome, **https://chatgpt.com/dots/home opens my existing Dot and displays its conversation history and message input**. The web sidebar also shows **Your dot**. This is an existing Dot that remains accessible on the web; the desktop app has lost its visible access path.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence on my existing installation/account; I do not have a deterministic fresh-account reproducer:

1. Use an existing Dot in the Windows desktop app.
2. Update from the previous installed release to **26.1016.51333**.
3. Reopen the app and find that the entire Dots sidebar entry is absent.
4. Check both the ChatGPT and Codex views: neither shows the entry.
5. Reinstall the desktop app: the entry is still absent.
6. Try **Ctrl + .** in the desktop app: it does not open the Dot.
7. Open **https://chatgpt.com/dots/home** in Chrome: the original Dot and its history load.

### What is the expected behavior?

A Dot I was already using should remain reachable from the desktop app after an update.

If a capability or configuration request fails, please show an actionable error and a supported recovery option instead of silently removing the entire entry point.

### Additional information

Desktop logs after the reinstall, around **2026-10-21 06:53 UTC**, record successful Dot room and history fetches:
- `roomKind=dot`, `stage=client.room_fetch`, `outcome=success`
- `roomKind=dot`, `stage=client.history_fetch`, `outcome=success`
- The corresponding network responses have HTTP status **200**.

These observations do **not** establish the root cause or prove that all desktop capability checks succeeded. I am not claiming that the Dot was deleted or that access was intentionally revoked.

Related: **#55783** reports a similar missing desktop entry on **macOS with the same app version**. This report adds the Windows environment, unsuccessful reinstall, and non-working shortcut.

I understand that bugs happen, and I appreciate the work going into the app. But losing an entire feature entry immediately after an update, spending time troubleshooting and reinstalling, and ending up in exactly the same state is extremely frustrating. I should not have to guess whether a feature I was already using has been removed.

The web page gives me temporary access, but I need the desktop entry restored. Please investigate this regression and provide a concrete recovery path that preserves existing conversations, local tasks, and computer connections. Reinstalling has already been tried and has not resolved it.

prs.title: [codex-login] Serialize managed ChatGPT token refreshes
prs.body:
## Stack

- Base: #23546

## Summary

- serialize managed ChatGPT refresh-token redemption across Codex processes sharing the same `CODEX_HOME`
- make waiters reuse credentials another process already refreshed and persisted
- apply the same serialization to proactive near-expiry refresh and reactive managed refresh recovery

## Why

Managed ChatGPT refresh tokens rotate when used. The base PR expands the existing pre-request refresh predicate to include a five-minute near-expiry window. Without serialization, multiple Codex processes can observe the same token in that window, redeem the same refresh token concurrently, and cause an avoidable reuse failure.

The pre-existing semaphore protects callers within one `AuthManager` only; this PR adds a file lock for managed refreshes across processes and rechecks stored auth after waiting on that lock.

## Validation

- `bazel test //codex-rs/login:login-all-test`
- `just fix -p codex-login`
- `just fmt` runs Rust formatting successfully, then its Python SDK Ruff step cannot install `openai-codex-cli-bin==0.131.0a4` on this Linux environment because no compatible wheel is published.

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: kind/customer-issue
labels.description: Issues that were reported by customers

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

In certain cases, the main agent spends many turns, iterations, making incremental changes in hopes of solving a small issue. For example, if a typecheck or linter comes back with numerous failures. The main agent may spend many turns/tokens to help get the build into a healthy state. 

This is one such subtask (also including fixing a broken build) that could be delegated to a subagent such as the generalist to outsource the fix and return to the main agent with a working build. 

Considerations/Objectives:
- Investigate getting the model to use the generalist in subtasks such as this
- evaluate if calling is consistent and provides enough feedback back to the main agent to prevent any hallucinations of state (does the generalist let the main agent know what changes it had to make / if the fix couldn't be fixed without further changes)
- Does the main agent provide enough context for the generalist to successfully accomplish its tasks? Or could this require a way for the main agent to share more context?
- Add behavior evals to see if the behavior is followed consistently.

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: /compress command is not persistent across session resume

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/small
labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `/compress` command, which summarizes chat history to save tokens, is not persistent across session exits and resumes. When a user runs `/compress`, the in-memory chat history is correctly replaced by a summary, but this change is not written back to the session file on disk. Consequently, when the session is resumed later (using `--resume` or `/resume`), the CLI loads the original, uncompressed history from the session file, effectively losing the compression.

**Repro Steps:**
1. Start a chat with `gemini`.
2. Build up some history with several messages.
3. Run `/compress` and wait for completion.
4. Exit the CLI.
5. Resume the session with `gemini --resume latest`.
6. Observe that the history has reverted to its uncompressed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Running `/compress` should persist the compressed history (the summary) to the session file on disk so that subsequent resumes of the same session correctly load the compressed state.

### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

OS: darwin (macOS)
Version: Current (detected in local development)

</details>

### Login information

N/A (General bug in persistence logic)

### Anything else we need to know?

Investigation shows that in `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, the `tryCompressChat` method correctly replaces the `this.chat` object with a new `GeminiChat` initialized with the compressed history:
```typescript
this.chat = await this.startChat(newHistory, resumedData);
```
However, the `ChatRecordingService` (which manages the session file) is initialized with `resumedData` (which points to the existing session file) but is not explicitly instructed to overwrite the file's message history with the new `newHistory`. The `initialize` method in `ChatRecordingService` merely points to the existing file without clearing or updating its messages.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(core): prevent command substitution guard bypass via shell wrapper flags
prs.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes a command-substitution guard bypass in `stripShellWrapper()` that could occur when a POSIX shell wrapper contains intermediate or chained command-line flags before the `-c` execution flag.

The affected command forms were not consistently recognized as shell wrappers. As a result, the command payload could remain wrapped in quotes when it reached `detectCommandSubstitution()`, causing command substitution inside the payload to be treated as literal text during detection even though the shell would execute it.


## Vulnerability

`stripShellWrapper()` previously expected the POSIX shell wrapper to have `-c` immediately after the shell executable.

For example, a command such as:

```text
bash -c 'echo $(whoami)'
```

was recognized correctly.

However, equivalent forms containing intermediate shell options were not:

```text
bash -e -c 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -o pipefail -c 'echo $(whoami)'
sh -l -c 'echo $(whoami)'
```

Chained short options such as:

```text
bash -lc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -exic 'echo $(whoami)'
```

could also bypass the existing wrapper detection.

### Why this matters

The command-substitution detection logic operates on the command after the shell wrapper has been stripped.

When the wrapper was not recognized, the payload could remain as:

```text
'echo $(whoami)'
```

The command-substitution detector interprets the single-quoted content as literal text and therefore does not identify the `$(...)` expression.

The shell, however, receives the original command and executes the substitution.

This creates a discrepancy between what the security guard analyzes and what the shell actually executes.

## Root Cause

The previous implementation relied on a single wrapper-matching regular expression that assumed the `-c` execution flag appeared directly after the shell executable.

It did not account for valid POSIX shell options appearing before the execution flag.

The core issue was therefore not the command-substitution detector itself, but the incomplete shell-wrapper normalization performed before detection.

## Fix

This PR replaces the overly restrictive POSIX wrapper matching with a deterministic token scanner.

The scanner:

* Recognizes `sh`, `bash`, and `zsh` wrappers.
* Handles whitespace-separated shell options before `-c`.
* Handles valid chained short options ending in `c`, such as:

  * `-c`
  * `+c`
  * `-lc`
  * `-xc`
  * `-ec`
  * `-exic`
  * `+xc`
* Correctly consumes arguments for options such as:

  * `-o`
  * `+o`
  * `-O`
  * `--rcfile`
  * `--init-file`
* Supports quoted and backslash-escaped option arguments.
* Fails closed when an unexpected positional token appears before the command-execution flag.
* Preserves the existing Windows shell handling for:

  * `cmd.exe /c`
  * `powershell -Command`
  * `powershell -NoProfile -Command`
  * `pwsh -Command`
* Preserves the existing payload unquoting and POSIX double-quoted payload parsing behavior.

The termination flag validation is deliberately conservative:

```ts
/^[+-][a-np-zA-NP-Z]*c$/
```

This allows valid short-option chains ending in `c` while excluding argument-taking `o/O` flags and malformed or unrelated tokens.

## Security Regression Coverage

Regression tests were added for intermediate and chained shell flags, including:

```text
bash -e -c 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -o pipefail -c 'echo $(whoami)'
sh -l -c 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -lc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -ec 'echo $(whoami)'
bash -exic 'echo $(whoami)'
zsh -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
sh -xc 'echo $(whoami)'
bash +xc 'echo $(whoami)'
```

Additional coverage verifies detection of:

* backtick command substitution
* process substitution
* safe commands without substitution
* escaped spaces in intermediate option arguments

Negative cases ensure arbitrary tokens are not incorrectly treated as the `-c` termination flag, including:

```text
bash --exec ...
bash --rc ...
bash file.c ...
bash -1c ...
bash -c- ...
bash -c/foo ...
bash -oc ...
bash -xoc ...
bash -ce ...
```

## Validation

The following checks were run successfully:

* `src/utils/shell-utils.test.ts` — **91/91 passed**
* `src/tools/shell.test.ts` — **95/95 passed**
* ESLint — **0 errors, 0 warnings**
* TypeScript typecheck — **0 errors**
* `git diff --check` — **clean**

## Scope

Only the following files are changed:

```text
packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.ts
packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.test.ts
```

No dependencies or unrelated components were modified.

## Related Issue

Relates to #29685

prs.title: fix(cli): only auto-nudge genuinely empty continuations and await the nudge
prs.body:
## Summary

When a tool-loop continuation came back with no visible text, `useGeminiStream` automatically sent a nudge (`[System: You successfully executed a tool but returned an empty response...]`). It did this as a fire-and-forget promise from inside the stream loop, and it only checked that the text buffer was empty. As a result the nudge also fired when the stream ended for reasons that are **not** an empty model response, including **after the user pressed Esc**. In that case it silently undid the cancellation and started a new request. This PR only nudges genuinely empty continuations and sequences the nudge properly.

## Details

**Before** (`processGeminiStreamEvents`):

- The nudge condition was just `isContinuation && buffer is empty && attempts < 2`. That is also true when the stream ended with:
  - `UserCancelled`, or a signal aborted by Esc. `submitQuery` then resets `turnCancelledRef` and creates a new `AbortController`, so **the cancel is undone and the model is called again**.
  - `Error`: the error is shown, then another request is sent anyway.
  - `AgentExecutionStopped` / `AgentExecutionBlocked`: a hook asked the agent to stop and the nudge overrode it.
  - `MaxSessionTurns`, `ContextWindowWillOverflow`, `LoopDetected`.
  - `InvalidStream`, e.g. `NO_RESPONSE_TEXT`. Since #28934 the core already retries empty responses with its own nudge (`NO_RESPONSE_TEXT_NUDGE_MESSAGE`) before reporting this, so the CLI nudge was a second, stacked retry.
- The nudge was a floating `submitQueryRef.current?.(...)` call, started before the outer `submitQuery` had flushed its pending history item.

**After:**

- `processGeminiStreamEvents` records when the stream ended abnormally (the events above). It returns a new `StreamProcessingStatus.EmptyContinuation` only for a continuation that ended normally, was not aborted, and produced no text or tool calls.
- `submitQuery` handles that status after flushing the pending history item. It sends the nudge only if:
  - the turn was not cancelled (`turnCancelledRef`),
  - no newer query has started (`activeQueryIdRef`),
  - and the attempt limit is not reached.
- The nudge is **awaited**, so the request stays `Responding` until the nudge has finished.
- The nudge text is unchanged, moved to a module constant. The now-unused `prompt_id` parameter of `processGeminiStreamEvents` is removed.

**Not changed:** the issue also suggests skipping `geminiClient.addHistory` for completed tools in the cancelled path of `handleCompletedTools`. I left that alone. Those responses pair the model's `functionCall` turn that is already in history, and dropping them would leave an unanswered `functionCall`, which is the corruption the surrounding code works to avoid (see the comment in the `modelSwitchedFromQuotaError` branch). Happy to look at it separately if maintainers see a concrete repro.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29071

## How to Validate

```bash
npm run build --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core
cd packages/cli && npx vitest run src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.test.tsx -t "nudge"
```

New `auto-nudge on empty continuation responses` tests:

- an always-empty continuation is nudged exactly twice, all sends share the prompt id, and everything has finished by the time the continuation's own promise resolves
- no nudge when the stream ended with: an error, an invalid stream, a hook stopping the agent, a hook blocking the agent, a user cancellation, or the session turn limit
- no nudge when the user cancels (`cancelOngoingRequest`) while the continuation is still streaming

7 of these fail on `main` and pass with this change. The existing auto-nudge test (via `handleCompletedTools`) still passes. All CLI hook and `AppContainer` tests pass (68 files, 1278 tests), and typecheck and lint are clean.

prs.title: fix(core): make file credential store writes atomic and serialized
prs.body:
## Summary

The file-based credential store (`FileKeychain`, used when no native keychain is available) could **silently lose saved credentials** when two processes wrote at the same time. It could also **lock the user out of all saved credentials** if a write was interrupted. This PR makes writes atomic and serializes read-modify-write cycles across processes.

## Details

**Before:**

- `setPassword()` / `deletePassword()` did an unlocked whole-file read-modify-write. With two concurrent writers (e.g. an OAuth token refresh in one terminal and a login in another), both read the same snapshot and the second write erased the first's entry.
- `saveData()` used `fs.writeFile` directly on the live file. A crash or full disk mid-write left a truncated ciphertext. AES-GCM decryption of that always fails, so every later operation threw `Corrupted credentials file detected ...` until the user deleted the file by hand.

**After:**

- **Atomic writes:** `saveData()` writes to a unique `gemini-credentials.json.<uuid>.tmp` (mode `0600`) and `rename`s it over the credentials file. The live file is therefore always a complete old or new version.
  - Transient `EBUSY`/`EPERM` rename failures (Windows, file briefly open elsewhere) are retried with backoff, the same approach as `ProjectRegistry.save()`.
  - The temp file is removed if writing or renaming fails.
- **Cross-process serialization:** `setPassword()` and `deletePassword()` run under an exclusive `proper-lockfile` lock and re-read the file inside the lock.
  - `proper-lockfile` is already a dependency, used by `ProjectRegistry` and trusted folders.
  - `realpath: false` lets the lock be taken before the credentials file exists, so no empty (undecryptable) placeholder file is created.
  - Retries wait up to ~5 s. Stale locks from crashed processes are recovered by `proper-lockfile`'s default stale detection.
- **Reads** (`getPassword`, `findCredentials`) stay lock-free. With atomic renames they always see a complete file.

No change to the file format, encryption, or location.

I did not add a `.bak` self-heal generation, which the issue mentions as optional. With atomic writes, a truncated file can no longer be produced by this code. Happy to add it if maintainers want recovery for files corrupted by older versions.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29054

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/services/fileKeychain.test.ts src/services/gcmTruncationReproduction.test.ts
```

`FileKeychain` had no unit tests. This adds 10, using a real temp directory:

- basic set/get/find/delete, file removal on last delete, encryption at rest, no leftover temp or lock files
- **8 concurrent writers** (separate instances, standing in for separate processes): no entries lost
- **interleaved concurrent set/delete**: no entries dropped or resurrected
- **interrupted write** (partial temp write + `ENOSPC`): the existing file is byte-for-byte unchanged and still decrypts
- the lock is released after a failed write
- transient `EPERM`/`EBUSY` rename is retried; a permanent rename failure cleans up the temp file

The 5 tests covering the bug (both concurrency tests, the interrupted write, and both rename tests) **fail on `main` and pass with this change**.

Note: `keychainService.test.ts` has 5 failures on Windows both on `main` and on this branch. They come from WSL detection in that test's environment, and that test mocks `FileKeychain` entirely, so they are unrelated to this change.

prs.title: fix(a2a-server): handle unhandled rejection in scheduleToolCalls
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an unhandled promise rejection in `packages/a2a-server/src/agent/task.ts` caused by invoking `this.scheduler.schedule()` with `void`. When tool calls are queued and a task is aborted or cancelled, `CoreToolScheduler` legitimately rejects the promise, triggering an unhandled rejection that terminates the entire `a2a-server` process in Node.js 15+.

## Details

- Attached a targeted `.catch()` handler to `this.scheduler.schedule()` in `scheduleToolCalls`.
- Safely swallows expected abort and cancellation errors (`abortSignal.aborted`, `isAbortError`, and cancellation messages) so that aborting one task does not crash the server or affect other tasks.
- Logs unexpected scheduler errors via `logger.error`.
- Added regression tests in `packages/a2a-server/src/agent/task.test.ts` to ensure cancellation does not emit `unhandledRejection` and unexpected errors are appropriately logged.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29034

## How to Validate

1. Run the a2a-server test suite to verify the regression tests pass:
```bash
npm --prefix packages/a2a-server test
```

2. Verify TypeScript type checking passes without errors:
```bash
npm --prefix packages/a2a-server run typecheck

```

prs.title: fix(core): stop $ patterns corrupting prompt templates and {{args}}
prs.body:
## Summary

Prompt templates in core were filled with `String.prototype.replace(string, string)`. As a result, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$$` in model, tool or user text were treated as replacement patterns instead of being inserted as-is. That silently corrupted:

- edit instructions and file contents sent to the LLM edit fixer
- tool output sent to the summarizer
- conversation text sent to the session summarizer

The same problem affected `{{args}}` substitution in custom commands, including inside `!{...}` shell commands. This PR fixes all of these call sites by reusing the existing safe helpers. It adds no new utilities.

## Details

**1. `$` replacement patterns (the reported bug).** For example, `'$&'` in an edit's `old_string` was replaced by the placeholder token itself (`{old_string}`), so the model received a different search string from the one that failed.

**2. Placeholder injection in `llm-edit-fixer` (found while fixing #1).** The five placeholders were filled one after another. Any input that contained a *later* placeholder got substituted into instead of the template. Example: an instruction that mentions `{old_string}`, or code containing `{error}`. That moved user/file content into the wrong section of the prompt.

**Changes:**

- `packages/core/src/utils/llm-edit-fixer.ts`, `packages/core/src/utils/summarizer.ts`, `packages/core/src/services/sessionSummaryService.ts`:
  - Use the existing single-pass `safeTemplateReplace()` from `textUtils.ts`. It is already used by the Conseca policy prompts and already tested for `$&` and double-interpolation.
  - The templates switch from `{key}` to that helper's `{{key}}` placeholder syntax. Each placeholder appears exactly once, so the generated prompts are unchanged for normal input.
- `packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts`:
  - All five `replaceAll(SHORTHAND_ARGS_PLACEHOLDER, …)` calls now use the existing `safeLiteralReplace()`.
  - Custom command arguments containing `$` patterns now reach the prompt and the shell command unchanged.
  - The policy check still runs on the final resolved command.

`bugCommand.ts` also uses `.replace('{…}', …)`, but its values go through `encodeURIComponent`, which encodes `$`, so it is not affected and is left as-is.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29044

## How to Validate

```bash
npm run build --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/utils/llm-edit-fixer.test.ts src/utils/summarizer.test.ts src/services/sessionSummaryService.test.ts src/utils/textUtils.test.ts
cd ../cli && npx vitest run src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.test.ts
```

There are 6 new regression tests: $-patterns in all five edit-fixer inputs, placeholder injection in the edit fixer, $-patterns in summarizer and session-summary input, and $-patterns in raw and shell-escaped `{{args}}`. **All 6 fail on `main` and pass with this change.** The existing prompt-construction tests (including the exact-match summarizer prompt test) pass unchanged.

Manual check: create a custom command with `prompt = "Echo: {{args}}"` and run `/<command> cost is $& or $'`. On `main` the prompt shows `cost is {{args}} or …`. With this change it shows the input exactly.

prs.title: ci(evals): ignore test files in steering-signature detection
prs.body:
## Summary

`scripts/changed_prompt.js` decides whether the required `Evals (ALWAYS_PASSING)` job runs for a change. Its signature scan (`inputSchema`, `ToolDefinition`, `LocalAgentDefinition`, …) covered every file under `packages/core/src/`, **including `*.test.ts`**. Test files routinely declare stand-in MCP tools with `inputSchema` (e.g. `packages/core/src/ide/ide-client.sandbox.test.ts`, added by #29858), so PRs with **no prompt or tool change** were running the non-deterministic behavioral evals and failing on unrelated flakes.

Concrete case: #29744 only touches `packages/core/src/ide/`; its new `ide-client.server-restart.test.ts` contains `{ inputSchema: OpenDiffRequestSchema.shape }`, which opened the gate ([run 39826194193](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/actions/runs/39826194193), `Matched steering signature in core: inputSchema`). The run then failed on `plan_mode > should transition from plan mode to normal execution and create a plan file from scratch` — the same eval that failed with the identical tool-call chain for #29848 one day earlier ([run 39642817922](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/actions/runs/39642817922)). 17 existing test files under `packages/core/src/` outside `tools/` and `prompts/` already contain one of the signatures, so this will keep hitting other PRs.

This PR excludes test sources from the **signature** scan only. **Path-based** detection (`packages/core/src/prompts/`, `packages/core/src/tools/`, `evals/`) is unchanged and still includes test files — the same split `eval-pr.yml` already makes at the trigger level (`paths: … '!**/*.test.ts'`).

## Details

- `scripts/changed_prompt.js`
  - New `isTestFile()` (`/\.test\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$/`) and exported `detectSteeringChanges(changedFiles, getDiff, { steeringOnly, verbose })` containing the unchanged two-stage logic; the signature stage now filters test files before diffing.
  - `main()` is guarded with `process.argv[1] === fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` (same idiom as `scripts/get-release-version.js`) so the module can be imported by tests.
  - The per-file diff is obtained with `execFileSync('git', [...])` (no shell interpolation of paths). CLI contract is unchanged: `--verbose`, `--steering-only`, `true|false` on stdout, default-to-`true` on error, `PR_HEAD_SHA` / `GITHUB_BASE_REF` / `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` honoured — both callers (`chained_e2e.yml`, `eval-pr.yml`) are unaffected.
- `scripts/tests/changed_prompt.test.js` (new, 18 cases): test-file detection, path-based detection (incl. tests under `tools/` still triggering), `evals/` vs `--steering-only`, signature detection in production files, **regression: signature only in test files → `false`**, only non-test core files are diffed, verbose vs first-match semantics.

No workflow changes; no user-facing change.

## Related Issues

Related to #29744 (CI failure that surfaced this) and #29848 (same flake, same cause class). No dedicated issue exists for the gate heuristic.

## How to Validate

```bash
npm run test:scripts            # 16 files, 220 tests (18 new)
npx eslint scripts/changed_prompt.js scripts/tests/changed_prompt.test.js
npx prettier --check scripts/changed_prompt.js scripts/tests/changed_prompt.test.js
```

Behavioral check against real commits (fetch the refs first):

| Input | script on `main` | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PR_HEAD_SHA=65c12b25b` (#29744 head: only `packages/core/src/ide/`, `inputSchema` in a test file) | `true` | `false` |
| same, `--steering-only` | `true` | `false` |
| `inputSchema` added to a production core file (probe commit) | `true` | `true` |
| `PR_HEAD_SHA=c16100a55` (merge-queue commit that also changes `packages/core/src/tools/shell.ts`) | `true` | `true` (path match) |

```bash
GITHUB_REPOSITORY=google-gemini/gemini-cli PR_HEAD_SHA=<sha> node scripts/changed_prompt.js --verbose
```

Local CI parity on this branch (Linux, Node 20.20.2): `npm run preflight` green (clean, `npm ci`, format, build, `lint:ci` incl. actionlint/shellcheck/yamllint/prettier/tsconfig/sensitive-keywords, typecheck, `test:ci` for all workspaces + `test:scripts` + `test:sea-launch`).

prs.title: fix(core): allow trusted system paths on Android (Termux) for ripgrep resolution (#21836)
prs.body:
## Summary

Allow trusted system directory prefixes on Android/Termux environments in `isTrustedSystemPath()` so that native ripgrep binaries (e.g. installed via `pkg install ripgrep`) can be resolved and executed by `grep_search`.

## Details

In Termux on Android, ripgrep installed via package managers resides in `$PREFIX/bin` (`/data/data/com.termux/files/usr/bin/rg`). Previously, `isTrustedSystemPath()` only permitted standard FHS paths (`/usr/bin`, `/bin`, etc.) and Windows paths, causing system ripgrep on Termux to be rejected as untrusted and falling back to JavaScript file searching or failing.

This change:
1. Adds trusted prefix checks for Android (`platform === 'android'`), checking `$PREFIX/bin`, `/data/data/com.termux/files/usr/bin`, `/system/bin`, `/system/xbin`, `/bin`, and `/usr/bin`.
2. Preserves the security guardrail that rejects paths inside the current working directory to prevent search path interruption / RCE.
3. Adds comprehensive unit tests in `paths.test.ts` and `ripGrep.test.ts` covering trusted and untrusted paths on Android.



## How to Validate

Run unit tests for path validation and ripgrep resolution:
```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/paths.test.ts
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/tools/ripGrep.test.ts
```
Expected result: All tests pass, including Android/Termux resolution and untrusted path rejections.

prs.title: fix(cli): correct Thai and Lao SARA AM display width
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes a display width mismatch for Thai `SARA AM` (`U+0E33`, `ำ`) and Lao `SARA AM` (`U+0EB3`, `ຳ`) where `string-width` reports a combined width of `1` column for `Consonant + SARA AM` (e.g., `'กำ'`) while terminal emulators (`tmux`, `xterm.js`, VTE, glibc `wcwidth`) render them across `2` columns (`1 + 1`). This 1-column undercount per `SARA AM` caused full-width lines and bordered boxes (such as `InputPrompt` and streaming output) to physically overflow the terminal width, wrapping onto an extra terminal row and causing Ink's incremental line-erasure math to desynchronize—resulting in duplicate output lines ("spamming") and erratic prompt jumping.

## Details

- **Root Cause**:
  - Unlike Thai/Lao non-spacing above/below vowels and tone marks (`General_Category=Mn`, `wcwidth=0`), Thai `SARA AM` (`U+0E33`) and Lao `SARA AM` (`U+0EB3`) have `General_Category=Lo` (spacing letters with `wcwidth=1`).
  - However, Unicode UAX #29 assigns `Grapheme_Cluster_Break=SpacingMark` to `U+0E33` and `U+0EB3` (rule GB9a), causing `Intl.Segmenter` in `string-width` to merge them into the preceding base character's grapheme cluster and ignore their 1-column width (`stringWidth('กำ') === 1` instead of `2`).
  - Additionally, `@jrichman/ink` merges `0x0e33` and `0x0eb3` into the preceding character in `toStyledCharacters()` and measures the combined token with `defaultStringWidth` (`string-width`), allocating 1 column slot in Ink's virtual output buffer while the terminal advances the cursor by 2 columns.
- **Fix**:
  - Updated `getCachedStringWidth` in `packages/cli/src/ui/utils/textUtils.ts` to replace `[\u0E33\u0EB3]` with a 1-column ASCII space (`' '`) prior to calling `stringWidth`, ensuring each `SARA AM` is measured as 1 column whether standalone or combined with a consonant/tone mark.
  - Registered `setStringWidthFunction(getCachedStringWidth)` with Ink in `packages/cli/src/interactiveCli.tsx` (and in `packages/cli/src/test-utils/render.tsx` for `@xterm/headless` component tests) so Ink's layout, wrapping, cursor positioning, and virtual grid buffer use the corrected width and LRU cache.
  - Replaced direct `stringWidth` calls in `packages/cli/src/ui/components/InputPrompt.tsx` with `getCachedStringWidth` for consistent width measurement and caching across click hit-testing and ghost-text wrapping/padding.

## Related Issues

Fixes #25369

## How to Validate

1. Run unit tests for `textUtils` and `@xterm/headless` Ink rendering:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/ui/utils/textUtils.test.ts src/test-utils/render.test.tsx src/ui/components/InputPrompt.test.tsx
   ```
2. Start the interactive CLI inside `tmux` (`npm run start`) and type or stream Thai/Lao text containing `SARA AM` (e.g., `กำลังพิมพ์ข้อความ` or `น้ำ`). Verify that the bordered input box and streaming responses remain aligned within the terminal width without wrapping right borders or duplicating previous frames.

prs.title: fix(core): resolve relative file paths against active IDE workspace root
prs.body:
## Summary

Resolves relative file paths in `WriteFileTool`, `EditTool`, `ReadFileTool`, and `correctPath` against the active IDE workspace root (or nested Git repository root) tracked in `ideContextStore` rather than unconditionally using the initial fallback `config.getTargetDir()`. This prevents Gemini CLI in multi-root or parent-folder IDE workspaces (such as VS Code + WSL) from writing or editing files in a sibling repository while displaying a relative path that appears to belong to the active project.

## Details

- Added `resolveActiveWorkspaceDir` in `packages/core/src/utils/pathCorrector.ts`:
      - Returns `config.getTargetDir()` when IDE mode is disabled or when no active/open file is present in `ideContextStore`.
      - When IDE mode is enabled, locates the most specific workspace directory in `WorkspaceContext.getDirectories()` containing the active editor file.
      - If the matching workspace directory is a parent folder containing multiple nested Git repositories, walks up from the active file to detect the nested `.git` repository root.
      - Prevents path duplication when a relative path already starts with the subpath from `config.getTargetDir()` to the active nested repository.

- Updated `correctPath` (`packages/core/src/utils/pathCorrector.ts`) to check the active IDE workspace root first (both direct path and BFS lookup) before falling back to other workspace directories.

- Updated `WriteFileTool` (`packages/core/src/tools/write-file.ts`), `EditTool` (`packages/core/src/tools/edit.ts`), and `ReadFileTool`
  (`packages/core/src/tools/read-file.ts`) to resolve relative paths and format relative UI descriptions against `resolveActiveWorkspaceDir`.

- Added unit tests in `packages/core/src/tools/write-file.test.ts`, `packages/core/src/tools/edit.test.ts`, and `packages/core/src/utils/pathCorrector.test.ts`.
    
## Related Issues

Fixes #25527

## How to Validate

1. Run the unit test suites for `WriteFileTool`, `EditTool`, `ReadFileTool`, and `pathCorrector`:

prs.title: feat(cli): support git submodules in extension installs
prs.body:
## Summary

Support Git submodules when installing extensions from Git repositories.

Without this change, `gemini extensions install <git-url>` would clone the top-level repository but leave submodule directories uninitialized, which could result in incomplete or broken extension installs.

## Details

This updates the Git-based extension install flow to initialize and update submodules recursively after checking out the requested ref in `cloneFromGit(...)`.

The change is intentionally narrow:

## Summary

Fixes a bug where automatic migration of deprecated settings overwrites unrelated `${VAR}` / `${VAR:-default}` environment variable placeholders on disk with their expanded runtime values whenever those placeholders reside in the same top-level settings subtree (or target subtree) as a migrated key.

## Details

    - Added unit and regression tests in `packages/cli/src/config/settings.test.ts` verifying runtime expansion/coercion alongside raw `${VAR}` placeholder preservation across same-subtree and cross-subtree migrations.

prs.title: fix(core): preserve file search results across query changes
prs.body:
## Summary

File searches can silently omit valid results after an earlier query populates the result cache. For example, searching `Src` and then `Src*` hides lowercase paths that a fresh `Src*` search finds. Reuse cached results only for identical queries so a new query always starts from the complete candidate list.

## Details

- Remove the assumption that a longer query must match a subset of its string prefix's results. Fuzzy search uses smart case, while glob filtering is case-insensitive.
- Cover the same failure within glob matching: `!*.ts` followed by `!*.tsx` must recover `.ts` files excluded by the first query. Separating caches by matcher alone would not fix this case.
- Preserve exact-query cache hits, filtering, ordering, cancellation, file-watcher invalidation, and result limits. Rename the existing broad-to-narrow integration test to describe the behavior it checks.
- Each new glob query now filters the full candidate list rather than a cached prefix subset. Repeated queries remain cached; fuzzy matching already searches the full list. No settings, dependencies, or matching rules change.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29055.

## How to Validate

```bash
npm exec -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- vitest run src/utils/filesearch --coverage.enabled=false --reporter=dot
npm run typecheck -w @google/gemini-cli-core
npm run preflight
```

Before the implementation change, all four new integration cases failed: a nonempty fuzzy result, an empty fuzzy result, and negated-glob extension with fuzzy search enabled and disabled. The cache unit test also failed. With the fix, all 84 file-search tests pass, including existing file-watcher tests, and core type checking and targeted lint pass on macOS arm64 with Node.js 24.16.0.

Full preflight completed installation, formatting, all package builds, repository-wide lint, and type checking. Its workspace test run passed all 8,518 core tests, 182 A2A-server tests, 29 SDK tests, and 68 VS Code companion tests. The CLI run passed 7,431 tests and failed nine existing startup/workspace-trust cases in `src/gemini.test.tsx`.

Those same nine failures reproduce with the original cache source and built implementation restored. After restoring this fix, running that startup suite with `GEMINI_CLI_TRUST_WORKSPACE=true` (also set by `.github/workflows/ci.yml`) passes all 45 enabled tests (one skipped):

```bash
GEMINI_CLI_TRUST_WORKSPACE=true npm exec -w @google/gemini-cli -- vitest run src/gemini.test.tsx --coverage.enabled=false --reporter=dot
```

The setting was scoped to that test process; no persistent trust settings were changed.

The separate script suite initially passed 183 tests and failed 19 in `patch-create-comment.test.js`, whose helper invokes a script with an unquoted checkout path containing `Open Source`. All 202 script tests pass from an isolated copy of unchanged upstream sources at a path without spaces. All 17 SEA launcher tests also pass. The file-search suite was rerun after the baseline comparison and again passed all 84 tests.

The default `npm run preflight` invocation is therefore **not green** in this local environment; the failing cases pass with the environment/path corrections above. This is a draft while maintainers triage contribution eligibility and review the validation notes.

prs.title: fix(core,cli): emit ACP retry progress updates and enforce retry delay cap and model fallback
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes #29805.

In ACP (`--acp`) mode, when a model request hits a 429 quota or capacity exhaustion error, the CLI previously failed to emit any ACP progress signals while retrying, could treat multi-hour quota reset messages (`Your quota will reset after 14h31m12s`) as transient capacity exhaustion and sleep for hours, and did not persist model fallback transitions for non-interactive/ACP sessions or background utility models (`flash-lite`).

This PR addresses all three root causes:
1. **ACP Retry Progress Notifications**: Adds session attribution (`sessionId`) to `RetryAttemptPayload` and subscribes `acpSession.ts` to `CoreEvent.RetryAttempt`, forwarding retry progress as `agent_thought_chunk` updates with structured `_meta.retry` metadata (`attempt`, `maxAttempts`, `delayMs`, `error`, `model`) so ACP clients have visibility during retries.
2. **Retry Delay Budget Enforcement**: Excludes explicit quota-reset messages (`quota will reset after`) from transient capacity retry promotion and enforces `maxDelayMs` (and `MAX_RETRYABLE_DELAY_SECONDS`) in `retryWithBackoff`, promoting excessive retry delays to `TerminalQuotaError` so fallback is triggered immediately instead of sleeping for hours.
3. **Persistent Non-Interactive & Utility Model Fallback**: Resolves the failed model's own policy chain in `handleFallback` when a utility model (such as `gemini-3.1-flash-lite`) fails, enables `onPersistent429` fallback in `BaseLlmClient` and automatic fallback in `handleFallback` for non-interactive/ACP sessions, and preserves `ModelAvailabilityService` terminal states in `activateFallbackMode` so subsequent calls in the session skip exhausted models immediately.

## Details

- `packages/core/src/utils/events.ts`: Add optional `sessionId` to `RetryAttemptPayload`.
- `packages/core/src/core/baseLlmClient.ts`, `packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.ts`, `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, `packages/core/src/tools/web-fetch.ts`: Include `sessionId` when emitting `CoreEvent.RetryAttempt`, enable `onPersistent429` in `BaseLlmClient`, and respect `getFallbackOverride` during retries.
- `packages/cli/src/acp/acpSession.ts`: Subscribe to `CoreEvent.RetryAttempt` for the active session and emit `agent_thought_chunk` updates with `_meta.retry`; unsubscribe on `dispose()`.
- `packages/core/src/utils/retry.ts` & `packages/core/src/utils/googleQuotaErrors.ts`: Export `MAX_RETRYABLE_DELAY_SECONDS` and enforce `maxDelayMs` budget for both silent capacity retries and `RetryableQuotaError` backoff delays.
- `packages/core/src/fallback/handler.ts` & `packages/core/src/config/config.ts`: Resolve failed utility model policy chains, enable automatic fallback in non-interactive sessions when no UI handler is registered, and avoid resetting `ModelAvailabilityService` or overwriting the active chat model when a non-active utility model falls back.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29805

## How to Validate

- Run unit and integration tests:
  - `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/retry.test.ts src/fallback/handler.test.ts src/availability/autoRoutingFallback.integration.test.ts src/config/config.test.ts src/config/flashFallback.test.ts`
  - `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/acp/acpSession.test.ts`

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation or README (if applicable)
- [x] Added/updated unit tests
- [x] Tested changes locally
- [x] Highlighted any breaking changes (none)

prs.title: fix(cli): handle termination signals and prevent tool execution after cancellation in non-interactive mode
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an issue where Gemini CLI in non-interactive/headless environments could continue consuming delayed provider tool calls after receiving an OS cancellation signal (`SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`), execute local shell tool side effects, and submit repeated tool results.

## Details

1. **OS Signal Listeners in Non-Interactive Modes**:
   - In `nonInteractiveCli.ts` and `nonInteractiveCliAgentSession.ts`, `setupStdinCancellation()` only attached raw mode keypress listeners if `process.stdin.isTTY` was true. In non-TTY environments (Docker, CI, scripts, subshells), OS signals were not bound to the `AbortController`.
   - Replaced `setupStdinCancellation()` with `setupCancellation()`, which registers `process.on('SIGINT')` and `process.on('SIGTERM')` listeners regardless of TTY status, ensuring signals trigger `abortController.abort()`. Symmetrically cleaned up in `finally` blocks via `process.off`.
2. **Handle `UserCancelled` in Stream Loop**:
   - In `nonInteractiveCli.ts`, added handling for `GeminiEventType.UserCancelled` in the response stream event loop to terminate execution immediately via `handleCancellationError(config)`.
3. **Guard Tool Scheduling**:
   - Checked `abortController.signal.aborted` immediately prior to calling `scheduler.schedule(toolCallRequests, abortController.signal)` to prevent execution of any previously queued tool calls.
4. **Standard Cancellation Exit**:
   - Unified cancellation in `nonInteractiveCliAgentSession.ts` to call `handleCancellationError(config)`, ensuring the process consistently exits with code 130 upon cancellation.

## Related Issues

Fixes #28091

## How to Validate

Run targeted unit tests:
```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/nonInteractiveCli.test.ts src/nonInteractiveCliAgentSession.test.ts
```
Run full test suite:
```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli
```
Run linter and typecheck:
```bash
npm run lint && npm run typecheck
```

prs.title: fix(core,cli,sdk): discard buffered tool calls on mid-stream error or retry
prs.body:
## Summary

When a model stream emits one or more `ToolCallRequest` events and then fails mid-stream (`Error` / `InvalidStream`), retries mid-stream (`Retry`), or terminates abnormally (`UserCancelled`, `AgentExecutionStopped`, `ContextWindowWillOverflow`, `LoopDetected`, `MaxSessionTurns`), `GeminiChat` rolls back the incomplete model turn from `agentHistory`. Previously, several stream consumers retained the buffered `toolCallRequests` (and `Turn.pendingToolCalls`) and still scheduled them after the stream loop exited, producing an orphaned `functionResponse` turn with no preceding `functionCall` in `agentHistory`.

This change:
- Clears `this.pendingToolCalls` (and resets per-attempt state on `Retry`) in `Turn.run()` when a stream retries, aborts, stops, or throws.
- Clears buffered `toolCallRequests` and tracks `StreamProcessingStatus` in `useGeminiStream.ts` when `Retry`, `Error`, `InvalidStream`, `UserCancelled`, `AgentExecutionStopped`, `ContextWindowWillOverflow`, `MaxSessionTurns`, or `LoopDetected` occurs, preventing orphaned tool execution and suppressing empty-response auto-nudges on non-completed streams.
- Clears buffered `toolCallRequests` / `toolCallsToSchedule` on mid-stream `Retry` and terminal stream events across `nonInteractiveCli.ts`, `acpSession.ts`, `legacy-agent-session.ts`, `sdk/src/session.ts`, and `a2a-server/src/agent/executor.ts`.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29842

## How to Validate

- Run unit tests:
  - `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/core/turn.test.ts src/agent/legacy-agent-session.test.ts`
  - `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.test.tsx src/nonInteractiveCli.test.ts src/acp/acpSession.test.ts`
  - `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-sdk -- src/session.test.ts`
- Run `npm run typecheck` and `npm run lint`.

prs.title: fix(core): ensure all model turns with function calls receive thought signatures
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an issue where multi-turn agent conversations fail with HTTP 400 Bad Request (`Function call is missing a thought_signature in functionCall parts`) when historical model tool calls precede subsequent user prompts.

## Details

### Root Cause
In `GeminiChat.ensureActiveLoopHasThoughtSignatures`, thought signature enforcement was only applied to turns beginning at `activeLoopStartIndex` (the most recent user text prompt). Any historical model turn containing a function call prior to `activeLoopStartIndex` (such as a tool invoked earlier in a coding session, e.g. at position 58) was forwarded to the Gemini API without a `thoughtSignature`.

The Gemini API requires that every model turn containing function calls in the `contents` history payload must have a `thought_signature` on its first `functionCall` part. Consequently, once a session progressed past the initial tool turn, the Gemini API rejected the subsequent request with HTTP 400 `INVALID_ARGUMENT`.

### Fix
- Updated `ensureActiveLoopHasThoughtSignatures` in `packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.ts` to iterate across all model turns in `requestContents` rather than restricting to `activeLoopStartIndex`.
- Guaranteed that the first `functionCall` part of every model turn in history has a `thoughtSignature` (`SYNTHETIC_THOUGHT_SIGNATURE` if not already present).
- Preserved existing valid signatures and left parallel function calls (after the first in a turn) unsigned per Gemini API specifications.
- Updated and added regression test coverage in `packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.test.ts`.

## How to Validate

1. Run the targeted unit and regression tests in `@google/gemini-cli-core`:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
   ```
   Expected result: All 134 tests pass.

2. Run `a2a-server` test suite:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-a2a-server
   ```
   Expected result: All 16 test files pass (177 tests).

3. Run workspace typecheck and linter:
   ```bash
   npm run typecheck
   npm run lint
   ```
   Expected result: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

4. Manual verification across 8 cases:
   - Case 1: Standard Active Loop Tool Call — Verified first function call is signed.
   - Case 2: Multi-Turn Historical Tool Call — Verified historical Turn 1 and active Turn 5 both signed.
   - Case 3: Parallel Tool Calls — Verified first function call signed, subsequent calls unsigned.
   - Case 4: Existing Real Signature Preservation — Verified real encrypted signatures are preserved.
   - Case 5: History Without User Text — Verified model function call is signed.
   - Case 6: Deep Turn 58 Reproduction — Verified position 58 function call is signed.
   - Case 7: Text-Only and Empty Turns — Verified no spurious fields added.
   - Case 8: User Turns — Verified user parts remain unaffected.
