prs.title: fix(media): normalize AVIF inbound images like HEIC before provider execution
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Channel plugins passing inbound AVIF images through the documented path (`runtime.channel.media.saveRemoteMedia` → `toInboundMediaFacts` → `MsgContext.media`) reached providers unchanged, and OpenAI-compatible providers that accept only PNG/JPEG/WebP rejected the request — while the same image as PNG/JPEG/WebP worked. HEIC/HEIF already gets normalized to JPEG before provider execution; AVIF (Chrome screenshots, Android camera captures) had no such path, so every channel would need its own image codec to handle it.

## What Changed

The HEIC/HEIF normalization path in `src/media-understanding/image-input-normalize.ts` now also covers **AVIF** (`image/avif` and the `.avif` extension), converting through the same shared pipeline (`normalizeInputImageBuffer` → `convertHeicToJpeg`) so every channel benefits. `CONVERT_TO_JPEG_INPUT_MIMES` in `src/media/input-files.ts` is extended to match.

## Evidence

**Real-behavior proof (codec-equipped runtime: macOS 27.2 arm64, Rastermill decode via the native sips backend).** A real 1×1 AVIF attachment (417 bytes) passed through the production `normalizeImageDescriptionInput`:

```
Input : mime=image/avif bytes=417 header=0000 0018 6674 7970 6176 6966  ("ftypavif")
Output: mime=image/jpeg bytes=543 header=ffd8 ffe0  ("JFIF", JPEG SOI)
```

**Behavioral regression, red on base / green on head.** The new `image-input-normalize.normalize.test.ts` embeds real AVIF/HEIC attachments and exercises the production Rastermill decode path with no module mocks:

```
PR head (16eeb10d):  ✓ 4 passed (4)
   - converts real AVIF bytes to JPEG before image description
   - converts AVIF declared only by the .avif file extension
   - still converts real HEIC bytes to JPEG
   - leaves common images untouched

main production files, same test file:
   × converts real AVIF bytes to JPEG before image description
       → expected 'image/avif' to be 'image/jpeg'
   × converts AVIF declared only by the .avif file extension
       → expected undefined to be 'image/jpeg'
   ✓ still converts real HEIC bytes to JPEG
   ✓ leaves common images untouched
   Tests  2 failed | 2 passed (4)
```

On main the AVIF bytes reach the provider unconverted (`image/avif`) — exactly the reported bug. The earlier mock-based suite was removed; these tests fail if AVIF ever forwards unchanged again.


**End-to-end through the shipped CLI** (`openclaw infer image describe --file proof64.avif --model zai/glm-5.3-flash`, a real 379-byte AVIF attachment, 64×64 solid red):

```
{
  "ok": true,
  "capability": "image.describe",
  "provider": "zai",
  "model": "glm-5.3-flash",
  "outputs": [
    {
      "path": "/tmp/proof64.avif",
      "text": "The image shows a solid red square — a uniform bright red color (approximately RGB 255, 0, 0) with no other details, patterns, or objects present.",
      "kind": "image.description"
    }
  ]
}
```

The shipped `infer image describe` entry point took the AVIF attachment through `prepareImageDescriptionInput` (this PR's normalization), sent the converted image to the provider, and the vision model described the actual pixel content — the AVIF was decoded and delivered as a real image, not forwarded raw.

## On the decoder prerequisite (owner decision)

This keeps the shared conversion policy (option 1). The runtime prerequisite is the same one the existing HEIC path already has: Rastermill decodes HEIC/AVIF through native OS codecs (macOS `sips`) and common formats in-process; no bundled codec is added or removed by this PR. On a host without a native AVIF/HEIC codec, conversion fails with a Rastermill error **before provider execution** — the channel gets a clear conversion failure instead of shipping bytes the provider rejects, which is the recovery path. This matches the shipped HEIC behavior (PR #86037) rather than introducing a new compatibility class.

## CI

- `pnpm tsgo:test` clean locally; check-test-types green on 42f70a8c.
- The 17 pre-existing failures in `image.resources.test.ts` (infra project) reproduce on clean `main` without this PR — unrelated.

Fixes #180508

prs.title: fix(agents): keep agent.run drain deadline monotonic across clock skew
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the host wall clock is rewound mid-drain (NTP correction or manual time change), `openclaw` can wait far longer than the configured timeout before giving up on pending `agent.run` jobs. `waitForAgentRunsToDrain` (in `src/agents/run-wait.ts`) computes the remaining wait budget with `Date.now()`, but that budget is consumed by `agent.wait`'s monotonic timer — a cross-clock-domain mismatch that inflates the wait by the size of the rewind.

- **Problem**: the drain deadline is a wall-clock epoch (built from `Date.now() + timeout`), yet the remaining budget is re-read with `Date.now()` on every iteration while being spent by a monotonic timer. A 90s wall-clock rewind turns a 5s budget into ~95s of waiting.
- **Solution**: convert the wall-clock deadline to a monotonic deadline once at the function entry (`performance.now() + max(0, deadlineWallAtMs - Date.now())`), then drive the whole drain loop off `performance.now()` so the remaining budget is immune to wall-clock jumps.
- **What changed**: `src/agents/run-wait.ts` (deadline conversion at entry; loop condition, `remainingMs`, and `retryDelayMs` now use `performance.now()`), plus one regression test in `src/agents/run-wait.test.ts`.
- **What did NOT change**: the function signature, its only caller (`subagent-followup.ts`), and the wall-clock contract of `resolveRunWaitDeadlineAtMs`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The entry of `waitForAgentRunsToDrain` is the canonical single point to convert the wall-clock deadline to the monotonic domain. The conversion reads `Date.now()` and `performance.now()` in the same synchronous step, so no wall-clock jump can be inserted between them in real runtime (clock corrections land between event-loop ticks, not mid-sync-block). Keeping the conversion here rather than changing `resolveRunWaitDeadlineAtMs` preserves that helper's wall-clock contract for any other callers.

- **Best fix**: yes — a single entry conversion plus three mechanical `Date.now()` → `performance.now()` swaps is the minimal correct change; no guard/branch needed.
- **Alternative**: rewriting `resolveRunWaitDeadlineAtMs` to return monotonic values was rejected because the function also normalizes caller-supplied wall-clock epochs (`deadlineAtMs`) that must keep their wall-clock meaning.
- **Risk**: the fix relies on the two clocks being read in one synchronous step (true in production). It does not address the sibling wall-clock read in `subagent-followup.ts`'s outer loop (tracked separately).

## User Impact

Operators running long-lived agent turns (`agent.run` drain waits) get accurate timeouts: a 5s drain deadline now stays ~5s even if the host wall clock jumps by minutes, instead of silently stretching the wait by the jump size. No behavioral change when the wall clock is stable.

## Evidence

**Real isolated-Gateway elapsed-time proof, multi-input matrix.** Starts the REAL shipped Gateway (`startGatewayServer`) once, then drives the REAL drain owner `waitForAgentRunsToDrain` with its **default callGateway** (no transport stub): with no in-process Gateway context this forces the shipped Gateway client transport (`callGateway` → real WebSocket → real `agent.wait` handler). A **genuinely-pending descendant run is reported on every refresh**, so the drain loop runs until its deadline actually expires. We measure the **real wall elapsed time until the deadline expires** and capture the **real `agent.wait` response over the WebSocket** (`status=timeout` — the genuine round-trip from the real handler). A wall-clock rollback is injected (via a `Date.now` proxy) between the drain deadline seed and the loop's remaining-budget reads, across a 3-input (budget, rewind) matrix in one Gateway run.

**Raw terminal output (verbatim, head `239b0157bd6c`)**:

```console
$ real-gateway-elapsed-proof.mts postfix   # this PR
3000/-60000: agent.wait [2999] status=timeout | real wall elapsed 3069ms
5000/-90000: agent.wait [4999] status=timeout | real wall elapsed 5034ms
8000/-120000: agent.wait [7999] status=timeout | real wall elapsed 8032ms
PASS: drain deadline expired at the budget across all matrix inputs

$ real-gateway-elapsed-proof.mts prefix    # origin/main
3000/-60000: agent.wait [63000] status=timeout | real wall elapsed 63061ms
5000/-90000: agent.wait [95000] status=timeout | real wall elapsed 95057ms
8000/-120000: agent.wait [128000] status=timeout | real wall elapsed 128049ms
BUG REPRODUCED: drain deadline inflated by each rollback
```

**Before/after matrix — real elapsed time until the drain deadline expires** (genuinely-pending run, real WS `agent.wait` round-trip returning `status=timeout`):

| budget / rewind | origin/main (`Date.now()`) | this PR (`performance.now()`) |
|---|---|---|
| 3,000ms / −60s | **63,061 ms** (inflated ~63s) | **3,069 ms** (bounded) |
| 5,000ms / −90s | **95,057 ms** (inflated ~95s) | **5,034 ms** (bounded) |
| 8,000ms / −120s | **128,049 ms** (inflated ~128s) | **8,032 ms** (bounded) |

In every matrix cell the unpatched drain **stays blocked for budget+rewind seconds of real time** after a wall-clock rollback, while the patched drain **expires at the budget**. This is the shipped-Gateway elapsed-time path with real request/response round-trips (the previous transport-stub evidence exercised neither).

**Regression test** — `keeps the agent.wait budget bounded when the wall clock rewinds mid-drain` fails on unpatched code (RED `expected 95000 to be less than or equal to 5000`) and passes after the fix (GREEN); `vitest run src/agents/run-wait.test.ts` → `35 passed (34 baseline + 1 new)`.

- **Not tested**: sibling `deadline - Date.now()` read in `subagent-followup.ts`'s outer loop; shifts injected via a `Date.now` proxy (not a real host NTP step); the pending run is a synthetic genuinely-pending descendant (real model runs avoided for nondeterministic timing).
- **Collision check**: 300 most recent open PRs' changed files don't touch `src/agents/run-wait.ts`; same-anchor PRs #175639/#166728/#173035 fix the pattern in other modules.

prs.title: improve: reduce desktop sidebar toggle layout work
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Expanding or collapsing the desktop sidebar repeatedly lays out the large session list and chat while its width animates.

## User Impact

The desktop sidebar opens and closes with less main-thread work. Its resting layout, 52 px rail, keyboard toggle, reduced motion, connection flyout, RTL clipping, resize behavior, and mobile drawer remain intact.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the desktop navigation at its expanded width and animate its clipping edge. Reserve the final content width once instead of interpolating grid columns and navigation width every frame. The existing layout owner retains the transition; there is no new state, cache, dependency, or eager import. A connection flyout explicitly uses the actual grid width and disables clipping while open.

The two existing E2E tests now check painted/hit-testable width and reserved content space instead of equating the physical panel width with its visible width. Existing large-catalog interaction probes remain report-only.

## Evidence

The original shared-Mac run showed a large desktop work reduction but one 1,725.58 ms automation-wall tail. Per coordinator instruction, the complete original run is retained and ten more interleaved A/B pairs were run on a quiet Blacksmith Testbox. All 160 follow-up outcomes passed. No quiet-host median/p95/min/max cell regressed over 20%, including session switching and both model-picker steps. In the combined sidebar distribution, desktop wall p95 improved 809.38 → 728.19 ms; mobile wall p95 moved 356.92 → 390.96 ms (+9.54%, inside the band). The original maximum remains visible below; its cause was not proved and it did not recur on the quiet host.

| Quiet-host sidebar metric | Desktop base → candidate | Mobile base → candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Wall median | 746.68 → 474.86 ms | 342.45 → 325.32 ms |
| Wall p95 | 841.58 → 523.47 ms | 391.88 → 392.87 ms |
| Main-thread task median | 694.18 → 396.98 ms | 146.21 → 147.26 ms |
| Script median | 164.68 → 93.03 ms | 38.82 → 39.27 ms |
| Layout median | 39.69 → 15.16 ms | 0 → 0 ms |

### Measurement contract and environment

Production renderer with synthetic Gateway: 1,000 sessions, 400 messages in each switched transcript, 1,000 models, 500 Cron jobs; desktop 1440×1000 and mobile 390×844. Serial A/B pairs use identical immutable bundles within each host. Acceptance uses untraced CDP metrics, with visible outcomes and interval requests; automation-to-assertion wall time includes Playwright/IPC/frame waits and is not INP. Existing source-mapped traces identify repeated style/layout during the width transition. No clocks or transport delays were simulated.

Original host: Darwin arm64, 32 logical CPUs, Chromium 156.0.8078.4, load 31.62 / 22.72 / 22.09. Follow-up: Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01m5jv97ecattsyhfsge96q0ef`, Linux x64, **4 observed CPUs** and about 15 GB usable RAM (the requested tier did not establish delivered capacity), Chromium 151.0.7922.0; initial load 0.47 / 0.16 / 0.05, benchmark manifest 0.63 / 0.21 / 0.09. [Testbox run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39864371066).

Cross-host combined distributions are the requested decision aid, not a controlled same-machine latency claim. Each within-host A/B comparison is controlled. Model steps were additional guard cells in the follow-up (n=10/side); sidebar and session-switch combine to n=20/side.

The timed bundles are the preserved candidate on `78b12ecec7a0383293cb351114d1a3820e4cc470`: baseline index SHA-256 `de56ae91b1c321d5f01c956c4c708258f4fbd4b10239209c24523d2ea2871b0d`, candidate `e9237b7cac733682a1397fe30c69435e0be1224b7dfd6bff0770589161149098`. The candidate patch was committed as `9e0192012d5`, then current main `3412694c197` was merged without changing these four files. Final-head builds/checks use `0cf06731554`.

prs.title: fix(gateway): renaming a session group takes 230 ms on a three-agent Gateway
prs.body:
Closes #167716

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: renaming a session group takes about 230 ms on a Gateway with three configured agents and ten on-disk agent stores, even when the group holds one session.

## User Impact

User impact: group rename and delete actions return promptly even when databases from retired agents remain on disk. Empty groups do not wait for unrelated session stores. Web and native clients need no changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The membership snapshot already identifies the stores that hold members of the group. Sweep only those stores instead of every store discovered on disk, including retired agents' stores.

Retirement still rereads all stores in its transaction and refuses to retire a group that has members. If a session is assigned in a skipped store while the mutation runs, it keeps the source group and the request can be retried.

## Evidence

Session-group regression suite: **26 tests passed**. Core production typecheck and the owning Gateway test typecheck pass.

Regression tests in `src/gateway/session-groups.test.ts`, run with the source change reverted and then enabled:

| Test | Source change reverted | With the change |
|---|---|---|
| "sweeps only the stores that hold members of the group" | `expected [ 'main', 'other' ] to deeply equal [ 'main' ]` | One sweep for the rename; none for the empty group |
| "retains a group when a member is assigned in a store the sweep skipped" | Rename resolves because the later sweep moves the late member | Rename rejects with "still has members"; the late member keeps the old group, and a retry moves it and retires the group |

Regression coverage exercises skipped unrelated stores, late assignments in skipped stores, retained source membership, and a successful retry. Category writes preserve session recency and catalog retirement retains its independent membership check.

**Timing:** fresh temporary state per variant, ten real SQLite agent stores, three configured agents, and one member in the renamed/deleted group. Each cell reports the median of three repeated requests after an initial warmup, with the observed range in parentheses.

| Operation | Main | With the change |
|---|---:|---:|
| Delete an empty group, one process with real SQLite workers | 186 ms (178–259) | 10 ms (9–10) |
| Rename a one-member group, loopback Gateway RPC | 228 ms (220–230) | 26 ms (24–73) |
| Delete an empty group, loopback Gateway RPC | 237 ms (212–244) | 16 ms (15–22) |
| Delete a one-member group, loopback Gateway RPC | 279 ms (262–314) | 21 ms (21–28) |

AI-assisted: Claude Code and Codex.

prs.title: fix: preserve native CLI sessions across completion turns
prs.body:
Related: #178982

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes native CLI conversations losing their session when an owner/client turn is followed by an internal completion turn and then another owner turn.

## User Impact

Tool declarations stay stable across those turns, while execution still checks current owner authority, client capabilities, and delivery context. No configuration migration is required. This is a shared-runtime fix, not a Claude-only fix. Focused boundary tests cover the changed contracts, and contributor-supplied authenticated Claude CLI evidence covers owner → completion → owner continuity on runtime head `2edffaf5d811`; the later CI-repair head `e5146f94ffa8` changes no runtime implementation. The current integration head `84c9eb5777a0` incorporates pinned main `013240515205` and preserves this fix across upstream lifecycle and tool-refusal changes. Earlier live runs remain prior-head evidence, not exact-head reruns of this integration. Contributor-supplied follow-up evidence also covers production-transport authorization, read-result rejection after revocation, and a stable-release upgrade. Contributor evidence on `c19837bc3077` records no fork dispatch or binding write when a registered native fork is interrupted during awaited preparation, alongside a successful allowed control; its mechanism and timing limits are recorded below.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep turn-dependent authorization at execution instead of adding and removing tools from the session catalog. This covers core tools, Codex tools, capability-gated plugin tools, and ClickClack discovery, and preserves updated native-session bindings after completion turns.

The adoption also repairs exec background-parameter schema drift, preserves class-backed plugin descriptors while gating callbacks, and avoids reporting an already-committed Codex fork as failed after a late ownership change. It adds no tool-name hash exemptions. The shared callback override replaces duplicate wrapping logic; remaining growth is the complete call-time authorization cutover and regression coverage.

Contribution: adapted from @Marvinthebored's [recovery branch](https://github.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/tree/fix/178982-stable-tool-declarations), with the reported exec regression and independent-review findings repaired.

## Work sessions

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/16662a3f-9198-4c14-b09e-c08323bfd5a4)

## Evidence

- [Live fork/revocation proof from @Marvinthebored](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179363#issuecomment-6344815555), built from `c19837bc3077`: an owner agent turn invokes the registered `codex_threads` fork with `attach: true` through the Control UI while an app-server wrapper holds the preparatory `thread/read` for 30 seconds. With `chat.abort` or `sessions.reset` during the hold, the recorded outcome is no subsequent `thread/fork`, no binding row, and no additional rollout. The allowed control with the same hold dispatches the fork, writes an active binding, and adds a rollout; a non-owner direct invocation is gated before any app-server request. This is contributor-run production-path evidence, not an independent rerun in this sandbox. The linked comment includes the request trace and observed state, and offers redacted raw files.
- [Authenticated live continuity proof from @Marvinthebored](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179363#issuecomment-6316094871): an isolated macOS Gateway driven through the Control UI reproduced a `reason=prompt-tools` native-session reset on base `f29ecf310b2c` (including a second control run). On exact PR head `2edffaf5d811`, with the built revision checked via `dist/build-info.json`, owner → subagent completion → owner turns all resumed one parent Claude CLI session with no reset. This is contributor-run evidence, not a run performed in this sandbox. Supplemental production observations and the 774-test batch include additional local patches and are not treated as exact-head proof.
- [Follow-up live authority and upgrade proof from @Marvinthebored](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179363#issuecomment-6331081185), on runtime head `2edffaf5d811` (unchanged by `e5146f94ffa8`): owner calls succeed; non-owner calls to `codex_plugins` are gated without app-server traffic; read-only callers fail the transport scope check; webhook turns without operator authority cannot invoke either protected tool. Owner → non-owner → owner agent turns retain one native session, whereas the base control resets twice. Session creation by an `operator.write` agent turn succeeds on both base and head and is not treated as an authorization regression.
- The same follow-up reports shared-token rotation while a read-only `plugin/list` call is pending: the direct invoke returns HTTP 403, `Gateway requester authority changed`, without returning the list. An owner-authorized abort also stops the agent turn without plugin data reaching its transcript; a non-owner abort is rejected. These runs establish result rejection, not prevention of an already-issued read or pre-write revocation.
- Stable-upgrade comparison in that follow-up: state created by npm `openclaw@2026.10.5` is snapshotted and restored separately for base and PR builds. Doctor repairs/migration and config validation agree across builds; the agent database moves from version 25 to 31 after the reported two Doctor repair passes. Both builds retain the pre-upgrade codeword and transcript events and rewrite the native binding to the session serving the resumed turn. Both have the same one-time `prompt-tools` reset after upgrade and no reset on the second turn. This is contributor-run evidence with detailed output in the linked comment, not an independent rerun here; raw logs are offered there on request.
- Formal SDK API comparison completed on `f29ecf310b2c` → `2edffaf5d811`: one added export (`tool-plugin.gateAgentToolExecution`), 158 exports affected through reachable declarations, and no removed exports or entrypoint changes. The five distinct declaration deltas add the gating helper/availability predicate and the returned `sandboxSessionPolicy` field; acknowledgement digest `bb6f245c`. Both frozen-revision renders and temporary-worktree cleanup completed successfully.
- Full production build, SDK declaration build/export integrity, core and extension source typechecks, and extension-test typecheck passed.
- Focused regression batch: 26 files / 509 tests passed. Repair-focused reruns also passed; their overlapping test counts are not added to that total.
- The class-descriptor and post-commit fork regressions failed before their repairs and passed afterward. Owner/completion/owner preparation verifies stable declarations, tool hash, and native binding.
- Touched-file lint, formatting, docs checks, and whitespace checks passed. Final independent review found no actionable P0–P2 findings.
- The publication candidate was checked against the complete reviewed patch, including both new source files.
- CI repairs in `e5146f94ffa8` resolve the four actionable findings in [the prior ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179363#issuecomment-6314324989): Gateway consumers now assert retained declarations and call-time denial, including unchanged persisted state/no handler or kickoff; two mocks preserve real module exports, with their two retired ratchet entries removed; SDK budgets account for exactly the already-added gating helper (+1 public export, +1 callable export), with no new exemption. No runtime implementation changed from the contributor-proven head `2edffaf5d811`.
- Repair validation: all five affected suites passed (48 tests total: SDK surface 6, session creation 25, safe bins 2, rename 2, construction routing 13); three affected core-test compiler graphs and scripts typecheck passed; touched lint, formatting, mock-factory ratchet, and whitespace checks passed.
- [ClawSweeper’s completed exact-head re-review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179363#issuecomment-6314324989) on `84c9eb5777a0b3f3380c569ad9e759d01369f2f7` (2026-10-22 22:44 UTC) reports **Before merge: None; Findings: None; Security: None** and **Ready for maintainer review**. It confirms the prior conflict request is resolved and that scheduler-scoped reads, private refusal receipts, execution availability metadata, and guarded binding settlement survive the integration. Contributor proof remains sufficient with its prior-head, contributor-run, and mechanism/timing qualifications preserved below; no additional proof is requested. The re-review acknowledgement is complete. The review’s CI-pending sentence was written before CI settled; the exact-head result below supersedes that snapshot. This is a maintainer handoff, not a merge or merge authorization.

- Earlier main integration `996b68b74cc8`: integrated pinned main `ae50346e0df0`. Resolved the SDK export-budget/facade and widget-schema conflicts while retaining upstream `openRecord`/`ToolArgumentValidationError` exports and widget inlining, plus this PR's stable declarations and call-time checks. The first targeted run caught a duplicate `isAgentToolExecutionAvailable` export introduced by the merge; the equivalent duplicate was removed and the run passed. All seven selected test files pass (widget, SDK surface/facade, and prompt-prefix stability), as do core/scripts typechecks, touched lint with zero warnings/errors, formatting, and whitespace checks. The four integration-repair files were read back from the published head and match the tested workspace. GitHub reported that head mergeable at publication. An additional local review attempt aborted without a verdict; the completed prior-head ClawSweeper review remains distinct from this mechanical integration.

- Post-integration CI repair `c19837bc3077`: [the core test-type job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39769429948/job/119794195771) and [the affected Node-test job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39769429948/job/119793652665) failed for the same stale `loadSessionEntry` reference in the session-rename test. Four calls now use the existing `sessionToolsEntry` fixture helper, which delegates to the same state accessor; assertions are unchanged. The Gateway-root test compiler reproduced all four TS2304 errors before the repair and passes afterward. Both session-rename tests pass, as do touched-file lint (zero warnings/errors), formatting, and whitespace checks. The published commit was read back: exactly one test file, four substitutions, no runtime change.

- Current main integration `84c9eb5777a0`: resolved all three textual conflicts against pinned main `013240515205`. Retained upstream scheduler-scoped automation reads and private refusal receipts, together with the PR's descriptor-preserving callbacks and execution availability checks. Upstream removed heartbeat turn paths; the now-obsolete `preserveCliSessionBinding` / `preserveBinding` argument chain is removed rather than restoring suppression of accepted completion bindings. The existing cold preserved-state regression fails if the upstream suppression is retained, then passes with this integration. All 129 tests in five focused files pass (four runner shards, 214.47 seconds): CLI attempts, CLI admission/settlement, prompt-prefix stability, turn authority including scheduler reads, and Code Mode refusal delivery. The scoped test/compiler graph, seven-file lint (zero warnings/errors), formatting, and whitespace checks also pass. Independent local review reported no actionable P0–P2 findings; one input chunk contained only status/path metadata and the other the selected staged source diff, so this is a scoped source review, not independent execution. The complete candidate is 59 files (+1,253/-500) against the pinned base; the seven integration repair files were read back byte-for-byte against the tested workspace. No migration, permission expansion, or replacement authorization mechanism is introduced.

**Documented proof limitations:**

- Parts 1–2 establish unauthorized-caller rejection and rejection of a read result after revocation. Part 3 now exercises abort/reset during a writing tool's awaited preparation and records no later fork dispatch or binding persistence. It does not isolate which mechanism stopped the operation: the model received an MCP disconnect, the wrapper records requests rather than read responses, and reset also aborted the active run. It therefore does not independently prove the specific live-authority assertions fired. Revocation between the fork response and binding commit, device-token revocation, and a mid-call owner-status change were not tested. ClawSweeper accepted this outcome-based proof with those limits; no bypass was observed and it requests no additional proof.
- The stable-upgrade evidence now supplied preserves conversation data and functional continuity, but not the identical native-session ID across the first upgraded turn: both base and head reset once when the tool catalog changes. No PR-specific migration or data loss was observed in that comparison. The earlier review identifies no concrete data-compatibility defect and confirms no schema or serialized field is added.
- All 29 core-test compiler graphs passed, but the aggregate command failed its existing 720-root budget preflight (observed counts 722–728). This patch does not change that root configuration or core test-file membership.
- The dirty-source ClickClack cold-import screening run was unqualified; no performance improvement is claimed.
- The earlier local review attempt for integration `996b68b74cc8` aborted without producing a verdict and is not counted as passing. The current `84c9eb5777a0` candidate received the scoped local review described above.

**Current-head CI:** green on integration head `84c9eb5777a0b3f3380c569ad9e759d01369f2f7` (verified 2026-10-22 after CI completed at 22:58 UTC). The [CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39866175282) and [aggregate gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39866175282/job/120137109936) passed: “No failed or timed-out jobs” and “Full CI validated the immutable workflow revision.” Every selected prerequisite group succeeded; the known-main-red exemption was false. The [commit-status CI gate, dependency review, and security-sensitive review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39868638271) also passed. The completed observer’s fully paginated 22:58:59 UTC snapshot contained 146 exact-head checks (83 passed, 62 skipped, 1 neutral), with none failed or pending; the parent independently verified the aggregate log and successful status gates rather than treating its capped managed check list as complete. GitHub reports this head conflict-free (`mergeable: true`, merge state `clean`). The PR remains open and unmerged for maintainer review.

**Prior test-repair CI:** green on exact test-repair head `c19837bc30774068cb8b5c33bab52f39cc525ae3` (verified 2026-10-22). The [CI aggregate gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39771467896/job/119809335776) passed with “No failed or timed-out jobs” and “Full CI validated the immutable workflow revision”; all selected prerequisite groups succeeded, with no known-main-red exemption. The [commit-status CI gate, dependency review, and security-sensitive review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39774344448) also passed. Both previously failing jobs—[core test types](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39771467896/job/119801377568) and [compact-small-16 tests](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39771467896/job/119800765591)—now pass, as do all three PostgreSQL conformance shards. The final managed check inventory is capped/truncated, so no complete final check count is claimed; completion is established by the inspected aggregate gate and successful commit-status gate. Integration head `996b68b74cc8` had the two same-cause failures documented above; these were repaired on `c19837bc3077`. These CI results do not validate the later `84c9eb5777a0` integration.

**Prior-head CI:** repaired head `e5146f94ffa8` was green (verified 2026-10-22): [CI run 39699950080](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39699950080) succeeded; all 199 check runs in the 10:46 UTC fully paginated snapshot settled (86 passed, 112 skipped, 1 neutral, zero failures or pending checks), including all three PostgreSQL conformance shards. [The CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39702109032), dependency review, and security-sensitive review statuses passed. prs.title: improve(ui): select existing photos and videos from the composer
prs.body:
Part of #180298.

## What Problem This Solves

Videos are discoverable through File but excluded from the explicitly named Photo action in the shared composer.

## User Impact

Chat and New Session gain **Photos & videos**, which requests existing images and videos together with multiple selection where supported. Intentionally image-only composers keep their existing image-only picker and reject videos; Safari retains **Attach…**. Camera’s **Upload photo** remains image-only.

**Draft proposal, not ready or approved for merge.** Production-browser and sanitized visual proof are recorded below. Vitor can still test on his own OpenClaw; native iOS/Android chooser behavior is not certified by emulation.

This is only the existing-media slice. Camera capture and unrestricted File behavior, including its video route, are preserved. Safari gains the explicit media action beside its existing **Attach…** route. This does not solve or accept native gallery/camera duplication inside Files as the final umbrella UX; clean Files routing and capture capability labels remain separate workstreams. No generic Attach-only fallback is introduced.

## Why This Change Was Made

The media action uses a dedicated input and the existing admission, preparation, preview, draft and send owners. Keeping the image-only input protects Camera’s existing caller. Opening a picker does not upload anything or start video compression; oversized-video compression still requires explicit consent. No custom gallery, recorder, state store or permission changes are added.

Proposed and directed by **Vitor Cepeda Lopes (@TheAngryPit)**. AI-assisted implementation.

## Work sessions

- [Original discussion with @TheAngryPit](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/dfd1f162-7d1d-4dc0-a7e0-0a65c7817bd8)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/e3844cef-eda3-469a-83d3-fbadcd26fb8e)

## Evidence

- **Published/tested-source head:** `224dc4e8f8b6b080006fe57dd123cb9ff4c0e9dd`, branch `openclaw/tidal-crab`, prepared official-main base `8e6990a1820ff62f9c92e008df7ede471efbf1d0`. All 12 changed files were fetched from the immutable published commit and match the locally tested/reviewed source byte-for-byte. Publisher: `roboclaw-bot`; every published commit carries the required TheAngryPit co-author trailer.
- **35 production-browser scenarios passed across four files:** actual mixed image/video selection and explicit sends through Chat and New Session, cancel/reselect and draft retention, initial hidden-input styling, activation geometry across viewport changes, camera lifecycle/native-input routing, video previews/release, invalid media, size handling and explicit compression consent. This is the actual built Control UI with synthetic Mock Gateway responses and inspected wire requests, not a separate mock UI or a live provider-delivery test.
- Browser run: **82.20 s Vitest / 94.064 s complete command**. Existing platform/geometry file: 25 scenarios, 51.299 s; it exercises real dropdown gestures, mounted input geometry, viewport transitions and camera boundaries that jsdom cannot prove. prs.title: fix(scripts): clean older PR clones after template refresh
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Follow-up to #181022: a clean failed PR clone can still be refused by cleanup after its shared template refreshes to a newer commit.

## User Impact

Older failed clones can be removed through the supported cleanup command while preserving operator changes, untracked and ignored files, and clones whose original seed can no longer be verified.

## Why This Change Was Made

The template backlink proves provenance, but its current index is not the old clone's baseline. Cleanup now builds a temporary index from the PR's retained `temp/pr-<number>` seed, refreshes that private index, and checks tracked content and all untracked files. The shared template index stays untouched. The existing metadata, live-cwd, operation-lock and final directory checks remain in charge of deletion.

## Evidence

prs.title: improve(ui): download about 3.3% less JavaScript over gzip
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/121497. Preserves the Brotli quality-10 improvement in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/180972.

## What Problem This Solves

Control UI clients using gzip download more JavaScript than necessary with the current build-time encoder.

## User Impact

**About 3.3% less complete-route JavaScript over gzip, with identical decoded assets and unchanged requests.** Brotli quality 10, HTTP encoding, browser code, and performance budgets are unchanged. No migration or user action is required.

The tradeoff is build-only CPU: the measured gzip stage adds about 2.27 seconds wall / 2.19 CPU-seconds per 40.3 MB corpus. This is not a page-load latency claim. The new dependency is an exact, integrity-pinned WASM package, not a host-native library; cross-OS validation and reproducible upstream WASM compilation are not claimed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use `libdeflate@0.1.0` at one uniform level 11 in the existing sidecar producer. Level 12 saves only another 1,685 bytes over all 2,076 top-level JavaScript/CSS assets while costing about 1.56 seconds more per encoding pass. Keep final-on-disk input reads, source-map exclusions, four-at-a-time compression and joined failure cleanup, and existing cache invalidation. Pako remains only as a development/test comparison, not an alternative production encoder.

## Evidence

Acceptance rule, set before measurements: meaningful gzip savings around 3% at initial entry, ready New Session/Chat, and first session creation; identical decoded assets/request graph and Brotli; unchanged strict gates. Compare actual portable levels 11/12 on the same current-main build, not previous native-library measurements.

Source baseline: `6893519fbd6062612b2c0c9e809369608b3aadc2`. Same-source production builds, Linux x64, Node 26.12.1. Browser rows use the real production HTTP handler/background file owner over loopback, fresh Chromium contexts, gzip responses, synthetic RPCs and a valid strict-JSON config fixture. They are not live-provider/full-Gateway authorization tests.

| JavaScript workload | Requests (unchanged) | Pako baseline | WASM level 11 | Savings |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Initial entry | 7 | 315,952 B | 305,152 B | 3.418% |
| Ready New Session | 20 | 957,289 B | 925,674 B | 3.303% |
| Ready Chat | 25 | 1,421,151 B | 1,374,486 B | 3.284% |
| New Session → first created chat, cumulative | 32 | 1,542,453 B | 1,491,728 B | 3.289% |

- Browser captures have identical asset paths/raw bytes/Brotli bytes, zero page/request failures, and a usable composer after first creation. Every requested JS/CSS gzip response matches its sidecar and decodes to the original file.
- All **2,080 gzip + 2,080 Brotli sidecars** decode identically. Every gzip sidecar re-encodes byte-identically on **Node 24.22.1 and 26.12.1, Linux x64**; gzip headers contain no time/name/host variation. All raw runtime assets and Brotli bytes are unchanged. One diagnostic Mermaid sourcemap varies only in generated Rolldown reference IDs; maps have no compression sidecars. No encoder code appears in browser source maps.
- `pnpm build`, actual UI builds, unchanged strict `pnpm ui:check-performance`, sidecar validation, targeted UI-config/test typecheck, focused lint (zero warnings/errors), formatting and `git diff --check` pass. Canonical `pnpm test` runs all **55 tests in four config/precompression/cache/build files** successfully (68.38 s wall, including artifact-lock waits). The changed stronger-gzip regression is red on base (25,158 is not less than 25,158) and green on the candidate. Test CI seconds are pending.
- A subsequent build reuses the content cache and preserves the new sidecars (3.61 s, including validation). The configuration, UI manifest and lockfile already belong to the cache key; no new cache exists.
- **Completed independent AutoReview:** Codex AutoReview, P0–P2, full compression/build/cache-owner context: `scoped-clean`, no actionable findings. The reviewer checked source and supplied evidence, not independently rerun tests. Cross-OS/architecture and upstream compiler reproducibility remain validation gaps for hosted review/CI; no merge or deployment is requested.

<details>
<summary>Portable encoder qualification and timing details</summary>

Exact npm integrity matches the lockfile. The MIT license includes wrapper and upstream attribution. The [published source revision](https://codeberg.org/EvanHahn/libdeflate.js/src/commit/a5f02605f65b67c9d094f1f4a5cbafe38c226969) pins [libdeflate 1.25](https://github.com/ebiggers/libdeflate/tree/c8c56a20f8f621e6a966b716b31f1dedab6a41e3). Its checked-in Emscripten recipe produces single-file, synchronous WASM with no filesystem dependency; the npm package has no production dependencies or install script. Compiler version is not pinned upstream, and the distributed binary was not independently rebuilt. Package age admission passed without an override. This is not the earlier native libdeflate 1.23 experiment.

`node ui/scripts/bench-gzip.mjs <built-dist> 5`: 2,076 top-level JS/CSS files, 40,263,998 raw bytes. Five serial interleaved passes per encoder; decode/hashing and file I/O outside the timer. Shared host: 128 available CPUs, initial load 42.27/27.75/20.98.

| Encoder | Total gzip bytes | Wall median / p95 (range), seconds | CPU median / p95, seconds |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| Pako 9, legacy hash, memLevel 6 | 12,180,203 | 2.964 / 3.356 (2.942–3.356) | 3.038 / 3.362 |
| **WASM libdeflate 11** | **11,750,210** | **5.232 / 5.370 (5.157–5.370)** | **5.232 / 5.384** |
| WASM libdeflate 12 | 11,748,525 | 6.796 / 7.509 (6.590–7.509) | 6.789 / 7.278 |

Level 11 saves 429,993 B / 3.530% across this corpus. Eleven tiny assets grow by just 13 bytes combined (maximum 3 B); no per-file policy/fallback is added. Full standalone builds were 47.56 s baseline and 29.12 s candidate on a busy shared host, **one run each**; that variance does not establish a build speedup. The encoder-only paired measurement is the cost comparison.

Strict build-manifest route accounting independently passes: New Session 953,681 → 922,126 B at 19 requests; Chat 1,417,543 → 1,370,938 B at 24 requests. Browser-ready captures above include the additional observed runtime request instead of hiding it.

Simplification: replace the encoder call at its existing owner, with no new production state, worker, configuration, or serving path. The additional script exists only to make the encoder cost/size comparison repeatable; existing regression suites retain lifecycle and cache proof.

</details>

Credit: Requested by @jacobtomlinson.

## Work sessions

- [Original discussion with @jacobtomlinson](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/9022d7f6-f546-48d1-9b98-dd26621e322d)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/cdb9849e-f669-4d67-abd7-b9ab21aa0e4a)

## What Problem This Solves

Large model catalogs and expanded automation inventories do unnecessary work during warm interactions. A production-renderer audit identifies the costs and removes two measured sources of waste.

## User Impact

The 1,000-model picker uses about one-third less script time. Filtering 500 loaded automation jobs uses 42–44% less script time for a single pasted query. Existing routes, selectors, keyboard behavior, action authority, and visible layout stay intact. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Model search invalidated every option binding even when its scalar presentation facts were unchanged. Scoped Solid memos now stop those unchanged values at the row. Automation rows mounted three hidden menu items apiece; the existing `Menu lazy` contract removes 1,500 hidden items and 3,000 DOM nodes until a menu is opened. First-open menu behavior is covered separately.

The first typing comparison exposed variable request coalescing: desktop median intermediate `cron.list` calls rose from 13.5 to 16.5; mobile 15 to 15.5. That burst comparison was rejected as unequal work. The accepted filter comparison uses one pasted query, asserts exactly one request, and preserves `cron-search-typing` as a separate diagnostic. prs.title: fix(qianfan): DeepSeek replies arrive all at once instead of streaming
prs.body:
Closes #163657

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: replies from Qianfan-served DeepSeek models are held until the full response is generated and then delivered as one block, even with block streaming on. Two-platform reproduction in the issue (2026.9.5 on Windows, 2026.9.7 on Linux), with a cURL control showing the raw API emits proper SSE deltas, so the loss is client-side.

## User Impact

User impact: Qianfan users on DeepSeek models (deepseek-v4-pro, deepseek-v3.2) see replies stream incrementally again, matching the same models through the volcengine provider. No config or migration needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The qianfan manifest had no `providerRequest` block at all, so capability resolution treated the endpoint as not supporting streaming usage and every qianfan request went out without `stream_options.include_usage`. The volcengine provider, which serves the same DeepSeek family through the same openai-completions adapter, already declares `supportsStreamingUsage` for both of its providers. Qianfan's v2 chat completions API documents `stream_options.include_usage` on the exact base URL in the manifest (`https://qianfan.baidubce.com/v2`), so the declaration is safe for the whole catalog, ERNIE models included.

The declaration is provider-level (the manifest schema has no per-model flag), which matches how volcengine declares it.

## Evidence

Request-shaping path traced end to end on current main (`ccab514b100`): manifest `providerRequest.providers.qianfan.openAICompletions.supportsStreamingUsage` → plugin metadata snapshot → `resolveProviderRequestCapabilities` (`supportsOpenAICompletionsStreamingUsageCompat`, src/agents/provider-attribution.ts) → `resolveOpenAICompletionsCompat` (`supportsUsageInStreaming`, packages/ai) → `params.stream_options = { include_usage: true }` in packages/ai/src/transports/openai-completions-params.ts. Without the manifest entry, the defaults resolver cannot turn this on for qianfan: it is a configured non-OpenAI endpoint, so the `!usesConfiguredNonOpenAIEndpoint` fallback never fires.

- New manifest contract test in `extensions/qianfan/index.test.ts`, mirroring the volcengine one: `pnpm test extensions/qianfan/index.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` → 4 passed, 22.9s wall.
- `pnpm test src/plugins/bundled-manifest-contract-plugins.test.ts src/plugins/manifest-registry.provider-metadata.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` → passed.
- `pnpm test test/plugins/bundled-provider-auth-literal-parity.test-support.ts --maxWorkers=1` → passed.
- autoreview (codex, branch vs origin/main): scoped-clean, no accepted/actionable findings, patch assessed correct.

Gap I want to be explicit about: I don't have a Qianfan API key, so the live end-to-end streaming check rides on the issue's two-platform reproduction and the reporter's cURL control. The request-side half of the fix is fully traced in source; the exact spot where a missing usage chunk turns into held-back delivery is the one link I could not pin from source alone (the same flag is the only difference from the working volcengine path for this model family). A maintainer with a key can confirm in one run by watching a qianfan DeepSeek reply stream.


## Runtime proof (added 2026-10-04)

The gap note above is now closed. Ran the gateway against an isolated mock that emulates the reported Qianfan DeepSeek quirk (usage-only final chunk only when asked, otherwise one held block), at head 358cb449:

- PR state: request carries `"stream_options":{"include_usage":true}` (verbatim body logged by the mock), channel delivers 12 incremental deltas over ~3.3 s.
- Control with the manifest boolean flipped off on the same head: request has no `stream_options` at all, channel sits silent 4.8 s then delivers the whole reply as one delta, the reported behavior.

Full timelines and setup details: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/163698#issuecomment-5971723272

prs.title: fix(ui): retain completed turn recaps after delayed session updates
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes completed chat turns permanently losing their runtime/token recap when delayed session state briefly presents anonymous activity after local run retirement. This reproduces the managed-media `.chat-turn-recap` timeout seen in #180809 and #180889.

## User Impact

Completed answers retain their recap through that handoff. A newly submitted turn, a different identified run, or a session/agent/connection change still replaces the watched turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway can legitimately publish active session state without an exact run set while terminal persistence finishes. After the local terminal status mask expires, that row can produce an anonymous working indicator. The recap owner previously treated it as a new turn and discarded the run it had observed. Later matching terminal metadata then had no watched run to complete.

The recap owner now retains that observation through passive anonymous activity. The transcript supplies explicit new-input intent from its existing visible queue. No deadline increases, polling, new state owner, or Gateway persistence changes.

## Evidence

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Original CI failures | Both have zero recap DOM nodes, a cleared local run, and matching persisted assistant / done-row identities with finite runtime. |
| Mounted pane regression | Red on the base at the missing recap; green with the fix. Exercises real run adoption, `chat.final`, the five-second status-mask expiry, deferred descriptor reconciliation, and the retained assistant bubble. All 3 tests in the file pass. |
| Existing recap contracts | All 27 `chat-progress.test.ts` tests pass. |
| Existing transcript rendering | All existing 27 rendering cases pass. |
| UI typecheck / targeted lint / formatting | Pass. The first CI run caught optional diagnostics returning `undefined`; normalized them to `null` and the exact failing E2E test-type graph now passes locally. |
| Production Knip | Pass. |
| Independent review | No actionable P0–P2 findings. |
| Linux real-Gateway stress | **Base: 1/50 failures (2%); fix: 0/50.** The base failure at iteration 14 is the exact recap timeout with matching done/assistant IDs and a 485 ms terminal runtime. |
| Startup | 316,383 → 316,396 B gzip (+13 B, within 64 B build variance); 1 → 1 CSS request. |
| Chat route | 1,417,825 → 1,417,863 B gzip (+38 B, within build variance). |

Both isolated Linux builds report the existing startup-baseline violation (316,272 B limit); the candidate adds no bytes beyond the allowed build variance. Both stress runs requested the same 16-vCPU Testbox class and received 4 CPUs / approximately 15.4 GiB RAM. They used cached compiler output and unchanged test assertions and timeouts. [Base run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39859947926), [candidate run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39859860760). The wrapper recorded settled command exits of 1 and 0, respectively; delegated Actions runs may show cancellation when their leases are stopped. The tested production commit is `c6f4a105156`; later commits only strengthen the regression test and normalize absent diagnostic fields.

Production LOC: 1,031 → 1,044 (+13). Test/E2E LOC: 1,129 → 1,288 (+159). The added fixture exercises the actual pane lifecycle instead of assigning rendering flags. Effects, render effects, listeners, DOM queries, flush calls, and owner APIs in the touched production files remain 0 → 0.

Before/after screenshots below use only the synthetic managed-media fixture. The before capture is the naturally reproduced timeout; the after capture includes its restored recap.

prs.title: fix(cron): session automations ignore the selected context window on native runs
prs.body:
Closes #177523

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: automations that run in an existing conversation (`sessionTarget: "session:<key>"`) ignore that conversation's selected context window on native (non-CLI) runtimes, so a session set to 200K is budgeted, compacted and sized as 1M whenever a scheduled turn runs in it.

## User Impact

User impact: a scheduled turn in a session pinned to 200K now runs with the same 200K budget as the user's own turns in that session (auto-compaction threshold, provider-side compaction trigger and the recorded session budget all follow the selection). Sessions without a selection, isolated jobs and CLI-backed runs keep their current behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cron prompt executor passed `sessionEntry.contextWindow` only on its CLI branch; the embedded runner reads the selection solely from its run params, so native cron runs fell back to the model's default window. The selection now lives in the executor's shared run-param builder, the same shape `openclaw agent` already uses, so every runtime path receives it. Production change is one line moved (+1/-1).

## Evidence

Real behavior, isolated Gateway (fresh `HOME` / state / config, own port) inside an offline network namespace: the provider's API host resolves to a local TLS stand-in that records request bodies; synthetic API key; external connectivity blocked (`ENETUNREACH`). A shipped catalog model that declares selectable windows `200k` / `1m` (default `1m`), with an explicit `models.providers.<provider>.models` entry for it on its default route. Two sessions created via `sessions.create`: one with `contextWindow: "200k"`, one without. One `--session session:<key>` automation per session, run with `openclaw cron run <id> --wait`.

Request sent by the automation turn (`context_management.edits`) and the persisted session budget after the run:

```text
session                 build                          compact trigger   tool-clearing trigger   stored contextTokens
200K-pinned             before (106f720e24f)           700000            300000 / 50000          1000000
200K-pinned             after  (7dfbe38ac70)           140000            60000 / 12500           200000
no selection (control)  before (106f720e24f)           700000            300000 / 50000          1000000
no selection (control)  after  (7dfbe38ac70)           700000            300000 / 50000          1000000
```

Before the fix the pinned session behaves exactly like the control (1M budget although it stores `contextWindow: "200k"`); after it, only the pinned session moves to its 200K window.

Regression test (`src/cron/isolated-agent/run.session-key-isolation.test.ts`): a stored `session:<key>` entry with `contextWindow: "200k"` must reach the runner on both runtimes. On the base the embedded case fails (`contextWindow` missing from the runner request) and the CLI case passes; with the fix both pass (18/18 in the file).

Local gates on the touched files: `oxfmt --check` clean; `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` pass; `git diff --check` clean; the whole `src/cron/isolated-agent` suite plus the cron auth-continuity integration test pass (54 files, 471 tests). `oxlint` reports `max-lines` 701/700 on `run-prompt-executor.ts`; the base reports the identical count (the file is already over the cap on `main`, and this change is line-neutral), so it is not introduced here.

What was not tested: CLI-backed automation runs end to end (needs a CLI login; that branch already passed the value and is covered by the test case); fallback attempts to a model without the selected option (handled by the existing resolver, which falls back to that model's default).

AI-assisted; the contributor reviewed the change and is responsible for it.

## What Problem This Solves

Agent execution and host utilities expose private helpers and modules that have only one production consumer.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change. Auth and tool authority, public SDK/CLI/config/protocol contracts, lazy imports, and durable user state remain unchanged. The standalone session-memory backend and its machinery are untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

prs.title: fix(openai): GPT-Live Talk bypasses the managed proxy on egress-restricted hosts
prs.body:
Fixes #175794

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: GPT-Live Talk fails with "Realtime provider error" on egress-restricted hosts, because its media WebSocket bypasses the managed proxy (`proxy.proxyUrl`) and dials OpenAI directly.

## User Impact

User impact: Talk with a GPT-Live model over `gateway-relay` and API-key auth now connects through the configured managed proxy. If the proxy refuses the tunnel, the session fails visibly and never falls back to a direct connection. Hosts without a proxy see no change and no added startup cost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Since #154119, the GPT-Live direct media socket runs in a `worker_threads` worker so audio keeps flowing during Gateway stalls. `startProxy` installs the managed proxy through Proxyline's `installGlobalProxy`, which patches `http`/`https` and the global agents only in the JS isolate that calls it. The media worker is a separate isolate with no hooks, so `ws` dials directly. The worker does inherit the env that `startProxy` exports (`HTTP(S)_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`, `OPENCLAW_PROXY_ACTIVE`, `OPENCLAW_PROXY_CA_FILE`).

The worker now builds its `ws` agent from that inherited env with the public SDK helper `createNodeProxyAgent({ mode: "env", targetUrl })` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/fetch-runtime`. It also opens the socket with the `WebSocket` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/websocket-runtime` instead of a bare `ws` import. On Bun, bare `ws` resolves to Bun's built-in adapter, which ignores `agent`; the first revision of this PR failed the Bun CI shard for exactly that reason. `provider-websocket` received the same switch in #147085. This matches the Slack relay, which pairs the same two SDK helpers.

- **Routing policy stays with its owner.** The helper applies `NO_PROXY`, so the default `gateway-only` loopback bypass still holds, and it normalizes `wss:`→`https:`. It also resolves the managed proxy CA through the existing env fallback for runtimes that inherit only env (`resolveActiveManagedProxyTlsOptions`).
- **The worker isolation invariant holds.** The agent is built inside the worker from plain env, and no Agents or factories are cloned through `workerData`.
- **It fails closed.** A refused or broken tunnel surfaces as the worker's existing error/close path. There is no direct retry.
- **No cost without a proxy.** The helper's module graph (Proxyline, undici, fetch guard) measured about 250–280 ms of module load in the compiled build. It is imported only when the inherited env has a `*_proxy` variable. That check is a superset gate only; the helper still makes the routing decision. The SDK `WebSocket` costs about 29 ms to load, versus about 20 ms for bare `ws`.

Alternatives not taken:
- Calling core `ensureInheritedManagedProxyRoutingActive()` in the worker. It is a `src/infra` internal that extensions must not import, and it would install process-global hooks inside a media worker.
- Changing only `OpenAIRealtimeBridge`, the file named in the report. GPT-Live models use the Quicksilver bridges, so that would not reach this path.

Out of scope:
- The WebRTC path, used for OAuth/subscription models. Its media is UDP/ICE and cannot traverse an HTTP CONNECT proxy. Its call setup goes through guarded fetch in the Gateway isolate, which already honours the managed proxy. That needs separate boundary proof, as ClawSweeper noted.
- Logging the underlying provider error at warn. The worker posts a detail-free `{type:"error"}` by design (redaction), so this belongs in a follow-up.
- The main-thread `new WebSocket` fallbacks. On Node they run in the Gateway isolate, where Proxyline's patched `http.request` replaces `ws`'s `createConnection` with its agent. Under Bun, their bare `ws` imports also resolve to Bun's adapter and are not routed. That is a sibling gap across the OpenAI realtime sockets (`realtime-quicksilver-session.ts`, `realtime-quicksilver-gateway-bridge.ts`, `realtime-voice-bridge.ts`) and is better handled as a follow-up than folded into this fix.

## Evidence

**Regression tests.** They use the real `OpenAIQuicksilverWorkerSocket.create` → worker with a synthetic CONNECT proxy and a local `ws` target, in `extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket-worker.test.ts`:
1. `tunnels media through the managed proxy and exchanges audio`: default `gateway-only` env, with a target host (`gpt-live.openai.test`) that only the proxy can resolve. The test asserts `CONNECT host:port`, open, and 960 PCM bytes echoed back intact.
2. `fails closed without a direct connection when the proxy refuses the tunnel`: `loopbackMode=proxy` keeps the loopback target directly reachable, then the proxy answers 403. The test asserts close, one transport error, and **zero** target connections.

RED on `upstream/main` (964d3238270), with only the test file changed:
```
FAIL ... tunnels media through the managed proxy and exchanges audio
AssertionError: expected [] to deeply equal [ 'gpt-live.openai.test:60171' ]
FAIL ... fails closed without a direct connection when the proxy refuses the tunnel
AssertionError: expected 'open' to be 'close'
Tests  2 failed | 2 passed (4)
```
GREEN with the fix: 4/4 on Node locally.

**Bun:** there is no Bun runtime on this host, so CI's `bun:changed-extensions-config` shard is the Bun proof, and it gives a RED/GREEN pair:
- `a0765150ae3` used a bare `ws` import, which Bun resolves to its own adapter. Both new tests failed there with the main symptoms (`expected [] to deeply equal [ 'gpt-live.openai.test:40881' ]`, `expected 'open' to be 'close'`).
- `bc2a833fdb7` uses the SDK `WebSocket`. Both tests pass on Bun (211 ms and 157 ms), and the socket test files pass in full (3 files, 12 tests); see [the job log](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39078428712/job/117530540972). The two new tests take about 0.9 s and 0.8 s; the file's wall time is about 23 s with `--maxWorkers=1`, mostly Vitest transform.

**Acceptance commands** (all passing locally on Windows):
- `pnpm test extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket-worker.test.ts extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket-adapter.test.ts extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket.runtime.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 3 files, 15 tests passed.
- `pnpm test src/infra/net/node-proxy-agent.test.ts src/infra/net/proxy/proxy-lifecycle.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 2 files, 23 tests passed.
- `pnpm build`: passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions` and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`: clean. Type-aware oxlint (`run-oxlint-shards.mts --only=extensions`, `extensions/openai`) and `oxfmt --check`: clean.

**Compiled-worker proof.** After `pnpm build`, a standalone Node script imports the built adapter (`dist/extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket.js`). The adapter spawns the built `dist/extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket.worker.js`. The script points it at the synthetic proxy with exactly the env keys `applyProxyEnv` exports.

<details open>
<summary>With this PR</summary>

```
=== scenario 1: managed proxy admits the tunnel (loopbackMode=gateway-only) ===
media url: ws://gpt-live.openai.test:63609 (host is unresolvable without the proxy)
adapter spawned worker: dist/extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket.worker.js
proxy: CONNECT gpt-live.openai.test:63609 -> 200, tunnel to 127.0.0.1:63609
target: WebSocket connection #1 from 127.0.0.1:63612
adapter: open
target: session.input_audio.append (960 PCM bytes) -> echo session.output_audio.delta
adapter: received 1 audio chunk(s), first 960 bytes
adapter: close 1000
PASS: startup opened through the proxy
PASS: echoed PCM returned intact
PASS: no transport errors
PASS: exactly one target connection (the tunnel)
=== scenario 2: managed proxy refuses the tunnel (loopbackMode=proxy) ===
media url: ws://127.0.0.1:63613 (directly reachable; must still go through the proxy)
adapter spawned worker: dist/extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket.worker.js
proxy: CONNECT 127.0.0.1:63613 -> 403 Forbidden (refused)
adapter: close 1006 ; errors: GPT-Live media worker transport failed
PASS: startup failed closed
PASS: adapter reported one transport error
PASS: target saw zero connections (no direct fallback)
RESULT: PASS
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Control: same build with the two agent lines removed from the compiled worker (equivalent to main)</summary>

```
=== scenario 1: managed proxy admits the tunnel (loopbackMode=gateway-only) ===
media url: ws://gpt-live.openai.test:49842 (host is unresolvable without the proxy)
adapter spawned worker: dist/extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket.worker.js
adapter: close 1006 
adapter: received 0 audio chunk(s), first 0 bytes
FAIL: startup opened through the proxy
FAIL: echoed PCM returned intact
FAIL: no transport errors
FAIL: exactly one target connection (the tunnel)
=== scenario 2: managed proxy refuses the tunnel (loopbackMode=proxy) ===
media url: ws://127.0.0.1:54452 (directly reachable; must still go through the proxy)
adapter spawned worker: dist/extensions/openai/realtime-quicksilver-socket.worker.js
target: WebSocket connection #1 from 127.0.0.1:54455
adapter: open; errors: 
FAIL: startup failed closed
FAIL: adapter reported one transport error
FAIL: target saw zero connections (no direct fallback)
RESULT: FAIL
```
</details>

No live OpenAI call was made, and none is needed for the routing boundary. The reporter's Docker/Android environment was not reproduced; the synthetic proxy stands in for their egress-restricted host.

prs.title: chore: capture worker CPU in Gateway startup benchmarks
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Gateway startup and restart CPU profiles omit workers that set their own Node startup arguments, leaving incomplete evidence when evaluating startup performance.

## User Impact

No Gateway behavior changes. Developers can capture the main thread and worker threads with the same benchmark option; restart gains the existing startup profiling option.

## Why This Change Was Made

The benchmark preload propagates profiling arguments when runtime workers replace `execArgv`. Node's default profile filenames distinguish process and thread IDs. The benchmark's sanitized child environment also preserves an explicitly disabled compile cache so baseline and candidate use the same mode.

## Evidence

A native worker capability probe reproduced the gap: passing CPU flags only to the parent emitted a main-thread profile; the preload emitted separate main and worker profiles even with explicit empty worker arguments. All 74 tests across the startup, restart, and shared benchmark suites pass. Type-aware scripts lint, formatting, and diff checks pass; independent review found no actionable findings. A `qaRuntime` build completed successfully. The initial broad lint configuration rejected the required external dependency store; the repository scripts configuration completed successfully. No product performance improvement is claimed by this instrumentation change.

### Acceptance rule, recorded before Gateway measurements

Flow: Gateway startup / restart, using the committed startup and restart workloads against exact-head `qaRuntime` builds, Node 26.12.1, isolated synthetic state, and disabled Node compile caching. The primary case is `default`; add `fiftyPlugins` if a plugin owner changes. Cold means a fresh process and fixture, not an OS filesystem-cache flush. Warm restart means the supported in-process restart signal after readiness.

Startup must reach HTTP readiness and complete the benchmark WebSocket session RPC. Restart must recover `/readyz`, with its readiness trace and successful completion. Record readiness, completion, first session RPC, restart downtime, process-tree CPU, peak RSS, and startup/restart phases where available. Capture separate `node --cpu-prof` runs for the main thread and initial workers; profiled time is not compared against unprofiled time.

Count operations first using frozen SQL harness v3.1.4, including boot, restart, and warm-turn SQL statements, requests, and main-thread SQL. Attribute imports, process spawns, repeated registry/catalog work, and serial waits before choosing a product change. Moving work to a worker or after readiness is not a total-work saving.

For a product candidate, interleave baseline and candidate ABAB with at least five samples per arm for cold startup and warm restart separately. Hold the campaign timing lock, and start timed samples only when the one-minute load is below 24. Report median, p95, and min–max. After more than one hour waiting for capacity, report counts and CPU-profile evidence with wall-clock latency explicitly unmeasured.

A candidate wins only when measured work falls and median readiness or CPU improves by at least 5%, without worsening another user-facing median or p95. Investigate smaller adverse moves rather than calling them noise; a regression of 20% or more in any cell stops the candidate. Boot/restart SQL and main-thread SQL must hold or fall; warm-turn SQL and request counts must not increase. Mandatory migrations, credential custody, admission, and integrity checks remain before the operations they protect.

### Baseline attribution on the instrumentation head

The product code matches `ce9941f4db620f6ad7ff7611ec293c8d4bc7fb1b`; only the benchmark instrumentation differs. Both frozen-harness runs passed all 14 turns, restart, and cleanup. These are two observations of the same product, not a before/after comparison:

| Observation | Whole SQL / requests / MAIN | Boot | Process-restart boot | Warm causal median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initial | 2944 / 802 / 96 | 301 / 92 / 49 | 292 / 102 / 37 | 45 / 11 / 0 |
| With source maps | 2966 / 799 / 97 | 288 / 88 / 49 | 293 / 102 / 38 | 45 / 11 / 0 |

Source maps reduced unattributed statements/requests from 2206/533 to 19/15. Boot phase boundaries and background work account for same-head variation; no reduction is claimed here.

Native diagnostic captures produced 17 startup profiles (main plus 16 workers) and 38 profiles over initial startup plus in-process restart. Both diagnostic runs exited cleanly. The loaded, profiled startup observed 11.05 s HTTP readiness, 14.68 s process-tree CPU, and 1162.9 MiB peak RSS. The loaded restart observed 9.03 s HTTP readiness and 15.69 s process-tree CPU. These single profiled observations are attribution only, not a latency baseline or A/B result.

The restart's main-thread profile attributes about 3.85 s of sampled blocking time to `isCliRuntimeProvider` enumerating all plugin setup backends from the cron migration description path. Synchronous native dependency capture and filesystem operations dominate that stack. This points to the existing targeted CLI-backend resolver as a prospective product fix; this PR does not make it. Required schema/admission, credential custody, initial session projection, and recovery ordering remain unchanged.

A supplemental module-load observer run exceeded the benchmark's shutdown deadline and is excluded from CPU/latency evidence. Existing startup traces provide import-stage attribution; the observer result is not treated as a successful profile. The completed unprofiled baseline follows.

### Completed unprofiled baseline

All ten samples were admitted with one-minute load below24 under the campaign timing lock, completing before the one-hour fallback deadline. Cold means a fresh process and fixture, with OS filesystem caches retained. These are baseline observations, not an A/B comparison.

| Metric | Cold median | Cold p95 | Cold min–max | Restart median | Restart p95 | Restart min–max |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| HTTP ready, ms | 9374.8 | 11120.2 | 9009.1–11120.2 | 5759.3 | 21981.7 | 5463.8–21981.7 |
| First session RPC, ms | 9372.1 | 11117.3 | 9043.1–11117.3 | — | — | — |
| Downtime, ms | — | — | — | 5751.5 | 21975.5 | 5457.7–21975.5 |
| Process-tree CPU, ms | 10850 | 11570 | 10160–11570 | 10440 | 15410 | 7540–15410 |
| Peak RSS, MiB | 1092.47 | 1098.59 | 1057.02–1098.59 | 1441.09 | 1466.80 | 1122.02–1466.80 |

Five samples per mode, nearest-rank p95. Keep the adverse second restart: it started at load23.06, then host load rose above40 during the run. It reached readiness in21981.7ms and consumed15410ms process-tree CPU. No observation is discarded. Every sample reached readiness. Cold shutdowns were5/5clean; restart samples1and2 exceeded the existing short teardown grace and were SIGKILLed after successful readiness. Restart samples3–5 did not. These two samples prove readiness, not clean shutdown; the separate frozen workload and original native profiles retain clean-shutdown proof.


### Open-PR overlap check

The shared inventory of 2,938 open PRs targeting main has two other PRs touching these files. Their heads were rechecked before readiness: #179929 at `cccbc6532a51bbf38b571519c1153b50d152a801` and #177141 at `c9f464482229bc5677fc8c0f8f8176ff6fc913cf`. Base-only versus base-plus-candidate `git merge-tree` keeps the same conflict paths: 4→4 and 11→11 respectively. This patch adds no conflicts.

prs.title: fix(plugins): reload edited bundled code without restarting the gateway
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: edited bundled plugin code remains stale after an explicit plugin reload, requiring a Gateway restart.

## User Impact

Operators can explicitly reload selected bundled plugins without restarting the Gateway or replacing unaffected plugin siblings. Compiled installations must rebuild first; reload does not rebuild code. Host and SDK edits still require a Gateway restart.

Native ESM graphs cannot be unloaded, so repeated explicit code replacements can retain additional graphs until process exit. Ordinary startup and inventory refresh retain the existing shared-loading path.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the existing captured-generation, worker preparation, and recovery owners only for explicit replacement IDs. Capture plugin trees and plugin-only build chunks using existing ownership metadata, while resolving host/shared imports to their canonical modules. Missing compiled ownership metadata fails with a rebuild instruction. Recovery retains the selected generation’s source bytes and ownership facts. No new configuration, dependencies, or parallel reload subsystem.

The simplification pass keeps capture policy in one module and preserves ordinary inventory reuse. Existing artifact contracts and native package classification are moved to focused owners to keep loader files within size limits. Necessary production growth represents ownership transport and shared-module resolution; the regression matrix covers distinct source/compiled loading boundaries.

## Evidence

- Reproduced the original Gateway regression: edited helper B still executed A before the fix.
- Gateway reload suite: **8 passed**, including edited bundled code, retained siblings, and replacement retry/drain behavior.
- Worker, recovery, and bundled-code suites: **26 passed**. The four-layout matrix covers source TypeScript, compiled CJS, compiled ESM, and runtime overlays; checks plugin-only chunk replacement, canonical host shared state, deferred imports, and captured recovery after source removal.
- Full isolated build passed. Core production and plugin-platform test typechecks passed. Final changed-file lint, formatting, and diff checks passed; the post-extraction loader/recovery rerun passed all 13 tests.
- Documentation anchor audit reported six broken anchors in unchanged files; neither changed documentation page introduces or changes links.
- Independent autoreview: no actionable P0–P2 findings; reviewer inspected supplied source but did not execute tests.
