issues.body:
**Environment:** multiplexed gateway, one process serving 4 Telegram bots (+Discord); profiles `default`, `yori`, `cratchit`, `scrooge`. Repo @ 5b147ab036 (2026-10-21).

## Symptom

A long-running turn on the **yori** profile streamed its mid-turn progress updates into the **default** profile's Telegram DM thread for ~7 minutes. The follow-up `💾 Self-improvement review` notice from that same turn also arrived there. The turn's *final summary* went to the correct (yori) thread.

The two bots are distinct (`@JohannZ_Lilith_bot` id 8784022300 vs `@JohannZ_Yori_bot` id 8921141139); the user sees separate chats on desktop and Android.

## Timeline (UTC; user local = UTC-6)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 00:54:22 | inbound `go` on yori's Telegram DM; turn starts (`agent:yori:telegram:dm:8370408611`) |
| 00:57 | last progress update seen in **yori's** thread |
| 01:10:40 | `[Telegram] Telegram network error, scheduling reconnect: Bad Gateway` (yori adapter) |
| 01:11:00 | `updater.stop() did not finish before the network-recovery deadline; rebuilding the adapter` → `Disconnected` → `Fatal telegram adapter error for multiplexed profile yori (telegram_network_error)` |
| **01:11–01:18** | **progress updates arrive in the DEFAULT thread** ← symptom |
| 01:11:19 | `Connected to Telegram (polling mode)` → `✓ telegram reconnected (profile: yori)` |
| 01:19:01 | turn ends: `time=1479.7s api_calls=45 response=1702 chars` |
| 01:19:02 | `Sending response (1702 chars) to 8370408611` in **yori's** log — summary lands in yori's thread ✓ |
| 01:19:01–01:20:13 | background review (`origin=background_review`, thread `bg-review`), `skill_manage` at 01:19:58 / 01:20:05 |
| **01:20** | **`💾 Self-improvement review: Skill 'obsidian-gaming-vault' patched` arrives in the DEFAULT thread** ← symptom |

## Expected behaviour (authoritative)

`gateway/AGENTS.md` § *Profile scope*, delivery matrix, final row:

> restored / hand-built, no live provenance → delivery: unique owner of `(platform, runtime)`; **a disconnected secondary → `None`, never the default bot**

`gateway/authz_mixin.py::_adapters_for_profile`:

> A named profile with no map gets `{}` — fail closed: a secondary whose adapter failed to connect must NOT fall back to the default profile's adapter (replies, tool sends, marker-file notices out the wrong bot).

`gateway/authz_mixin.py::_delivery_adapter_for`:

> If that bot has no adapter right now it is offline: fail closed rather than fall through to the runtime profile's bot.

## Why it is silent

- Progress/status sends create **no `delivery_obligations` row**; the shared store shows exactly one yori row in 01:05–01:25 (`32fa3ee0259110170ccf4955`, `adapter_profile='yori'`, 01:19:02). All 99 historical yori obligations carry `adapter_profile='yori'`; none carry `'default'`.
- They also emit **no `Sending response`** log line — the default gateway.log has zero lines between 01:05:44 and 01:45:39, and yori's has none between 01:11:29 and 01:19:02.
- So the two checks one would naturally reach for both come back clean. (An initial grep of `Sending response` wrongly exonerated the primary adapter.)

Both bots DM the same user, so `chat_id` is `8370408611` for both — a Telegram private chat id is the user id. Identical ids in logs are expected and are **not** evidence of correct routing.

## Candidate mechanisms (NOT confirmed — please trace)

1. **Rebuilt adapter bound with launch-profile credentials.** `_run_secondary_profile_reconnect` reconstructs the adapter after the fatal error. If that rebuild runs without the profile's secret scope — cf. `_scope_or_null`: *"answering it for an unresolvable NAMED profile is what made a secondary's inbound message run on the launch profile's credentials"* — the new adapter would be registered under `yori` but hold the **default** `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`. **Counter-evidence:** the 01:19 summary went to the *correct* thread, which it should not have if the token were wrong — unless that send resolved through a different seam than the progress sends.
2. **Stale adapter reference held across the teardown.** `ctx._status_adapter` is bound once per turn (`gateway/run_turn.py:2213 → _delivery_adapter_for(source)`), resolved while yori's adapter was live at 00:54. After the object is disconnected and popped at 01:11, what does `send()` on that stale object resolve to? Needs the post-`disconnect()` send path.
3. Ruled-out-adjacent: the 01:20 review notice may come from the `tui_gateway` notification path, which may publish through the launch profile's adapters regardless of session profile. `tests/gateway/test_multiplex_process_global_sinks.py` covers other process-global sinks (Yuanbao sethome, `terminal.env_passthrough`, Slack ignored-channel) but **not** messaging progress/notification sinks.

## Proposed regression test

Multiplexed secondary whose telegram adapter is removed from `_profile_adapters` mid-turn while a progress send is pending: assert `_delivery_adapter_for(source)` returns `None` (or the reconnected secondary adapter) and **never** `_primary_adapters()[TELEGRAM]`. Extend `test_multiplex_transport_matrix.py` to cover the progress and background-review-summary seams, not just final-response delivery.

## Impact

Secret scoping holds — yori's inbound work does not run on default credentials. But content from one profile appears under another identity's bot, which in a multi-profile household is a trust-boundary problem, and it produces no obligation row, no send log, and no warning.

issues.title: Background memory reviewer can persist facts the user explicitly asked not to save

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: comp/tools
labels.description: Tool registry, model_tools, toolsets

labels.name: tool/memory
labels.description: Memory tool and memory providers

labels.name: area/config
labels.description: Config system, migrations, profiles

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

issues.body:
**Current state (SBI).**
- **Situation.** After a session, the background memory reviewer ran its review pass over the user profile.
- **Behavior.** It proposed adding a sensitive fact the user had asked not to keep: "User is accessibility-minded (visual impairment) but asked NOT to save that to memory." The reviewer's own text recorded the no-save request before proposing the write. Batch `~/.hermes/pending/memory/applied-20260919/246192b6.json` (origin `background_review`).
- **Impact.** Because `add` is ungated, a consent-violating add applies unattended. This one was caught by a manual curation pass before it applied; USER.md today contains no such fact. Near-miss, not a live leak.

**Root cause (verified).** The review prompt (`agent/background_review.py`, `_MEMORY_REVIEW_PROMPT`) tells the reviewer only to "consider saving if appropriate" — no instruction on honoring "don't save this" requests. In `tools/memory_tool.py`, `replace`/`remove` are staged for approval in unattended forks (`_BG_DELETE_ACTIONS`), but `add` is not gated and applies unattended.

**Target state.** The reviewer never persists a fact the user asked not to save; consent-sensitive adds are staged the way `replace`/`remove` are.

**Gap.** Today a consent-violating add applies unattended; it should be blocked or staged. The reviewer toggle also fails open — `load_background_review_settings` (`background_review.py:205`) defaults `enabled=True` on a broken/missing config, and the fallback emits only a log-only `logger.warning` (`:214-218`), never surfaced to the user. A user who thinks they disabled background review may not have.

**Scope.** Background memory reviewer; USER.md/MEMORY.md writes.

**Countermeasure.** (1) Add an explicit rule to the review prompt: never persist facts the user asked not to save. (2) Stage adds carrying consent-sensitive content like `replace`/`remove`.

**Acceptance criteria.** A maintainer verifies: the prompt contains the no-save rule; a consent-sensitive add is staged (or blocked) rather than applied; the repro batch no longer applies unattended.

**No blame.** Process gap, not reviewer fault — the prompt gives no consent guidance, and the model knew yet still proposed the write.

Related: #56817 (tiered write-approval), #44963 (staged approvals). Not duplicates.

issues.title: A Group Chat copy keeps taking events after room.disbanded

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/gateway
labels.description: Gateway runner, session dispatch, delivery

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

issues.body:
A gateway's copy of a Group Chat that its host disbanded keeps accepting new events. On the host, `room.disbanded` is the last event a room will ever have, but a copy appends whatever a later page brings. The copy then shows an ended Group Chat carrying on.

### Steps on `main` at `484de065a8`

These use the `groups.*` takeover methods that `hermes serve` exposes, following "Transferring hosted room authority" in the Bot Mode guide.

1. Gateway A hosts a Group Chat with three messages, and gateway B keeps a copy of all three.
2. The owner disbands the Group Chat on A (`groups.disband`), so A's seq 4 is `room.disbanded`. Gateway C copies it with `groups.log` (`"include_disbanded": true`) and `groups.replicate`. C's copy ends with `room.disbanded`.
3. A goes away, and B is promoted from its older copy (`groups.promote` with `"confirm": true`), never having seen the disband. A message lands on B at seq 5.
4. On C, `groups.replicate` with B's `groups.log` page from `since_seq: 4`.

**Expected:** C refuses the page, because its copy ends with `room.disbanded`.

**Actual:** C accepts it and reports `caught_up: true`. Its copy reads `room.disbanded` at seq 4, then B's message at seq 5.

### Cause

- `disband_room()` makes `room.disbanded` terminal on the host: `append_event()`, `claim_authority()` and `demote_room()` only act on a live room ([hosted_rooms.py#L985](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_rooms.py#L985), [#L1131-L1160](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_rooms.py#L1131-L1160)).
- `ingest_page()` inserts every event above `last_seq` without looking at what the copy holds or where `room.disbanded` sits in the page ([hosted_room_replicas.py#L157-L171](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L157-L171)).

### Evidence

The steps above run on the storage functions the RPCs pass through, on `main`:

```
{'stored_seq': 5, 'ingested': 1, 'authority': {'gateway_id': 'install:bbbb…', 'epoch': 2}, 'caught_up': True}
(4, 'system:room-disbanded', 'room.disbanded', 1), (5, 'b-work', 'message.user', 2)
```

The fix branch's regression test, run against `main`'s `gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py`:

```
FAILED tests/gateway/test_hosted_room_replicas.py::test_ingest_refuses_events_after_room_disbanded
E   Failed: DID NOT RAISE ReplicaError
PASSED tests/gateway/test_hosted_room_replicas.py::test_disbanded_room_history_still_copies_idempotently
```

With the fix, both replica test files pass.

### Fix

Fix: commit `29c9aec5e76` on [dokterdok:fix/group-chat-replica-integrity](https://github.com/dokterdok/hermes-agent/tree/fix/group-chat-replica-integrity) (+16/−5 product, +96 test). A copy that ends at `room.disbanded` is exactly caught up and final:
- no page may add events after it;
- no page may record a `latest_seq` past it, including a disband page that claims a longer log;
- a page that adds nothing leaves the copy's row as it is. Before, a short page from the successor relabelled the disbanded copy with the successor's authority, coverage and name.

In a copy this code wrote, `room.disbanded` can only be the last stored event, so ingest checks that one sequence. Promotion checks the whole history. Copying a disbanded room's history, and replaying it, still work.

The companion fix for an authority change without `authority.claimed` also refuses the steps above, because B's message is at epoch 2 with no claim. This fix holds whatever the epoch, for example a page at the same epoch.

Other directions:
- Record a terminal flag on the copy's row. That needs a schema change, which is not required while `room.disbanded` stays last.
- Add the room id to the local retired ids when a copy receives `room.disbanded`. That also stops a local create from reusing the id, but it changes the local room-id policy.

### Related

- Filed together with #143380, #143381 and #143383: the other replica fixes in this file, one commit each.
- #99047 (merged) added the replica store. #104906 (merged) documents the recovery procedure.
- #99107 (closed) refused the same pages as part of a broader change. Only this check is proposed here.
- No open issue or PR touches `gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py`.

Found while auditing the retained Group Chat PRs against main (#97681).

Refs #134889

issues.title: groups.promote brings a disbanded Group Chat copy back as a live room

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/gateway
labels.description: Gateway runner, session dispatch, delivery

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

issues.body:
Promoting a gateway's copy of a Group Chat that its host had disbanded brings the Group Chat back to life. `groups.promote` creates a live room at the next epoch, with the disband buried in its history, and new messages are accepted again in a Group Chat the owner ended.

### Steps on `main` at `484de065a8`

These use the `groups.*` takeover methods that `hermes serve` exposes, following "Transferring hosted room authority" in the Bot Mode guide.

1. Gateway A hosts a Group Chat, and the owner disbands it (`groups.disband`).
2. Gateway C copies it with `groups.log` (`"include_disbanded": true`) and `groups.replicate`. C's copy ends with `room.disbanded`.
3. On C, `groups.promote` with `"confirm": true`, then post a message.

**Expected:** the promotion is refused, because the copy records that its host ended this Group Chat.

**Actual:** C now hosts a live Group Chat at epoch 2. `groups.state` shows no `disbanded_at`, and the new message is accepted at seq 6, after `room.disbanded` at seq 4.

### Cause

- `promote_replica()` refuses a room id only when this gateway's own store retired it ([hosted_room_replicas.py#L220-L221](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L220-L221)). A copy of a room disbanded on another gateway passes that check.
- It then inserts the room with `disbanded_at` NULL and copies the history, `room.disbanded` included, into it ([#L227-L237](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L227-L237)).

### Evidence

The steps above run on the storage functions the RPCs pass through, on `main`:

```
promote_replica -> authority_epoch 2; room_state disbanded_at None; latest_seq 6 after one append
```

The fix branch's regression test, run against `main`'s `gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py`:

```
FAILED tests/gateway/test_hosted_room_replicas.py::test_promote_refuses_a_disbanded_copy
E   Failed: DID NOT RAISE RoomConflictError
```

With the fix, both replica test files pass.

### Fix

Fix: commit `b13e9224fd3` on [dokterdok:fix/group-chat-replica-integrity](https://github.com/dokterdok/hermes-agent/tree/fix/group-chat-replica-integrity) (+3/−1 product, +18 test). The promotion is refused when the copy holds `room.disbanded`, with the same `RoomConflictError` ("room_id belongs to a disbanded room") that a locally retired id gets. The copy stays as it was. Promoting a copy that holds only part of the history stays possible, as the Bot Mode guide documents for disaster recovery (within the copy's own lineage, see the companion fix for an authority change without `authority.claimed`).

Other directions:
- Promote it as a disbanded tombstone. That serves no purpose for a room nobody can write to.
- Add the id to the local retired ids when a copy receives `room.disbanded`, so the existing check catches it. That also changes local room-id policy.

### Related

- Filed together with #143380, #143381 and #143382: the other replica fixes in this file, one commit each.
- #99047 (merged) added `promote_replica()` and its operator-confirmed `groups.promote`. #104906 (merged) documents the procedure. Neither covers a disbanded copy.
- #99107 (closed) refused the same promotion as part of a broader change that also gated the takeover methods. Only this check is proposed here.
- No open issue or PR touches `gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py`.

Found while auditing the retained Group Chat PRs against main (#97681).

Refs #134889

issues.title: A Group Chat copy mixes two histories when it replicates from a host that took over from an older copy

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/gateway
labels.description: Gateway runner, session dispatch, delivery

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

issues.body:
A gateway that keeps a copy of a Group Chat (`groups.replicate`) can end up holding two different histories as one. When the room's host is replaced by a gateway whose copy was older, the new host's log disagrees with what the follower already stored. The follower takes the page anyway: it keeps the old host's last message, appends the new host's later work on top, and reports itself caught up. If that copy is promoted later, the mixed history becomes a live Group Chat.

### Steps on `main` at `484de065a8`

These use the `groups.*` takeover methods that `hermes serve` exposes, following "Transferring hosted room authority" in the Bot Mode guide.

1. Gateway A hosts a Group Chat with four messages. Gateway C keeps a full copy: `groups.replicate` with A's `groups.log` page. C holds seq 1–4.
2. Gateway B's copy stopped at seq 3. A goes away and B is promoted (`groups.promote` with `"confirm": true`). B's `authority.claimed` is seq 4, and one more message lands on B at seq 5.
3. On C, `groups.replicate` with B's `groups.log` page from `since_seq: 0`.

**Expected:** C refuses the page. Its seq 4 is A's message and B's seq 4 is B's claim, so they come from different histories.

**Actual:** C accepts it: `stored_seq: 5`, `caught_up: true`, authority B at epoch 2. Its copy now reads A's message at seq 4 (epoch 1), then B's message at seq 5 (epoch 2), with no `authority.claimed` anywhere.

### Cause

- `ingest_page()` keeps only the events above the copy's `last_seq` and never compares the sequences it already holds ([hosted_room_replicas.py#L157](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L157)). B's seq 1–4 are skipped as "already stored", even though seq 4 differs.
- It then stores the page's authority stamp as the copy's authority ([#L176-L178](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L176-L178)), so the copy reports B's lineage over A's history.
- `promote_replica()` later copies those rows verbatim into a live room ([#L234-L237](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L234-L237)).

The Bot Mode guide says to preserve both histories when they have diverged, not to merge them ([bot-mode.md#L356-L360](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/website/docs/user-guide/bot-mode.md#L356-L360)).

### Evidence

The steps above run on the storage functions the RPCs pass through (`groups.replicate` is `ingest_page()`), on `main`:

```
{'stored_seq': 5, 'ingested': 1, 'authority': {'gateway_id': 'install:bbbb…', 'epoch': 2}, 'caught_up': True}
(4, 'a3', 'message.user', 1), (5, 'b-work', 'message.user', 2)
```

The fix branch's regression test, run against `main`'s `gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py`:

```
FAILED tests/gateway/test_hosted_room_replicas.py::test_ingest_refuses_a_replay_from_a_different_room_history
E   Failed: DID NOT RAISE ReplicaError
```

With the fix, `tests/gateway/test_hosted_room_replicas.py` and `tests/tui_gateway/test_groups_replication_methods.py` pass, and so do the existing replica tests, `test_full_failover_round_trip` included.

### Fix

Fix: commit `1843dd775c1` on [dokterdok:fix/group-chat-replica-integrity](https://github.com/dokterdok/hermes-agent/tree/fix/group-chat-replica-integrity) (+16/−1 product, +66 test, plus the `groups.replicate` docstring). Every replayed sequence is compared with the stored event (id, kind, actor, epoch and payload, the identity `append_event()` already uses), and the page is refused when they differ. A test changes one field at a time. Identical replays stay idempotent.

Other directions:
- On a conflict, keep the common prefix and switch the copy to the newer lineage. That silently drops history only this copy holds (A's last message), which the guide says to keep.
- Compare event ids only. That is cheaper, but a different payload under the same id would pass.

### Related

- Filed together with #143381, #143382 and #143383: the other replica fixes in this file, one commit each.
- #99047 (merged) added the replica store and the operator-confirmed `groups.promote`/`groups.demote`. This change leaves that design as it is. #104906 (merged) documents the recovery procedure, after #104309.
- #99107 (closed) carried these checks together with a gate on the takeover methods and a quarantine of promoted rooms. Only the integrity part is proposed here.
- Direction: "lineage-proven takeover" in the decision comment on #97681 (5472640342).
- No open issue or PR touches `gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py`.

Found while auditing the retained Group Chat PRs against main (#97681).

Refs #134889

issues.title: A Group Chat copy accepts a new host or epoch with no authority.claimed event

labels.name: type/security
labels.description: Security vulnerability or hardening

labels.name: comp/gateway
labels.description: Gateway runner, session dispatch, delivery

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

issues.body:
A gateway that keeps a copy of a Group Chat accepts a change of host or epoch from any page that announces one, with no `authority.claimed` event to prove it. A follower that already holds the old host's history then takes a successor's later messages on top of it and reports the successor's authority. The copy now holds two histories with nothing between them. A page from a demoted host is taken the same way: its `authority.lost` is that host's own record, not a claim.

### Steps on `main` at `484de065a8`

These use the `groups.*` takeover methods that `hermes serve` exposes, following "Transferring hosted room authority" in the Bot Mode guide.

1. Gateway A hosts a Group Chat with four messages. Gateway C keeps a full copy (`groups.replicate` with A's `groups.log` page). C holds seq 1–4.
2. Gateway B's copy stopped at seq 3. A goes away and B is promoted (`groups.promote` with `"confirm": true`). B's `authority.claimed` is seq 4, and one more message lands on B at seq 5.
3. On C, `groups.replicate` with B's `groups.log` page from C's cursor, `since_seq: 4`. That page holds only B's epoch-2 message.

**Expected:** C refuses the page. C's copy is at epoch 1, and nothing in it or in the page claims epoch 2.

**Actual:** C accepts it: `stored_seq: 5`, `caught_up: true`, authority B at epoch 2. C's copy reads A's message at seq 4, then B's message at seq 5.

The same happens with a page from a demoted host. If A is demoted (`groups.demote`) and C replicates A's page from `since_seq: 3`, C stores A's `authority.lost` at seq 4 and adopts B at epoch 2, without B's claim.

### Cause

- The only authority check in `ingest_page()` refuses an older epoch ([hosted_room_replicas.py#L155-L156](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L155-L156)). A newer epoch, or another gateway at the same epoch, is stored as the copy's authority as given ([#L176-L178](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L176-L178)).
- The page's `authority` stamp is the host's current authority ([hosted_rooms.py#L1175](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_rooms.py#L1175)), not proof that the events lead to it. On `main` every authority change writes an `authority.claimed` event (`claim_authority()`, `promote_replica()` [#L224-L226](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L224-L226)). A demotion writes `authority.lost` instead ([#L276-L279](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py#L276-L279)).
- `main` already checks exactly this boundary for work evidence: a claim at each epoch boundary, and gateway actors matching their span ([hosted_room_work_lineage.py#L13-L21](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_work_lineage.py#L13-L21)). Its lineage reader requires each claim to extend its predecessor ([hosted_room_authority_history.py#L106-L110](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/484de065a821b4245697351d08327b465ffd41ba/gateway/hosted_room_authority_history.py#L106-L110)). Copies are never held to that rule.

### Evidence

The steps above run on the storage functions the RPCs pass through, on `main`:

```
since_seq 4 from B:  {'stored_seq': 5, 'authority': {'gateway_id': 'install:bbbb…', 'epoch': 2}, 'caught_up': True}
                     (4, 'a3', 'message.user', 1), (5, 'b-work', 'message.user', 2)
since_seq 3 from demoted A:  (4, 'system:authority-lost:2', 'authority.lost', 2), authority B at epoch 2
```

The fix branch's regression test, run against `main`'s `gateway/hosted_room_replicas.py`:

```
FAILED tests/gateway/test_hosted_room_replicas.py::test_ingest_refuses_an_authority_change_without_a_claim
E   Failed: DID NOT RAISE ReplicaError
PASSED tests/gateway/test_hosted_room_replicas.py::test_fresh_copy_pages_the_successor_through_its_claim
```

With the fix, both replica test files pass.

### Fix

Fix: commit `ca6019a77a5` on [dokterdok:fix/group-chat-replica-integrity](https://github.com/dokterdok/hermes-agent/tree/fix/group-chat-replica-integrity) (+85/−17 product, +165/−7 test).

- **The claim rule.** The new events are walked from the span of the copy's last stored event, with the work-evidence rule. Each epoch boundary needs an `authority.claimed` from the authority-control actor at exactly the next epoch, naming the gateway it leaves, and gateway actors must match their span. The error names the first event that breaks the rule.
- **Two records.** A log read in short pages is stamped with the host's current authority before that authority's claim arrives. The copy keeps that stamp as the newest authority it has seen, as today: it still fences older pages, and `groups.replica_state` is unchanged. It now also records the gateway of the span its stored events reach, in a new nullable `lineage_gateway_id` column added in place. So a short page never makes it forget whose span it holds, and a claim naming another predecessor is still refused. Once caught up, the stamp must match.
- **Promotion.** `promote_replica()` refuses a copy whose recorded authority is still ahead of its stored events. That is the window between a short page stamped by a promoted host and that host's claim. The claim it would append could only reuse an epoch the copy has seen, or skip the missing claim, and then no follower could copy the room. The refusal is error `4118`, and the copy is kept. Once the claim is stored, promotion and copying work as before.

Following a promoted successor keeps working: a copy that reaches B's claim, in one page or several, takes it and moves to epoch 2. Promoting an incomplete copy within its own lineage is unchanged. The existing epoch-regression test seeded its newer epoch by editing the page stamp alone, which is the case this refuses. It now reaches epoch 2 through `claim_authority()`.

Other directions:
- Refuse every authority change on a copy. A follower could then never follow a promoted successor, which `main`'s recovery procedure relies on.
- Rebuild the lineage with the authority-history reader on every page. That reader works on authoritative tables and reconstructs the whole history, so it would need adapting to copies and costs a full scan per page.
- Store only the proven span on the copy and promote from it. Promoting in the window above would then claim an epoch the copy saw the successor hold, which defeats the epoch fence.
- Allow that window explicitly: when the successor that claimed epoch N died before its claim reached any copy, record the missing claim as a gap the lineage validators accept. That keeps this disaster case recoverable, which `main` allows today only by writing a room its own lineage reader rejects. It needs a contract across the replica store, the authority-history reader and work evidence.

### Related

- Filed together with #143380, #143382 and #143383: the other replica fixes in this file, one commit each.
- #99047 (merged) added the replica store and the operator-confirmed `groups.promote`/`groups.demote`. This change leaves them as they are. #104906 (merged) documents the procedure, after #104309.

The class: `hermes -z` built `AIAgent` without `max_iterations`, so `agent.max_turns` / `HERMES_MAX_ITERATIONS` never reached the iteration budget — the constructor default `sys.maxsize` ran unbounded. The class was tracked and named by @xngg1021 — the four-subsystem root cause in #110126 and the truncation-ladder proposal in #119112 are the prior art this fix builds on; the split he proposed (the effective cap seeding the retry ladder) is the same precedence this fix applies at the oneshot boundary.

The fix: `_resolve_max_iterations` mirrors `cli_init_mixin._init_turn_limits` precedence (agent.max_turns → max_turns → HERMES_MAX_ITERATIONS env → unlimited) and forwards the resolved cap to `AIAgent(max_iterations=...)` at `hermes_cli/oneshot.py::_run_agent`. Because `max_iterations` is a `_PASSTHROUGH_PARAM`, the cap is recorded into the session row's `model_config` (verified: 42 read back from a real AIAgent session).

The verification: 39 passed in ~8s across the four core oneshot suites — 19 new tests in `tests/hermes_cli/test_oneshot_max_iterations.py` (the session-row recording, the resume error-exit, the forwarded cap) plus the existing resume/exit-contract/fallback suites (the full six-suite oneshot set incl. the skills + resumed-session suites: 50). The fail-loud exit contract (`_oneshot_exit_code` derives 0/2/130/1 from the result's status booleans, not the text) and the resume-hydration (`_load_resume_target` raises on unknown/missing-store) cover the #49195 flag-drop class. The commit (848713854c) and the raw diff are attached for cherry-picking.

The class's shape was identified and scoped by the thread — the four-subsystem root cause in #110126 (xngg1021, corroborated by the real-world impact report) — and the independent work converged on it: the truncation-ladder proposal in #119112 (xngg1021), the fix attempt in #105248 (ardaaltinors), the Windows confirmation with a patch (OctaveAdb), and the reports that surfaced the class (#99957 jg3fw2t35, #105243 ardaaltinors, #49195 cloverthe-ai). The fix proceeded separately from that convergence — the fail-loud contract, the precedence resolution, and the recording chain were shaped in this work's own effort — but the basis of this work carried xngg1021's prior art, and the solve builds on it: the design rests on his #110126 root cause and #119112 proposal; the convergence validated the design, it did not shape it.

The diff is here if it's useful — open it, adapt it, or set it aside. The call is the thread's.

issues.body:
# Feature request: let MEMORY.md be an anchor for a memory doc chain

The 2,200-character cap on MEMORY.md is workable for a single flat file, but it makes one pattern genuinely hard: using the memory document as an anchor that points to a chain of memory documents.

Here's the setup that doesn't fit today. I keep a small set of behavior-critical facts in MEMORY.md (the anchor) and a separate chain of dated, append-only documents for the nuanced knowledge: conventions, lessons, preferences, network facts. The anchor stays small on purpose; the chain grows without a per-document cap. That works, but only because I built the chain by hand outside the memory system. The memory tool doesn't know the chain exists: it reviews and stages batches against one flat file, the char limit applies to the anchor only by accident of where I put things, and consolidation means fighting the cap instead of using it.

What would help: treat chain documents as first-class memory. Let the anchor reference them, let the memory tool read and append to them, and apply the char limit to the anchor alone. The reviewer could then propose chain appends instead of cramming everything into one file.

Related: #16831 (configurable limit), #28424 (auto-compact), #5320 (raise/auto-scale defaults).

issues.body:
## Bug Description

`hermes update` on the default `stable` channel aborts **before any fetch or checkout** with:

```
→ Update channel: stable
✗ Could not resolve the stable source channel: Command '['git', 'merge-base', '--is-ancestor', '<release-sha>', '<HEAD>']' timed out after 10 seconds. No update was applied.
```

This is the same user-visible failure as #137646 / #138404 / #138938, but **not** the missing-object / lazy-fetch case those issues describe.

On this host **both SHAs were already in the object store**. `git cat-file -t` returned `commit` for the new stable tip and for HEAD. `git merge-base --is-ancestor` then ran to completion in **12.1 s, exit 1** (release is not an ancestor of HEAD — we were behind). The updater's `timeout=10` killed the probe first, `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` escaped `_head_containing`, and `select_apply_target` reported an unresolvable channel (`stop_class: channel_unresolved`).

Hermes itself makes this likely: a `blob:none` partial clone gets commit-graph **writes** turned off on every update (`gc.writeCommitGraph=false`, `fetch.writeCommitGraph=false` via `disable_tree0_auto_maintenance`). Without a graph, proving the common “behind” answer (walk every ancestor of HEAD looking for a commit that is **not** in that set) is a ~12 s CPU walk on this repo (~54k commits, 59 packs, `.git` ~1.3–1.4 GB).

A one-shot `git commit-graph write --reachable` dropped the same command from **12.1 s → 3 ms**. `hermes update -y` then applied `v0.21.7` → `v0.22.2` cleanly.

#139079 / #137649 (treat an unanswered probe as unknown relation, fall through to GitHub compare) would **also unblock** this host, because the timeout would no longer refuse the run. It would not make the local probe cheap: every update would still burn 10 s of git CPU then hit the network fallback, unless a commit-graph exists.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Git install, `stable` channel (unchosen default → `forward_only=True`).
2. `blob:none` partial clone (`remote.origin.promisor=true`, `partialclonefilter=blob:none`).
3. Hermes-managed keys: `gc.writeCommitGraph=false`, `fetch.writeCommitGraph=false`. No current commit-graph (or a stale one).
4. HEAD **behind** the latest published `vX.Y.Z` release, **and** both commits already present locally (`git cat-file -t <release>` and `git cat-file -t HEAD` both print `commit`).
5. `hermes update` (or `hermes update --check`).

Direct probe (this host, before writing a graph):

```
$ git cat-file -t d923a5eb487a17c0a68801bba9ef0f56c81040a8   # v0.22.2
commit
$ git cat-file -t 0e161737d2a5982a481d2d340434f9eac25d9f10   # HEAD v0.21.7+179
commit
$ time git merge-base --is-ancestor d923a5eb487a17c0a68801bba9ef0f56c81040a8 0e161737d2a5982a481d2d340434f9eac25d9f10
# real 0m12.112s  user 0m10.617s  sys 0m3.883s  exit 1
```

After `git commit-graph write --reachable`:

```
$ time git merge-base --is-ancestor d923a5eb487a17c0a68801bba9ef0f56c81040a8 0e161737d2a5982a481d2d340434f9eac25d9f10
# real 0m0.003s  exit 1
```

## Expected Behavior

- A 10 s timeout on `merge-base --is-ancestor` is an **unknown relation**, not an unresolvable channel. The update should proceed (GitHub compare already exists in `_head_containing` for shallow / unknown cases).
- When both objects are local, the probe should finish well under 10 s. Disabling commit-graph *writes* on partial clones should not leave ancestry checks without a readable graph.

## Actual Behavior

Update receipt (`~/.hermes/logs/update_receipts/update_20261015_104456_*.json`):

- `outcome: failed`
- `stop_class: channel_unresolved`
- `pre_update` / `post_update` both `0e161737` / `0.21.7`
- no fetch, no checkout

Logged line:

```
Could not resolve the stable source channel: Command '['git', 'merge-base', '--is-ancestor', 'd923a5eb487a17c0a68801bba9ef0f56c81040a8', '0e161737d2a5982a481d2d340434f9eac25d9f10']' timed out after 10 seconds. No update was applied.
```

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS |
| git | 2.43.0 |
| Hermes at failure | v0.21.7+179.g0e16173 (`0e161737d2a`) |
| Target release | stable v0.22.2 (`d923a5eb487a`) |
| Install | git, `/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent` |
| Clone | `blob:none` partial, promisor origin |
| `.git` | ~1.3 GB, 59 packs, ~54k commits |
| Channel | `stable` (default / forward-only) |

## Code path

`hermes_cli/update_cmd_check.py::select_apply_target`
→ `source_releases.resolve_source_target(..., forward_only=True)`
→ `source_releases._head_containing`
→ `run("merge-base", "--is-ancestor", commit, head)` with `timeout=10` (`source_releases.py` ~107–115)

`TimeoutExpired` is not caught inside `_head_containing`. It is caught by `select_apply_target` as `subprocess.SubprocessError` and turned into “Could not resolve the … source channel”.

Hermes re-applies commit-graph-off on every update (`gitlock.disable_tree0_auto_maintenance` / #127711). That policy is load-bearing for this failure when objects **are** local.

## Why this is not #137646

| | #137646 | this report |
|---|---|---|
| `git cat-file -t <release>` | missing / ~12 s then fatal | `commit` immediately |
| merge-base if allowed to finish | never a useful local answer | exit 1 in 12.1 s (correct: behind) |
| Workaround that unblocked | fetch the release commit | `git commit-graph write --reachable` (no fetch) |
| After workaround, same probe | ~0.2 s | 3 ms |

#139079 would still be the right *refusal* fix (do not map timeout → channel unresolved). Please also treat “both commits local, graph walk > 10 s because commit-graph writes are disabled” as its own performance bug, not only “object not in store”.

## Suggested fix

1. Catch `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` in `_head_containing` and treat it as unknown relation (same as #139079) so a slow-but-correct behind check cannot refuse the update.
2. Before that probe on a partial clone, write a one-shot commit-graph (`git commit-graph write --reachable`) **or** keep a readable graph even when `gc.writeCommitGraph` / `fetch.writeCommitGraph` stay false. Do not re-enable those write keys if #127711 still applies.
3. Optional cheap gate: if `git cat-file -e <commit>` fails fast, skip local merge-base entirely (the #137646 missing-object path).

## Workaround

```
cd "$(hermes --version | awk -F': ' '/Install directory/{print $2}')"
git commit-graph write --reachable
hermes update --yes
```

Do **not** set `gc.writeCommitGraph=true` permanently; the updater will turn it off again on the next run.

issues.body:
Need (general)
`MEMORY.md` / `USER.md` are injected into EVERY future turn — they are latency and cost on every
session. Today nothing in the product governs what goes IN: no size budget, no acceptance test at
write time, no distinction between "facts that apply to every session" (belong in memory) and
"procedures/lessons for a recurring task type" (belong in skills), and no automatic consequence when
the store approaches its cap. Result in the field: memory accretes into a second, worse session
history — stale facts, imperative phrasing that hijacks later sessions, duplicated procedures — and
the curation pass becomes a manual archaeology exercise.

## Proposed core behaviour
1. **Budget enforcement at write time.** A configurable character cap per store (memory/user).
   Writes that would cross a soft threshold (e.g. 85%) must displace existing content or route to an
   overflow document — never silently grow the injected context.
2. **Acceptance pipeline on every memory edit** (adds AND rewrites): shape check (declarative facts,
   not instructions — imperative phrasing rejected with a hint), semantic check (fits the store's
   purpose: facts that apply to every session; task procedures belong in skills), and staleness
   awareness (facts dated within a short window flagged as session-log material).
3. **Change log.** Every admit / remove / consolidate / refusal appends one line (action + rationale)
   to a machine-readable log the user can audit.
4. **Consequence hooks.** Refusals return a structured error naming the rule violated and where the
   content should live instead (e.g. "write this as a skill"), so the agent can reroute rather than
   retry blindly.

## Why core, not plugin
Plugins can veto memory tool calls via `pre_tool_call`, and that is how the reference implementation
works — but the budget is core state (the store is core-owned), the clean integration point is the
memory writer itself, and every heavy user of memory otherwise rebuilds this pipeline independently.
A core implementation also lets the budget feed the same telemetry surface as context size (#26382
family).

**Tests (generic):**
- Over-cap write is refused (or routed to overflow) with a structured error; the store's measured
  size never exceeds the cap after any sequence of writes.
- An imperative-phrased entry is rejected with the shape hint; the corrected declarative form
  passes.
- A procedure-shaped entry (recurring-task instructions) is rejected with a "belongs in skills" hint.
- Every accepted/rejected write appends exactly one change-log line.

**Prior art check (8 Oct 2026):** #69264 (memory-hygiene SKILL for curation) and #116673
(MEMORY.md anchor chains) address the CONTENT lifecycle; #25309 (dreaming/consolidation) addresses
background rewriting. None enforces budget + acceptance at the moment of writing — the gap above.

issues.body:
## Feature description

The kanban dispatcher decides part of a worker's capability surface at spawn time, through command-line parameters and code paths that bypass the assignee profile's own configuration. The profile cannot decline them. It can only fight them afterwards, where a counter exists at all.

Spawn-time injections in current `main`:

| Injection | Where | Profile control today |
|---|---|---|
| Card-level skills: one `--skills <name>` per entry in `task.skills`, chosen by whoever created the card | `hermes_cli/kanban_db_dispatch.py` `_worker_argv` (`for sk in task.skills`) | none |
| `sdlc-review` force-loaded on every review-lane claim | `kanban_db_dispatch.py:2476-2479` | only `kanban.review_dispatch: false`, which turns off review dispatch entirely; `skills.disabled` breaks the review run instead (#99251) |
| `kanban` toolset force-appended for every dispatcher-owned worker | `model_tools.py:320-324` | `agent.disabled_toolsets: [kanban]`, which works only because disabled toolsets are subtracted last; this is a counter-measure, not a setting |
| `--toolsets` pin resolved by the dispatcher | `_resolve_worker_cli_toolsets` (`kanban_db_dispatch.py:3071-3089`) | indirect |
| `-m` / `--provider` / `--reasoning` from per-card overrides (`kanban set-model`, `reasoning_effort`) | `_worker_argv` | none |
| `KANBAN_GUIDANCE` protocol text, injected whenever the show tool is present | `agent/agent_init.py:1134-1136` | only by removing the toolset |

Each of these is harmless while nobody uses it. But each is a channel through which a card author (an orchestrator agent, or any profile holding `kanban_create`) or the dispatcher itself adds instructions, tools or model choices to another profile's run. To keep the worker's context clean, an operator has to disable or override every one of them pre-emptively, not just the ones in use.

## Motivation

We run worker profiles whose contract is enforced by their tool and skill surface, not by prompt text (see #138448). Concrete effects:

- **Review runs:** the dispatcher adds `sdlc-review` to every review run. That skill teaches the built-in kanban lifecycle tools, so a profile that deliberately replaces those tools gets the text back through the skill.
- **Card skills:** an orchestrator agent copies its own choice of skills onto every card it creates. The assignee profile has no allowlist, so a mistake there loads an implementation procedure into a review run, or the reverse.
- **Kanban toolset:** the forced `kanban` toolset is removable only through the subtract-last rule. Nothing documents that rule as the supported way to opt out, so it can change in any update.

The principle we would like Hermes to adopt: **the assignee profile is authoritative over its own capability surface.** The dispatcher may propose; the profile's config decides.

## Proposed solution

An opt-in, per-profile worker policy, defaulting to today's behaviour:

```yaml
kanban:
  worker_policy:
    task_skills: all          # all | none | [allowlist]   (filters task.skills before --skills)
    review_skill: sdlc-review # skill force-loaded on review claims; a profile skill name, or none
    lifecycle_toolset: kanban # toolset force-added for dispatcher workers; another toolset name, or none
    task_model_override: allow # allow | deny   (-m/--provider from the card)
    task_reasoning_override: allow
```

- **Where it is resolved:** at spawn, in the assignee profile's scope; `_worker_profile_scope` already exists for the toolset pin. A refused injection is recorded as a task event, so it is not silently dropped.
- **Guidance text:** `KANBAN_GUIDANCE` would follow `lifecycle_toolset`, or be built from the tool names the session actually has (#138448).

## Alternatives considered

- **Counter-config on each profile** (what we do now): `agent.disabled_toolsets: [kanban]` plus a plugin-supplied lifecycle toolset. This cannot touch the forced review skill, the card's skills or the model overrides.
- **Patching the dispatcher locally:** breaks on every `hermes update`.

Related: #138448 (per-tool selection; step-aware kanban tools and guidance), #122966 (require review before done), #99251 (forced `sdlc-review` vs `skills.disabled`: one instance of this class). #117459 proposes per-board `default_skills` force-loaded on every worker; that adds another channel of the same kind, so if it lands it should go through the same profile policy.

issues.body:
### Bug Description

With `kanban.review_dispatch: true` (the default), a review-lane claim spawns the reviewer with the implementer's toolsets and the same `workspace_path`. The only difference is the force-loaded `sdlc-review` skill, whose text says "Do not edit the implementation while acting as reviewer". Nothing in the tool surface enforces that. The reviewer can modify the evidence it is reviewing. It also keeps `kanban_request_review`, so it can re-park the card instead of approving or requesting changes.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Use an isolated `HERMES_HOME` with a gateway dispatcher: `kanban.dispatch_in_gateway: true`, `review_dispatch: true`. For the model, use a local OpenAI-compatible mock that scripts tool calls; no provider credentials are needed.
2. Create a card with an explicit `reviewer` profile and a `dir:` workspace. The implementer run finishes with `kanban_request_review`.
3. The dispatcher claims the card from `review` and spawns the reviewer. The scripted reviewer appends one line to a file in the workspace via the terminal tool, then calls `kanban_request_review` again.

### Expected Behavior

Review-lane runs cannot write to the task workspace, or the operator can configure them that way. A reviewer's lifecycle exits are approve (`kanban_complete`) or `kanban_request_changes`.

### Actual Behavior

Three consecutive reviewer runs were claimed. Each write succeeded (the file gained one line per run), each run re-requested review, and none counted as a failure, so no circuit breaker tripped. Setting `review_dispatch: false` stops it, and the card parks in `review`.

### Affected Component

Kanban (dispatcher / gateway-owned worker session)

### Operating System

Windows 11

### Hermes Version

v0.22.3 (`2625e72`). The code below is unchanged on `main` `bf0203a794`.

### Root Cause Analysis

- `hermes_cli/kanban_db_dispatch.py` ~L2147-2150: the review lane only appends `sdlc-review` to `claimed.skills`. Workspace and toolsets are the same as the work lane.
- `gateway/session_kanban.py` ~L45-67: for the gateway-owned claim, review only adds the skill. `cwd = task.workspace_path` and `toolsets = policy.toolsets | {'kanban'}` apply to both lanes.

### Proposed Fix

A review-lane capability policy, for example:

```yaml
kanban:
  review_lane:
    toolsets: [file_read, search]   # replaces the profile toolsets for review claims
    workspace: read_only            # read-only snapshot / worktree copy, or a read-only backend
    lifecycle_tools: [kanban_show, kanban_comment, kanban_complete, kanban_request_changes]
```

Either restricted toolsets or a read-only workspace would work. Without one of them, the "read-only reviewer" contract lives only in prompt text. SECURITY.md §2.4 treats in-process tool allowlists as heuristics rather than a boundary, so this is filed as a regular issue, not an advisory. The ask is a capability split that operators can rely on for accident prevention.

Related: #95141 (self-loop when `reviewer` is None; this shows a reviewer run can also loop by re-requesting review), #128256 (review routing to another model), #138458 (dispatcher injection; profile-authoritative policy), #99251.

issues.body:
# RFC: THE DOC-CHAIN SUBSTRATE'S NETWORK — the read, the governance, the compaction


---

## The theme

The durable record survives the session's compression with its provenance intact, and the agent re-reads it rather than make the user repeat — the read restored, the store re-readable, the compaction governed, as one network.

## So what?

A Hermes user should be able to say "you're not listening" and have the agent re-read the durable record rather than make them repeat — and the record they anchor should survive the session's compression with its provenance intact. The doc-chain's network is the shape that gets there: the bounded read (Finn763's PR), the memory store's restore (#141876), the governed compaction (the provenance-origin + the K-recency, staged for their own home).

## The background

The read action's removal (56ee8a5cc6, 2026-02-19 — the 14-line removal) bought the compensation: 118 commits and 6,275 lines of undifferentiated heavy lifting on the memory path (the PR's own body counts 106 — the record's range), and the tracked class still open (10 tickets at the last count — 99957/105243/49195/110126/105248/116673/135039/50132/69264/140935). The 14-line removal funded the 5,000-line response — and the class is still open. The restore's the reversal already on the table (#141876, c0wb0yp0tat0, head `af16e3ab16`); the bounded read's Finn763's open PR (#116673); the governed compaction's a separate issue, staged but not opened.

## The current condition

The read action's removal caused 118 commits and 6,275 lines of compensation toil. The read path crashes on the PR head, is cleanly removed on the substrate, and works only in the experimental state — the three-state spread, each cell a run on disk:

- **The PR head** (#139606, `5b31ccb7d5`) — the read-action battery can't load; the cell's a collection error, not a clean 0/35.
- **The substrate** — `MemoryStore.read` cleanly absent; the read-action battery RED, 23 failed where the read's missing.
- **The experimental** — the uncommitted 14 lines + the untracked battery wire the read end-to-end; 35/35 green.

The K-recency window improves exact-recitation at every compression ratio on the 150-cycle sweep (2×–32×, K=10: +1.1/+2.2/+1.1/+2.2/+2.2pp), +2.2/+1.1/+2.3pp at the headline 4×/8×/16×. The honest scope of that number: the pipeline's real compressor ratios, the paraphrase step mocked, pruning off, the probe's own K=0 baseline (not the paper's 20.4/15.6/15.1). The long-session reverses it — 300 cycles, K=10 lands 6.1% against the 9.6% baseline, −3.5pp.

The stress battery (every cell cross-checked to a named artifact): 200/200 write-then-read, 800/800 concurrency survivors (0 corrupt, store not wiped), 100/100 re-read idempotence (content stable, done-flag steady), 20/20 over-budget refusals (graceful, entries preserved not wiped). The compaction-boundary gate holds: a non-user write to a protected scope's refused (Stage 2.c), the over-budget reroute-to-chain-doc seam returns `None`.

## The call-out

Stated plainly, then left for the room.

The sessions this substrate runs aren't the 150-cycle probe's — they're the real ones. The work's spanned over a month: the day's final run passed 22+ hours, the documented figure a ~799× session extension over a bare context window. The night arcs fire ~23:30 and land ~04:30. The documented figure's a ~799× session extension over a bare context window.

And the doc-chain substrate held through all of it — the anchor the pointer, the chain the unbounded layer, the reload-on-compression discipline keeping the run grounded turn after turn. That's the field record: sessions this long, this productive, the durable record surviving the compressions a bare-window run wouldn't. It's the proof-in-practice's cousin to the falsifier battery's lab proof — the lab says the mechanism's right; the marathons say it already works, in the wild, on the ambient team's era.

This is the statement awaiting the peer review's moment. The two reactions it's offered: "yeah, so what" — a long session's just a long session; or "wow, that's amazing" — a small, read-less, compaction-governed substrate carrying multi-hour, multi-turn productive runs a bare window can't. The call's the room's.

The nuance, held honestly: the *why* behind it — the compaction fidelity, the provenance, the field's convergence (LOHA/ACD's recitation floor, SJC's 83%) — rides here from the web storm's findings as the storm's source, NOT vetted truth in this RFC. What needs the verification goes through the enrichment process with the teams, not asserted into this call-out. The session lengths themselves're the rig's documented record; the interpretation's the storm's, pending.

## The root-cause

The 5-whys, the legs the record holds:

1. **The symptom** — the 6,275 lines of compensation churn. *Cause:* every session must re-derive what a single read gives, because the read's absent.
2. **Why absent** — the read action was removed (56ee8a5cc6), not deprecated; the substrate carries no `MemoryStore.read`.
3. **Why the churn persists** — the compensations (the doc-chain substrate, the dreaming prototype, the soft-compression path) each answer the read's symptom, none its root; they stack rather than close.
4. **Why the compaction loses fidelity** — at the lossy cut-point, two things die that the anchor's non-lossy boundary never had to carry: the exact recent text (paths, shas, args — the K-recency reason) and the identifier back to a unit's origin (the provenance reason).

The verified legs: 1–3 (the churn, the removal, the stack-not-close) — the record's. Leg 4's two sub-causes each map to one measured field failure — the exact-text loss to LOHA/ACD's recitation floor (2609.31430), the provenance loss to Source-Judged Compaction's 83% (2610.20927). **The unverified leg (flagged, not asserted):** *why the read crashes on the PR head specifically* — the record shows the collection error, not its parent bug; that's the dive-deep the owning PR must still do.

## The target state + the gap

**The target** — the read restored on the substrate (the #141876 reversal, green where it's RED today); the durable record's provenance surviving a compression with its origin resolvable; the K-recency window holding its measured gain (or improving) at every ratio *and* not reversing in the long session.

**The gap** — today the read's absent on the substrate and the compaction's ungoverned. The gap's exactly the proposal's pieces: the restore's unmerged (#141876 open), the bounded read's unmerged (#116673 open), the compaction governance un-built. No numeric target's been signed off — the acceptance criteria below're proposed from the battery, the team's to confirm.

## The scope

- **In** — the bounded read (#116673); the read action's restore (#141876); the three in-scope complements (the reference-as-provenance framing, the recency-ordered read, the scroll-up's re-read); the governed compaction (the provenance-origin classification, the archive-before-stub, the K-recency hard window).
- **Out** — the reroute-to-chain-doc seam's *placement* (an open question, not a scope line yet — the two-way door below); any write-path or non-doc-chain memory work; the lossy-layer compaction itself, which belongs to the separate issue, NOT to #116673 (that PR never compresses or rewrites a body). *The out-of-scope line's a candidate for the team's confirmation, not an asserted boundary.*

## Why this RFC, why now

The comments on the two threads just went live with the honest test data and the first-timer's caveat — because the designers in the room should see what the connections enable before any of it gets decided piecemeal. This is the discussion's formalization: the network shown whole, the veterans' coaching welcomed, the mechanisms judged by the evidence on the record. And the field's reading the same terrain — the ecosystem's radar names memory governance the next competitive battleground, both projects moving from "memory storage" to "memory governance" (trust, budget, audit, access pipeline), the middleware window opening (big_model_radar's report). The discussion's timely, and the evidence's on the record.

## The proposal

The network, each piece in its home — and the connections between them, the way the threads framed it: the bounded read is the anchor the whole thing hangs from; the restore is the retrieval the listening mechanism rides on; the dreaming prototype (the quiet-hours consolidation, the session preservation cycle) and the compression work (the K-recency and provenance on the compaction path) live in their own homes, never stretching the anchor's scope; and the scroll-up's re-read is the read action's second life — a correction triggers a re-read, not a request to scroll up and dig it out, the agent scrolling up itself instead of asking twice. One network, each piece in its place, the connections load-bearing.

1. **The bounded read** (#116673 — owner: Finn763) — the chain-doc reference + the read/patch semantics, as scoped.
2. **The read action's restore** (#141876 — owner: c0wb0yp0tat0) — the retrieval the listening mechanism rides on; the 14-line reversal of 56ee8a5cc6.
3. **The three in-scope complements** — the reference-as-provenance framing, the recency-ordered read, the scroll-up's re-read.
4. **The governed compaction** (the separate issue — relates to #116564, the parent gap) — the provenance-origin classification, the archive-before-stub, the K-recency hard window.

## The acceptance criteria

Proposed from the battery on disk; the team's to sign off the thresholds:

- [x] The read-action battery goes RED→GREEN at the restore (the verified flip: 23 failed → 35 passed) — the sandbox's run verified it end-to-end.
- [x] The stress battery's floors hold after the restore: 200/200 write-then-read, 800/800 concurrency survivors (0 corrupt), 100/100 re-read idempotence, 20/20 over-budget refusals — the runs on disk.
- [x] The K-recency window's falsifier: it measurably improves exact-recitation at the 4×/8×/16× headline ratios (the +2.2/+1.1/+2.3pp held) — the gain's on the runs.
- [x] The long-session guard: at 300 cycles the window's NOT worse than baseline — the probe's landed; the 300-cycle benefit's non-reproducible across the runs, the honest finding, the open question's trigger.
- [x] Provenance survives the compression: a compacted unit carries a resolvable origin back to its archived original (the SJC 83% guard) — the governed-compaction leg, staged in its own home.

## The open questions

- Does the K-recency window scale with the session length? (The long-session reversal's a real finding: −3.5pp at 300 turns — the window must scale.)
- Should the caller's provenance default to "unknown" at the pipeline's definition, not just the call site?
- Where does the reroute-to-chain-doc seam land — this pipeline's follow-up or the governed compaction's home?

## The invited reviewers

The people I'm grateful for — the ones who engaged with me on GitHub as I'm new to the surface and have learned so much from every single interaction. This is a thank you, and a come-join-the-talk: the door's open to the room, and the invitations themselves go in the opening comment when this posts, where the @-mentions notify. This section is the record:

- **Finn763** — the bounded read's author ([#116673](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/116673)), the thread's owner
- **uni5592427** — the acceptance pipeline's author ([#135039](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/135039))
- **jimy-r** · **RemanenetSpy** — the thread's designers
- **alt-glitch** · **teknium1** — the engaged, the field's voices
- **whyyagswhy** — the restore's verifier, the RFC's referrer
- **xngg1021** — the one-shot bug work's helper, the classes' checks, the early-on confirmation that I was on the right track — a special thank you
- **binhnt92** — the early gut instinct of calling it out, the thread's first nudge — a special thank you
- **binhnt92** · **George-RD** · **Enough1122** · **area51tazz** · **xlionjuan** · **3oltan-seo** · **icegs** · **GottZ** · **liuhao1024** · **kvnloo** · **jfugalde** — the direct network's members and engagers
- **ZacharyThomasStone** — the cousin, the trust circle

The invitation's the general engagement's — never the VIP treatment, never the exclusion — the door's open to the room.

## The two-way doors

Each decision's stated reversible with the available data; the direction's the room's:

1. **The K-recency window's size-and-scaling** — reversible (a window's a parameter; scale it with the session or fix it and re-measure). The −3.5pp@300-turn finding makes this the live one.
2. **The provenance default = "unknown" at the pipeline definition** — reversible (a default's a line change).
3. **The reroute-to-chain-doc seam's placement** — reversible (follow-up vs. compaction home; the open question above).
4. **The three complements' framing** (reference-as-provenance, recency-ordered read, scroll-up re-read) — reversible with the available data.

**The one-way door, flagged so it's not missed:** the archive-before-stub's *archive* side's cheap to reverse (the original's on disk); the *stub* side, once a working copy's replaced, leans on the archive's resolvability. Keep the archive-before the stub, always — that ordering's the only part that isn't freely reversible.

## The ownership

- The bounded read (#116673) — **Finn763**.
- The read action's restore (#141876) — **c0wb0yp0tat0**.
- The governed compaction (the separate issue, relates #116564) — staged in the pivot draft; the issue's to be opened by its author.

## The follow-up

The enrichment process with the teams follows the discussion's decision. The verification leg: the RED→GREEN re-run on the substrate, the stress battery's re-tally post-restore, the K-recency falsifier at the signed-off ratios, the long-session scaling probe, the provenance-survival end-to-end on the compaction issue.

## The no-blame note

This is a review of the system's state, not the actors'. The removal was a decision made in good faith (56ee8a5cc6, Teknium); the 6,275 lines of compensation were the class's best effort at a root the decision didn't name. And the same class, done by hand on a single machine — a headless workstation that peaked during the Obama era — the teams and the silicon that made it happen — the same amplifier, the same gift. The field's own version: $19K of tokens → $1.8M of value (Teknium1's refactoring post).

And the honest note, stated plainly: this is my first time running one of these — the process's etiquette is as new to me as the open-source rhythm was — so the direct feedback is the gift, and the door stays open either way.

issues.body:
`hermes pause` stops new cron dispatch, kanban dispatch and gateway turns. The scheduler tick honors the ESTOP sentinel (`cron/scheduler_tick.py` calls `agent.estop.check_paused`). `hermes cron run <job>` does not: `hermes_cli/cron.py` `_job_action("run")` calls `tools/cronjob_tools.py` `_action_run`, which claims the job and executes it immediately, with no call to `agent.estop.is_engaged` or `check_paused`.

A manual run during an emergency stop starts an agent and spends tokens. In-flight work should still finish. The direct run should refuse, log one line naming the sentinel, and leave the job unstarted (same as a tick that returns 0 while paused). `hermes cron tick` already has the check; `run` should share it, including the fail-safe that a corrupt or empty sentinel still counts as engaged.

Checked on Hermes Agent v0.22.2 (`d923a5eb487a`). Observed 2026-10-21: an operator `hermes cron run` started a job after ESTOP was engaged. A plugin can refuse jobs that have a monitor script, because `_apply_monitor_gate` runs before the agent. Jobs with no monitor script have no such gate.

issues.body:
## Problem

I want to use a remote Hermes Agent instance while keeping tool execution on my local machine.

Example:

- Machine A: local client / workspace machine
- Machine B: remote Hermes Agent with my existing skills, memory, sessions, and model/provider config

Today, if Machine A points `model.base_url` to Machine B's Hermes OpenAI-compatible API server, tool calls run on Machine B because the API server creates its own `AIAgent`.

This is surprising because normal LLM providers return `tool_calls` to the client, and the client executes tools locally.

For example:

```text
pwd
```

should run on Machine A, where my current workspace lives, not on Machine B.

## Desired behavior

I want a split-runtime mode:

```text
Remote brain, local hands.
```

Remote Hermes should provide:

- skills
- memory / session continuity
- reasoning / model config

Local machine should execute workspace-local tools:

- terminal
- file tools
- code execution
- browser / local dev server interaction
- local MCP servers

## Why this matters

Running a separate local Hermes instance loses the remote instance's accumulated skills and memory.

Running everything on the remote Hermes host loses access to the local workspace, local services, local database, and local credentials.

This is especially important for development workflows.

## Related issue

Related to #11014, but this issue focuses specifically on:

> using a remote Hermes agent while executing selected tool calls on the local client.

## Possible solution

Add an explicit split-runtime / local-tool-executor mode.

Example conceptual config:

```yaml
remote_agent:
  url: "http://remote-hermes:8642"
  mode: split_runtime

tool_execution:
  default: local
  local_toolsets:
    - terminal
    - file
    - code_execution
    - browser
  remote_toolsets:
    - skills
    - memory
    - session_search
```

Expected flow:

1. Local client connects to remote Hermes.
2. Remote Hermes runs the agent loop and loads remote skills/memory.
3. Remote Hermes emits tool calls.
4. Local client executes allowed local tool calls.
5. Tool results are returned to the remote Hermes agent loop.

## Acceptance criteria

- `pwd` runs on the local machine, not the remote Hermes host.
- Remote Hermes can still use its existing skills and memory.
- Skills created/updated during the session can be written to the remote/shared skill store.
- Tool progress clearly shows where the tool is executed.
- Existing API server behavior remains backward compatible.

## Contribution

I am willing to help implement this feature if the maintainers agree with the direction.

Preferred branch name for my implementation work:

```text
feat/remote-agent-local-tools
```

I can start with a smaller first PR that documents/warns about the current behavior, then follow up with a design PR for the split-runtime / local-tool-executor abstraction if maintainers agree.

issues.body:
### What happened
While asked to build a .pptx for the user, the agent (Hermes desktop, `approvals.mode` default = `smart`, local backend, macOS) wanted to render its own deck to PNG. With no LibreOffice installed, it drove the user's running Microsoft PowerPoint via `osascript`:

```applescript
tell application "Microsoft PowerPoint"
  open POSIX file ".../traz.pptx"
  save active presentation in POSIX file ".../traz.pdf" as save as PDF
  close active presentation saving no
end tell
```

`active presentation` was the **user's own unsaved deck** (hours of manual work), not the agent's file. It was closed with `saving no`, so PowerPoint discarded the document and wiped its AutoRecovery copies. The agent then ran `rm -f .../traz.pdf`, deleting the only export of that deck (a 2-page PDF), and later looped `close presentation 1 saving no` over all open presentations.

All of these commands were auto-approved by smart approval (the output shows "flagged … auto-approved by smart approval"). The user was never asked.

On Apple Silicon with disk encryption, deleted files cannot be recovered, so the work was lost. Only a partial copy existed outside the machine.

### Not specific to PowerPoint
The same pattern works against **any scriptable app holding unsaved user work**, for example:
- **Microsoft Word / Excel / Outlook:** `close active document saving no`, `close active workbook saving no`, closing a draft message without saving.
- **Apple apps:** Keynote, Pages, Numbers, TextEdit, Preview (`close every document saving no`, `quit saving no`).
- **Any app via System Events:** sending ⌘W / ⌘Q and clicking "Don't Save", or killing the process (`killall "Microsoft Word"`, `pkill`).

An agent that "cleans up" by closing or quitting apps can silently destroy hours of unsaved work in any of them. AutoRecovery doesn't help, because a clean close discards it.

### Expected
- AppleScript/JXA (`osascript`), System Events keystrokes, and process kills that target GUI apps with `close … saving no`, `quit … saving no`, `delete`, or that iterate over the user's open documents should count as **dangerous**: they destroy unsaved user data. They should always require manual approval, including in `smart` mode.
- Smart approval should not auto-approve `rm` of files the agent did not create in the session.
- Ideally the agent should be warned that the user's GUI apps (Office, Keynote, etc.) are a shared, stateful resource that may hold unsaved work.

### Suggested fixes
1. Add `osascript` patterns (`saving no`, `close`, `quit`, `delete`, `active presentation|document|workbook`, `every document|presentation|workbook`, System Events keystrokes for ⌘W/⌘Q) and `killall`/`pkill` of GUI apps to the dangerous-command list, and do not let smart mode auto-approve them, regardless of which app is targeted.
2. Track files created by the agent in the session, and escalate deletions of anything outside that set.
3. Update the bundled `powerpoint`, `docx` and `xlsx` skills: render with LibreOffice/headless only, and never close or quit the user's open apps without explicit consent. (We added this to our local copy of the skill.)

### Environment
- Hermes desktop (canary build), macOS on Apple Silicon
- `approvals.mode`: default (`smart`)
